context: This paper details their submission to the 2019 7th year BioASQ competition for the Task-7b, Phase B Exact Answering Task, which includes Factoid, Yes/No, and List Type Question Answering. Their system is based on a contextual word embedding model using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) approach, fine-tuned for biomedical question answering using BioBERT, and achieved the highest MRR score for Factoid Question Answering in the third test batch set and the highest recall score for List Type Question Answering in the fourth test batch set.

This section introduces the BioASQ 7B (Phase B) semantic question answering task, in which systems must generate exact and ideal answers to biomedical questions, and describes the authors' BioBERT-based system, which they fine-tuned for the task. It reports that the system scored near the top for factoid questions across all batches—achieving the highest MRR for factoid question answering in the third test batch and the highest recall for list-type questions in the fourth test batch—and placed 4th for list-type and 3rd for factoid-type questions in the final test batch.

This section reviews prior BioASQ systems: Sharma et al. (BIBREF3) use a two-stage process that extracts relevant entities and ranks them with a supervised classifier; Wiese et al. (BIBREF4) propose a Fast QA-based neural network that predicts the answer span in a passage, trained on SQuAD and fine-tuned on BioASQ; and Dimitriadis et al. (BIBREF5) use a two-stage process with Metamap and BeCas to identify candidate sentences, represented as features and ranked by a binary classifier trained on candidate sentences, snippets, and correct answers from BioASQ, achieving a highest MRR of 0.4325 in the 6th edition. In contrast, the authors' own system is a neural network model based on contextual word embeddings (BIBREF1) that achieved an MRR of 0.6103 on one test batch for the Factoid Question Answering task

This section explains that BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a contextual word embedding model that returns contextual embeddings for words given a sentence, and can be fine-tuned for 11 different tasks including question answering. For question answering, the question and paragraph (context) are given as input, separated by a [Sep] separator, and fine-tuning involves adding a softmax layer that takes contextual word embeddings as input and learns to identify the answer span present in the paragraph. BERT was originally trained using masked words and next-sentence-prediction so that its weights are learned such that context is used in building word representations.

path: Comparison of Word Embeddings and Contextual Word Embeddings
context: This section explains that a word embedding is a learned vector representation where words with the same meaning have similar vector representations, and that word embeddings generated from models like word2vec are context independent, being returned regardless of where the words appear in a sentence or the sentiment of the sentence, whereas contextual word embedding models like BERT take the context of the word into consideration.

This section compares BERT and BioBERT, noting that both use the same architecture but BioBERT is pretrained on Wikipedia, PMC, and PubMed articles, making it better suited for biomedical text; it reports that BERT-Large fine-tuned on SQuAD 1.1 achieves an F1 score of 90.9 versus 88.5 for BERT-Base, and highlights that BioBERT's word-piece vocabulary lacks biomedical jargon, with future work aiming to train a BERT model from scratch on biomedical corpora to include such jargon.

The section describes the fine-tuning of BioBERT for the Factoid Question Answering task, where word tokenized embeddings of the question and context paragraph are fed into the model with '[CLS]' and '[SEP]' tokens appended, and a softmax layer predicts answer span indices in the paragraph. On test data, the model generates n-best predictions (n configurable) in decreasing order of confidence, and any reference to the 'answer returned by the model' refers to the top-ranked answer.

This section describes the setup for the factoid question answering task, where the training data is an aggregate of all BioASQ training datasets up to the 5th version, cleaned to 530 question-answer pairs and split 94:6 into 495 training and 35 testing examples. The data is converted to BERT/BioBERT format by computing the answer's 'start_index' (the index of the answer text in the context paragraph) using Python's built-in find() function, which returns -1 if the answer is not found, and the authors note that efficiently identifying the correct start_index when multiple instances of the answer text appear requires matching the instance to the question's context—a goal they could not achieve with readily available tools and leave for future work.

This section describes the training and error analysis of the BioBERT model on the BioASQ dataset for the factoid question answering task, reporting that reducing epochs from 50 to 12 improved test accuracy from 4% to 23.3%, that removing 70% of start_index:0 instances to balance the data yielded 26% test accuracy (with 32% strict accuracy on BioASQ test batch-2, placing 2nd), that tuning batch size from 400 to 32 produced more concise answers, and that fine-tuning with the SQuAD dataset (learning rate 3e-3, 3 epochs) boosted test accuracy to 44% (47% when trained on SQuAD alone).

path: Our Systems and Their Performance on Factoid Questions
context: This section describes the various UNCC systems and their variations tested on BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B factoid questions, which changed between batches according to three aspects: training on BioASQ data versus SQuAD, using BioASQ snippets versus documents from provided URLs as context, and adding or not adding the LAT (lexical answer type) feature, with entailment methods used only for Yes/No questions. The authors found that both BioBERT and entailment-based techniques provided value for biomedical question answering but had clear limitations, and that feature engineering produced mixed results with some errors corrected and new errors introduced without overall improvement.

path: Our Systems and Their Performance on Factoid Questions
LAT Feature considered and its impact (slightly negative)
context: The section explains that during error analysis, the model sometimes returned answers far from what was asked (e.g., returning the enzyme 'alanine aminotransferase' instead of the organ 'Liver' for the question "Hy's law measures failure of which organ?"), prompting the incorporation of Lexical Answer Type (LAT) and Focus Word concepts (as used in IBM Watson) to constrain answers to the expected entity type. Using the Stanford CoreNLP library (with POS tagging and dependency parsing) to extract LATs from questions, they integrated LAT into their UNCC_QA1 system in Batch 4, which underperformed their FACTOIDS system by about 3% in MRR but corrected such entity-type errors.

LAT Feature considered and its impact (slightly negative)
Assumptions and rules for deriving lexical answer type.
context: This section describes the LAT (lexical answer type) derivation rules based on question words and parts-of-speech tags (WDT, WRB, WP), using proximity-based window sizes (3 or 5) to identify Noun-Subject words as LATs, achieving 75% accuracy, and reports that the system using LATs was slightly inferior to the one without LATs, with errors typically involving selecting the wrong element of the correct type.

path: Our Systems and Their Performance on Factoid Questions
Impact of Training using BioAsq data (slightly negative)
context: Training on BioASQ data led to overfitting, yielding an abysmal 18% MRR in Batch 1 (QA1) and a slightly better 40% MRR in Batch 2 (QA1), which was the second-best result but 16% lower than the highest score. In Batch 3, the UNCC_QA3 system, fine-tuned on BioASQ and SQuAD 2.0 with context generated from relevant snippets, underperformed by about 2% in MRR compared to UNCC_QA1, which was trained on SQuAD but not BioASQ and won the category; the authors suspect the simplistic find() function could be improved.

path: Our Systems and Their Performance on Factoid Questions
Impact of Using Context from URLs (negative)
context: This section states that using full documents (with URL pointers provided in BioASQ) as context underperformed compared to using only the provided snippets, with UNCC_QA3 underperforming UNCC_QA1 by about 6% in MRR in Batch 5 and by 9% relative to the top performer.

path: Performance on Yes/No and List questions
context: This section states that although the work focused on Factoid questions, the authors also conducted experiments on List-type and Yes/No questions.

path: Performance on Yes/No and List questions
context: The section describes a simple entailment-based strategy for answering Yes/No questions: given a question, it iterates through candidate sentences to detect any contradiction with confidence over 50%, returning 'No' if found and 'Yes' otherwise. Using the AllenNlp entailment library, this approach outperformed the BioASQ baseline and improved performance by about 13% in macro F1 score compared to their other systems.

path: Performance on Yes/No and List questions
For List-type the URLs have negative impact
context: For List-type questions, the FACTOIDS system generated n-best answer predictions, then applied post-processing heuristics—tokenizing answers using separators ('comma', 'and', 'also', 'as well as'), eliminating tokens exceeding 100 characters (which BioASQ does not count as valid answers, as lengthy snippets reduce mean precision), and removing duplicates—to produce the final answer pool. In BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B, this approach yielded a highest recall of 0.7033 but low precision of 0.1119, illustrating the trade-off between the two measures.

This section summarizes the results of the UNCC system on BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B, showing mixed performance where the simple architectures and algorithm worked very well only in Batch 3, while observing both the value of contextual embeddings and feature engineering (LAT) but failing to combine them properly.

This section describes three systems—'UNCC_QA1', 'QA1', and 'UNCC_QA3'—used in the Batch 5 experiments for factoid questions in BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B. 'UNCC_QA1' was finetuned on SQuAD 2.0 with context generated from relevant snippets in the test data, 'QA1' added a 'LAT' feature and was also finetuned on SQuAD 2.0 using the same preprocessing, and 'UNCC_QA3' used the same fine-tuning as 'UNCC_QA1' but generated context from relevant documents whose URLs were included in the test data.
For List-type questions in BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B, the team's post processing helped in later batches but they never achieved competitive precision, although their recall was good.

This section states that using entailment can have a measurable impact on performance (at least with respect to a weak baseline), with the weak results presented in Table 3 for the Yes/No questions task.

This section states that the UNCC team shifted from extractive summarization (used in 2018's BioASQ Task-7B submission) to a BioBERT-based factoid question answering approach, addressing BioBERT's limitations through feature engineering with mixed results, and securing a best and a second best score across different test batches; they also performed reasonably well on Yes/No and List-type questions with a simple approach, found that adding the AllenNLP entailment system improved Yes/No performance (demonstrating that reasoning influences results), and made all data and software available on GitHub.

This section outlines future experiments, including developing a dense question answering neural network with a softmax layer that uses contextual word embeddings from BioBERT's last layer, tuning its hyperparameters (architecture shown in Fig. FIGREF30), and adding a 'LAT' contextual word embedding feature to assess whether it improves answer prediction accuracy without degrading BioBERT's embedding quality. It also mentions exploring domain-specific inference using the MedNLI dataset, clinical BERT embeddings, domain knowledge incorporation, and deeper discourse representations.
This appendix provides additional details about the implementations used in the UNCC Biomedical Semantic Question Answering Systems for the BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B.

This section explains that the authors used several variants of their systems when experimenting with the BioASQ problems, and that they apologize for system names that do not reflect the modifications made, which is why they provide this list to clarify the naming conventions.

This section states that the team preprocessed the BioASQ Task-7B test data into BioBERT format by generating context paragraphs, either by aggregating relevant snippets or by aggregating documents corresponding to the URLs provided in the BioASQ test data.

This section describes three QA1 systems: one that generated Context/paragraphs by aggregating relevant snippets from the test data and mapped them against the question text and question id (ignoring document content, with URLs provided in the original test data), fine-tuned on BioASQ data; a second that performed data preprocessing identically to test batch-1 and was fine-tuned on BioASQ data; and a third that added a 'LAT'/Focus word feature and was fine-tuned with SQuAD 2.0, generating Context/paragraph from relevant snippets provided in the test data.

This section describes the UNCC_QA_1 system, which is fine-tuned on the SQuAD 2.0 dataset, with a 'LAT'/'Focus word' feature added and fine-tuned on SQuAD 2.0, and for data preprocessing, the Context/paragraph is generated from relevant snippets provided in the test data.

This section describes the UNCC_QA3 system, which is finetuned on the SQuAD 2.0 and BioASQ datasets, with context/paragraph generated from relevant snippets (or relevant documents with URLs) provided in the test data. Its fine-tuning process is the same as that used for the UNCC_QA_1 system in test batch-5, with the only difference being in data preprocessing.

This section describes the UNCC_QA2 system, which uses the same fine-tuning process as UNCC_QA_1 but generates the context/paragraph from relevant documents whose URLs are included in the test data, and notes that UNCC_QA_1 achieved the highest MRR score in the 3rd test batch set.
This section states that the system is finetuned on the SQuAD 2.0 dataset, and that during data preprocessing, the context/paragraph is generated from the relevant snippets provided in the test data.

This section describes the UNCC team's approach to BioASQ Task-7B List type questions, using a fine-tuned model (QA1) that predicts top answers sent for post-processing, with context generated either by aggregating relevant snippets or by aggregating documents (URLs) from the BioASQ test data. The team achieved an F-Measure score of 0.0786 in test batch-2 using QA1 fine-tuned on BioASQ data, then improved to 0.2862 in the final test batch by fine-tuning on the SQuAD dataset and implementing post-processing techniques, with systems QA1, UNCC_QA_1, UNCC_QA3, and UNCC_QA2 returning top 20 answers in batch-3 and top 5 answers in batches 4 and 5.

For the first three BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B test batches, the system submitted 'Yes' to all Yes/No questions, then applied 'Sentence Entailment' techniques (referenced in section 6.0) to the fourth and fifth test batches, with the systems 'UNCC_QA_1' (test batch-4) and 'UNCC_QA3' (test batch-5) using this approach for Yes/No question answering.

path: Additional details for Yes/No Type Questions
context: This section describes the use of Textual Entailment in Batch 4 and 5 for 'Yes'/'No' question type, where the algorithm iterates through candidate sentences looking for any contradicting the question, returning 'No' if a contradiction is found (with a contradiction confidence threshold of 50%) and 'Yes' otherwise, using the AllenNLP entailment library to determine entailment between candidate sentences and the question.

path: Assumptions, rules and logic flow for deriving Lexical Answer Types from questions
context: This section describes the assumptions and rules used to derive Lexical Answer Types (LATs) from questions, distinguishing question types based on question words ('Which', 'What', 'When', 'How', etc.) and identifying them via parts of speech (POS) tags 'WDT', 'WRB', 'WP'. It states that the LAT or focus word is assumed to be a Noun following the question word and functioning as a Subject (identified by StanfordNLP dependency parsing tags 'nsubj' or 'nsubjpass'), with proximity to the question word used to resolve multiple subject nouns, and that for questions with 'When', 'Who', or 'Why', the question word itself serves as the LAT.

path: Assumptions, rules and logic flow for deriving Lexical Answer Types from questions
context: This section describes the rules for deriving Lexical Answer Types (LATs) from questions beginning with 'How', stating that the adjective following the question word is treated as the LAT (not necessarily immediately), that 'How' itself becomes the LAT when no adjective is present, and that when multiple adjectives appear, the one in close proximity following the question word is returned, with adjectives identified using the part of speech tag 'JJ'.

path: Assumptions, rules and logic flow for deriving Lexical Answer Types from questions
context: This section describes the rule for deriving Lexical Answer Types (LATs) from questions containing question words like 'Which' and 'What' where a Noun immediately follows the question word. It states that when the word immediately following the question word is a noun, the window size is set to '3', meaning the algorithm iterates through the next 3 words to check if any word is both a 'Noun' and 'Subject'; if so, that word is considered the LAT/Focus Word, otherwise the word immediately following the question word is considered the LAT.

path: Assumptions, rules and logic flow for deriving Lexical Answer Types from questions
context: This section describes the rules for deriving Lexical Answer Types (LATs) from questions containing question words like 'Which' or 'What' where the immediately following word is not a Noun: when the next word is not a Noun, a window size of 5 is used to iterate through the next 5 words searching for a word that is both a Noun and Subject (considered the LAT), otherwise the closest Noun following the question word is returned as the LAT. The paper states that the accuracy for LAT derivation is 75 percent, and notes that this simple logic can be improved as shown in BIBREF9 and BIBREF10, though whether such improvements produce gains in this particular task remains an open question.

This section proposes three future experiments: (1) building a dense question answering neural network that feeds contextual word embeddings from the last layer of BioBERT to predict answer spans (Fig. FIGREF30), (2) feeding only the contextual word embeddings of the Focus word/'LAT' and the paragraph/Context (neglecting the rest of the question text) to help the model identify the question's focus and map answers against it, validated by checking whether the cosine distance between the Focus word's contextual embedding and the actual answer's embedding is comparatively low, and (3) adding a better version of the 'LAT' contextual word embedding as an additional feature alongside the question text and Context embeddings to assess whether it improves answer prediction accuracy without degrading BioBERT's contextual embeddings.

This section presents figures and tables describing the UNCC BioBERT-based systems for BioASQ Task-7B Phase-B, including methods for finding lexical answer types (LATs) using POS tags and dependency parsing, BioBERT fine-tuned for question answering, and a proposed extension adding a network trained on question and paragraph embeddings with LAT and other semantic features. It reports findings that adding contextual LAT embeddings produced mixed results with no overall improvement, and notes that in Batch 3 the highest score was obtained while the relative distance between their best system and the top performing system shrunk between Batch 4 and 5.

This paper presents a feature-rich biLSTM model that uses a variety of linguistic and surface-level features to recover both core-word diacritics (CW) and case endings (CE) in Arabic text. The model surpasses all previous state-of-the-art systems, achieving a CW error rate (CWER) of 2.86% and a CE error rate (CEER) of 3.7% for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), and a CWER of 2.2% and CEER of 2.5% for Classical Arabic (CA), with resultant word error rates of 6.0% and 4.3% for MSA and CA respectively, highlighting the effectiveness of feature engineering for deep neural models.

This section introduces the problem of Arabic diacritic recovery, distinguishing between core-word (CW) diacritics and case-endings (CEs), and motivates its importance for disambiguation in applications like text-to-speech and educational tools. It presents two biLSTM-based DNN architectures—a character-level model for CW diacritics (informed by word segmentation and a unigram language model, achieving word error rates of 2.9% for MSA and 2.2% for CA) and a word-level model for CE recovery using a rich set of surface, morphological, and syntactic features (achieving CEERs of 3.7% for MSA and 2.5% for CA)—with MSA results outperforming state-of-the-art systems (Farasa at 10.7% and RDI at 14.4%) by more than 60%.

This Background section reviews prior work on diacritic restoration across languages, covering rule-based, HMM, CRF, morphological-analyzer-based systems (e.g., MADAMIRA, Farasa, ATKS), and neural architectures like the biLSTM used by BIBREF17, and reports their performance using word error rate (WER) and diacritic error rate (DER) on datasets such as the Quran (CA), FBIS, LDC CallHome ECA, LDC's Arabic Treebank (ATB), and An-Nahar Newspaper. It notes findings that Semitic diacritic recovery extends to most letters, that restoring context-dependent (CE) diacritics is more challenging than context-independent (CW) ones, that combining multiple features improves CE restoration, and that a large unigram LM is competitive for CW diacritic recovery, motivating the paper's introduction of feature-rich DNN models that reduce diacritization error rates by more than half compared

This section describes the training and test corpora used for the diacritizer: for MSA, a 9.7M-token diacritized corpus (about 194K unique surface forms, mixing MSA and CA across genres like politics and sports) used to train the RDI and Farasa diacritizers, and the WikiNews test set (70 MSA WikiNews articles, 18,300 tokens) covering politics, economics, health, science and technology, sports, and arts and culture; for CA, a 2.7M-token collection of fully diacritized classical texts from a book publisher, with 5,000 sentences (about 400k words) held out for testing and the rest used to train the CA models.

This section describes four feature types used in the core word diacritization model: CHAR (the characters), SEG (character position within word segments, using Farasa segmentation with 99% accuracy on the WikiNews dataset and B/M/E/S markers), PRIOR (diacritics observed per segment in the training set, encoded as binary vectors over the eight primitive diacritic marks a, i, u, o, K, N, F, and $\sim$, defaulting to 11111111 for unobserved segments), and CASE (a binary feature distinguishing core word diacritics from case endings).

This section describes a character-based biLSTM model for word diacritization, where each character is represented by a list of $m$ features, each with a randomly initialized embedding of size 50, concatenated into an $m\times 50$ vector fed into a biLSTM layer of length 100, followed by a dense layer of size 100. The model was trained with early stopping (patience of 5 epochs), a learning rate of 0.001, a batch size of 256, and an Adamax optimizer, using character sequences with word boundary markers and a maximum sentence length of 1,250 characters.

This section describes the features used for case ending (CE) recovery, including segmentation, POS tagging, and stem-templates obtained via Farasa (which has 96% POS accuracy on the WikiNews dataset), and explains that while Farasa's SVM-ranking approach requires explicit feature combinations, the DNN model's flexibility allowed inclusion of additional surface-level features (affixes, leading/trailing characters, gazetteer presence) that significantly lowered the case ending error rate (CEER).

The section describes a DNN architecture for case ending diacritization in which each input word is represented by a list of $n$ features, each with a randomly initialized embedding of size 100, concatenated into an $n\times 100$ vector per word. These vectors are fed into a 100-dimensional biLSTM layer with 75% dropout (chosen as the best among lower-rate side experiments), followed by a 100-dimensional dense layer with 15% dropout and softmax activation; side experiments adding more biLSTM layers or replacing softmax with a conditional random field layer showed no improvement, so the simpler model was adopted. Optimal parameters (e.g., dropout rate) were selected using a validation set, training with the "Adamax" optimizer, categorical cross entropy loss, a learning rate of 0.001, and early stopping with a patience of up to 5 epochs without improvement.

This section describes the experimental setup for the Core Word experiments, in which the authors used the Keras toolkit with a TensorFlow backend, reserved 5% of the training data for validation, and included the CASE feature (indicating whether a letter accepts a normal diacritic or case ending). They compared four feature setups—CHAR (characters only, the baseline), CHAR+SEG (characters plus segmentation information), CHAR+PRIOR (characters plus observed diacritized forms from the training set), and All (all features)—and optionally applied post correction using a unigram language model, reporting WER (word-level) and DER (character-level) error rates under relaxed scoring.

This section describes testing the MSA diacritizer and CA diacritizer on the WikiNews dataset and a held-out 5,000 sentences, respectively, reporting WER and DER results using different features with and without post correction, as shown in Table TABREF27.

For Modern Standard Arabic, combining all features (CHAR+PRIOR) achieved the best results, with post correction further improving performance, and the system beat the state-of-the-art against five other systems (Farasa, MADAMIRA, RDI, MIT, and Microsoft ATKS). Error analysis of 527 errors found that the most prominent error type (40.8%) was selecting a valid diacritized form that did not match the context, followed by transliterated foreign words (23.5%), Arabic named entities (10.6%), completely incorrect forms (10.8%), and cases where both forms were correct but differed (9.1%).

For Classical Arabic (CA) core word diacritization, CHAR+SEG and CHAR+PRIOR outperformed using characters alone, with CHAR+PRIOR better than CHAR+SEG, and combining all features yielding the best results; post correction had a larger positive impact than in MSA, achieving a best word error rate (WER) of 2.2% with post corrections, versus 8.5% WER from the best MSA system applied to the CA test set. Analysis of 500 errors (5.2% of errors) found the two most common error types were completely correct diacritized forms (38.8%) and correct forms not matching the context (31.4%), with additional errors from suffix/pronoun diacritics depending on case ending (13.2%), named entities (8.8%), and partial diacritization of the reference (4.4%).

This section describes the experimental setup for testing case ending recovery, outlining six feature configurations (word, word-surface, word-POS, word-morph, word-surface-POS-morph, and all-misc) that progressively incorporate surface forms, POS information, morphological templates, and character n-grams, and specifying that MSA was evaluated on the WikiNews dataset against Farasa, MADAMIRA, RDI, MIT, and Microsoft ATKS, while CA was evaluated on 5,000 held-out sentences compared against the best MSA system.

This section presents the results of the authors' feature-rich biLSTM model compared to other systems for Arabic case ending (i'rab) diacritic recovery, as listed in Table TABREF45, and includes an analysis of the errors made by their approach.

This section reports the MSA results, showing that the baseline DNN system outperforms all state-of-the-art systems and that adding features progressively improved performance, with surface-level features yielding the most gain, followed by POS tags and stem templates, and further gains from adding head and tail characters plus a list of sukun words and named entities, resulting in a proposed feature-rich system with a CEER approximately 61% lower than state-of-the-art systems. It describes the CE distribution and prediction accuracy (Figure FIGREF49), noting CEER of ~1% for the four basic markers kasra, fatHa, damma and sukun (appearing 27%, 14%, 9% and 10% respectively) and negligible errors for other CE markers, and Table TABREF30 breaks down all errors (1% of total) with common reasons and examples, such as guessing fatHa instead of damma (19.3%) due to POS

This section reports that POS tagging features produced the greatest improvements, followed by surface features, with all features combined achieving a WER of 2.5% and a CEER of 8.9% when the best MSA system was applied to Classical Arabic. It finds that the four basic case markers (fatHa, kasra, damma, and sukun) each had a CEER of approximately 0.5%, that detecting the virtual case mark was easy, and that all other case markers had negligible errors, while error analysis (Table TABREF31) shows that many errors are syntactic and morphological in nature and could be addressed with better POS tagging, indeclinability identification, and parsing.

This section reports full word diacritization (CW+CE) results comparing the authors' best biLSTM setup against other systems in the literature. For MSA, their system achieves a 6.0% WER versus the state of the art's 12.2%, and for CA it produces a 4.3% error rate, which is significantly better than using their best MSA system to diacritize CA.

This conclusion states that the feature-rich biLSTM model achieved a word level error of 6.0% for MSA CW and CE recovery (more than 50% lower than the state-of-the-art 12.2%) and a word error rate of 4.3% for CA, using surface, morphological, and syntactic features. The paper notes that semantic errors like incorrect attachment are difficult to fix but may benefit from dependency parsing, that feature categories may carry over to other languages while language-specific feature engineering is needed, and that consistent diacritization conventions are important for training and testing. Future work includes augmenting the CW model with POS tagging and a bigram language model, creating a multi-reference diacritization test set for words with multiple valid forms, examining features for Arabic parsing, and exploring character-level CNNs, pre-trained embeddings, attention mechanisms, and joint modeling for core word and case ending diacritics.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables, including the DNN model architectures for core word diacritics (Fig. 1) and case ending prediction (Fig. 2), along with feature descriptions (Table 1). It reports core word diacritization results (Table 2), error analyses for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Classical Arabic (CA) including case error accounting (Tables 4-6), case endings distribution and prediction accuracy (Figs. 3-4), and comparisons to state-of-the-art systems for core word diacritics (Table 7), MSA results (Table 8), and full diacritization (Table 9).

This paper defines "car-speak" as abstract language pertaining to a car's physical attributes, curates a reasonable dataset of car-speak language, and trains several classifiers to classify car-speak.

This introduction states that car buying in the US largely happens at dealerships, where the dealer acts as a "translator or classifier" that takes a natural language input (e.g., "I need a fast, family friendly, reliable car under $20k") and returns a list of car suggestions. It notes that nearly 50% of customers buy based on the sales representative's advice rather than their own research, and it outlines the paper's contributions: defining "car-speak," identifying appropriate training data for a Natural Language model, and developing a model that can classify car-speak and return a car.

This Related Work section reviews prior research on car sales and dealer interactions, citing Deloitte's report on the car-buying process and its distinct buyer phases (BIBREF0), Verhoef et al.'s findings on the importance of dealers in customer retention and purchase decisions (BIBREF3), Jeff Kershner's statistics on dealership sales focusing on small social interactions between dealer and buyer (BIBREF1, BIBREF4), and Barley's observations that users increasingly prefer technology/robots over dealers due to distrust of sales representatives (BIBREF2).

This section defines "car-speak" as abstract language referring to a car's physical attributes (e.g., "fast" could mean high horsepower or a sleek form factor), and explains that it appears throughout the car-buying process—from the Research Phase where buyers identify needs, to dealership communication, and finally the sales representative's internal classifier that translates car-speak into concrete attributes. It emphasizes that understanding car-speak is non-trivial, requiring mining people's ideas about cars to determine which vehicles qualify as "fast."

This section describes how the authors curate a car-speak dataset by scraping full-length car reviews from U.S. News & World Report's website (https://cars.usnews.com/cars-trucks) using web-scraping tools like beautiful-soup, gathering reviews for car models made between 2000 and 2018 to ensure relevance, justified by the finding that the average vehicle on U.S. roads is 11.6 years old (average manufacturing year 2006-2007).

The dataset contains 3,209 reviews about 553 different cars from 49 different car manufacturers. To translate and classify car-speak, the authors need to filter the dataset to keep only the most relevant terms, weight each word in each review to determine the most relevant ideas for classification, and train and evaluate various classification models.

This section describes filtering car reviews using the NLTK library by tokenizing each review and retaining only nouns and adjectives (the most salient parts of speech), leaving 10,867 words across all reviews, with Figure FIGREF6 showing the frequency of the top 20 words, including "saftey" and "luxury," which serve as examples of car-speak as abstract descriptions with associated physical characteristics.

This section describes using TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) as a reliable metric for finding relevant terms in documents, representing each review as a vector of TF-IDF scores with a length of 10,867, labeling each review vector with the car model it reviews (ignoring the year, since a single model generally retains the same characteristics over time).

We train K Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers on the review vectors prepared in Section SECREF8, evaluating them using 4-fold cross validation on a shuffled data set. Table TABREF10 reports the F1 micro and F1 macro scores for all classifiers, with KNN performing the best across all four metrics, which is attributed to the multi-class nature of the data set.

This conclusion summarizes the paper's approach to defining and identifying "car-speak" (Section SECREF3), gathering a dataset of vehicle reviews from U.S. News BIBREF5, and creating/testing several classifiers trained on this data. The classifiers did not perform particularly well but provide a starting point for future work, which includes using more complex models and testing classifiers on user-provided natural language queries for more practical evaluation.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables: Figure 1 illustrates the ambiguity of the word "fast" by contrasting two cars that both achieve high speeds, Table 1 shows excerpts from car reviews, Figure 2 displays the frequencies of the top 20 words in reviews, and Table 2 reports evaluation metrics for all classifiers.

This section states that fine-grained Named Entity Recognition detects and classifies entity mentions across diverse domains, but accuracy becomes limited when the type set spans several domains due to a lack of datasets with properly annotated entity boundaries covering a large spectrum of entity types. The work addresses these issues by combining state-of-the-art deep learning models (ELMo) with an expansive knowledge base (Wikidata), cross-validating the model on 112 fine-grained entity types based on the hierarchy from the Wiki(gold) dataset.

This introduction section defines named entity recognition (NER) and its role in NLP applications, then explains that fine-grained NER (FgNER) uses over a hundred hierarchical labels and relies on distant supervision (mapping entities to knowledge bases like Freebase, DBpedia, YAGO) to generate training data, which produces noisy labels and fails to distinguish between different mentions of the same entity. It reviews prior FgNER systems, including Ling et al.'s perceptron with 112 overlapping labels, Yosef et al.'s SVM classifiers with 505 types, Gillick et al.'s context-dependent approach with label pruning heuristics, Yogatama et al.'s embedding-based model, and Shimaoka et al.'s attention-based LSTM model, motivating a more generalizable scheme for learning entity representations.

This section describes the two datasets used to evaluate the model—OntoNotes 5.0, which includes texts from five genres (broadcast conversation, broadcast news, magazine, newswire, and web data) and is annotated with 18 categories—and Wiki(gold), whose training data was automatically generated via distant supervision mapping Wikipedia hyperlinks to Freebase (not used in this study) and whose test data was manually annotated, with 7 main categories that map directly to OntoNotes.

This section defines the evaluation metrics used in the study, explaining that NER requires identifying both entity boundaries and entity types under "exact-match evaluation," where an entity is correct only if both boundaries and type match the ground truth. It defines precision, recall, and F-1 scores in terms of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN), and describes both macro-averaged and micro-averaged F-1 scores, stating that the study uses the micro-averaged F-1 score because it accounts for label imbalances in the evaluation data and provides a more meaningful statistic.

This section explains that deep neural networks, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have transformed entity detection systems by learning long-term dependencies in sequential data, with LSTMs using forget gates and input gates to address the vanishing or exploding gradients problem and capture long-term or short-term dependencies.

This section describes the proposed NER model architecture, which uses ELMo word representations combined with a residual LSTM to learn morphological representations from the character sequence of each token, followed by a softmax layer as a tag decoder to predict entity types. The hyperparameters include a hidden-layer size of 512 for each LSTM, a dropout probability of 0.2, an ELMo embedding dimension of 1024, the Adam optimization method, a batch size of 32, 30 epochs of training, and implementation using the TensorFlow framework.

This section describes the entity linking (EL) process using Wikidata, where entities are identified via a lookup constrained by the most common name, with a redirection list ("Also known as") improving recall by 5-10%. It details clustering entities onto the 112 Wiki(gold) types using the NECKAr tool for person/location/organization, mapping via occupation or instance of, and using cosine similarity (minimum threshold 0.1) of entity descriptions with Word2Vec embeddings trained on Wikipedia to select the highest-scoring subtype.

This section reports the results, showing that the model achieves an 88% total F-1 score on the OntoNotes dataset and a 53% total F-1 cross-validation score on the 112-class Wiki(gold) dataset, with the other OntoNotes categories (date, time, norp, language, ordinal, cardinal, quantity, percent, money, law) scoring between 80-90% F-1 except for time (65%). The authors note that while Wiki(gold) results could be improved by training directly on that dataset, their aim is to present a framework easily modifiable to any domain hierarchy with acceptable out-of-the-box performance rather than tuning specifically to this class hierarchy.

This conclusion summarizes the proposed deep neural network model for fine-grained named entity classification that uses ELMo embeddings and Wikidata to learn context-based entity representations and augment labels into finer-grained subtypes, reporting performance comparisons on Wiki(gold) in Table TABREF20 and noting the model performs similarly to existing systems without being trained or tuned on that dataset, with future work including refining the clustering method to extend to types beyond person, location, and organization and to include disambiguation of entity types.

This section presents the datasets, model pipeline, and evaluation results: Table 1 gives dataset statistics, Figures 1-3 illustrate the 112 Wiki(GOLD) tags, the full model pipeline (ELMo token embeddings fed into a residual LSTM module, with detected entities linked to Wikidata), and example outputs, while Tables 2 and 3 report precision, recall, and F-1 scores on Wiki(GOLD) and OntoNotes, along with a comparison with existing models.

The paper proposes a Bayesian model of multilingual unsupervised semantic role induction that combines individual per-language models with latent variables capturing cross-language role alignments, and uses this generative framework to evaluate four training scenarios—monolingual data only, a parallel corpus, a parallel corpus with other-language annotations, and small amounts of target-language annotation—finding that the primary benefit of adding a parallel corpus comes from increased monolingual data rather than the cross-language alignments, which yield only small improvements even with labeled data available for the other language.

This section introduces Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) as an important NLP task and motivates unsupervised SRL, noting that parallel text across languages can provide word alignment information to improve role prediction. It proposes a joint Bayesian model for multilingual unsupervised semantic role induction, consisting of individual Bayesian models per language combined with crosslingual latent variables that incorporate soft role agreement between aligned constituents, and states that the paper investigates performance improvements across settings involving labeled and unlabeled data along with the annotation effort required to achieve similar gains with labeled data.
This section states that the paper uses a standard unsupervised SRL setup consisting of several steps, and that unsupervised semantic role induction corresponds to step 4 of this pipeline.

This section describes the monolingual base model, which is the Bayesian unsupervised semantic role induction model of garg2012unsupervised, where semantic roles are predicate-specific and the role inventory for each predicate is divided into Primary roles (PRs) and Secondary roles (SRs) to model role ordering and repetition preferences. The generative process uses PRs to model global role ordering and repetition preferences and intervals to provide limited context for SRs, with all multinomial and binomial distributions having symmetric Dirichlet and beta priors, and the crosslingual model consists of two copies of this monolingual model connected by crosslingual latent variables.

This section describes a multilingual Bayesian Semantic Role Induction model that couples monolingual models across languages by adding crosslingual latent variables (CLVs) derived from word alignments between aligned head words in parallel corpora, where each CLV is a multi-valued variable (induced via a Chinese Restaurant Process) defining peaky distributions over role labels per language to capture crosslingual role correspondences. It acknowledges that generating aligned roles twice (by both the monolingual process and the CLV) is a deficiency caused by the intractability of adding CLVs as conditioning variables (which breaks Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy), and notes the model scales gracefully to more than two languages and can be reused in semi-supervised settings such as source-to-target annotation with no labeled target data.

This section describes a collapsed Gibbs-sampling inference approach that samples role labels and cross-lingual variables (CLVs) as hidden variables, using closed-form Dirichlet-multinomial solutions for the monolingual model and additional role-generation probabilities for the multilingual model, with CLV sampling considering aligned-role probabilities and CRP-based selection; it concludes that trained parameters parse monolingual data using only the monolingual model, with crosslingual parameters ignored so that CLV information acts as a regularizer.

This section describes the evaluation methodology, which follows titovcrosslingual by evaluating only correctly identified arguments, using the lang2011unsupervised metric with three components: Purity (PU), Collocation (CO), and F1 (the harmonic mean of PU and CO). For each predicate, scores are computed using the total number of argument instances, instances in induced clusters, and instances with gold labels, then weighted by argument instance count and averaged over all predicates.

This section describes the baseline used in the experiments, which is the same one used by lang2011unsupervised and has been shown to be difficult to outperform. The baseline assigns a semantic role to a constituent based on its syntactic function (the dependency relation to its head), such that if there are a total of INLINEFORM0 clusters, the INLINEFORM1 most frequent syntactic functions get a cluster each, and the rest are assigned to the INLINEFORM2 th cluster.

This section describes the work of titovcrosslingual, which uses separate monolingual models per language with an external penalty term maximizing the proportion of aligned arguments sharing role labels across two languages, optimized via annotation projection-like inference that does not scale to more than two languages, and contrasts it with the monolingual model of BIBREF3, which incorporates a global role ordering probability and avoids the hard clustering by assigning role labels based on argument-keys (tuples of four syntactic features) by allowing constituents with the same features to receive different roles in different contexts.

This section describes the datasets used—about 40k EN and 36k DE sentences from the CoNLL 2009 training set and about 1.5M parallel EN-DE sentences from Europarl—with EN sentences parsed using MaltParser and DE using the LTH parser, all non-auxiliary verbs selected as predicates (about 3k EN and 500 DE predicates), yielding 3.4M predicate instances in EN and 2.62M in DE. Arguments for EN are identified using the heuristics of lang2011unsupervised (achieving an F1 score of 85.1% on CoNLL 2009 EN data, which the authors note makes their EN results incomparable to the 80.7% reported by titovcrosslingual due to implementation differences), while DE arguments use the LTH system (F1 of 86.5%), and

This section reports the main results of the Bayesian model for multilingual unsupervised semantic role induction (SRI) using 21 semantic roles, 2 pattern roles (PRs) and 19 semantic roles (SRs), evaluated on the CoNLL and Europarl (EP) datasets using precision of clustering (PU), coverage of arguments (CO), and F1 score. Across four settings—monolingual CoNLL training/testing (Line 1), monolingual training with additional EP data (Line 2), the multilingual model adding word alignments (Line 3), and bilingual training on EP with testing on CoNLL (Lines 4–5)—the model outperforms the Baseline in both languages, improves German with additional EP data, and achieves cross-lingual performance at least as good as titovcrosslingual's external penalty term (German F1=82.7%, English F1=83.7%), though English

context: This section describes an annotation transfer experiment where source-language role annotations in the CoNLL dataset are clamped using a predefined mapping (and not sampled during training) to obtain good parameter estimates, which are then used to sample source roles in the unlabeled Europarl data, with cross-lingual variation latent variables (CLVs) aiming to capture this improvement and enhance sampling and parameter estimates for the target language; Table TABREF28 shows small improvements in the target languages, attributed to the small percentage of aligned roles limiting the impact of cross-lingual information.

This section evaluates the monolingual model in a semi-supervised setting by randomly selecting a proportion of CoNLL sentences as "supervised sentences" with clamped role labels, comparing against a "supervised baseline" using MAP estimates for seen predicates, and measuring clustering performance. The findings show that at around 10% supervised sentences, the supervised baseline starts outperforming the semi-supervised model (equivalent to about 3.6k sentences in German and 4k in English), that 10% labeled sentences already cover 63% of predicates in German and 44% in English, and that for German about 3.5% (1260) supervised sentences achieve the same performance increase as 1.5M unlabeled sentences.

This Related Work section states that the paper builds on Titov's crosslingual unsupervised SRL work, which uses superlingual latent variables (originally proposed by Naseem et al. for POS tagging) to capture cross-lingual information, and cites semi-supervised transfer approaches by Pado and by Furstenau et al. who used graph-based and graph-alignment methods to transfer or measure similarity of semantic role annotations between English and German; for monolingual unsupervised SRL it references Swier's work on the British National Corpus using 54 verbs from VerbNet, the Bayesian models of Garg et al. and Titov, Grenager's generative model with its constrained parameter space, iterative split-merge and graph-partitioning approaches, and a survey of supervised SRL systems by Marquez et al.

The paper proposes a Bayesian model of semantic role induction (SRI) that uses crosslingual latent variables to capture role alignments in parallel corpora, which correlate roles across languages and regularize monolingual parameter estimates. Evaluating monolingual SRI with a large unlabeled dataset, bilingual SRI with a parallel corpus, bilingual SRI with source-language annotations, and monolingual SRI with a small labeled dataset, they find that increasing monolingual unlabeled data significantly improves SRI in German but not English, while adding word alignments yields small, non-significant improvements even with source-language labeled data—attributed to assumptions where only a small percentage of roles are aligned—and that annotating small amounts of data can easily outperform gains from large unlabeled datasets or parallel corpora.
This section states that the work was funded by the Swiss NSF grant 200021_125137 and the EC FP7 grant PARLANCE.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables, including Figure 4 illustrating the multilingual model with aligned cross-linguistic variables (CLVs) and parameter representations (PR3, PR2, SRM), Table 1 reporting main results with F1 scores and significance testing via stratified shuffling (p-value < 0.05), Table 2 showing results for the multilingual model using labeled source language data, and Figure 5 depicting F1 performance with a portion of data labeled.

This paper describes the Team Copenhagen system, which placed first in the CoNLL--SIGMORPHON 2018 shared task on universal morphological reinflection (Task 2) with an overall accuracy of 49.87. The system uses an encoder-decoder architecture over character sequences with three core innovations: a wide context window, a multi-task learning approach with the auxiliary task of MSD prediction, and multilingual training.

This section describes the paper's approach to Task 2 of the CoNLL–SIGMORPHON 2018 shared task on universal morphological reinflection, which generates an inflected word form from its lemma and context. The authors start from the shared task's baseline seq2seq model with attention and achieve the best overall accuracy of 49.87 by introducing three augmentations: (1) using an LSTM to encode the entire available context, (2) employing multi-task learning with an auxiliary MSD prediction objective, and (3) training the auxiliary component multilingually over sets of two to three languages. They find that encoding the full context improves performance by 11.15 percentage points on average (though increasing variance), and that multi-task learning with multilingual training and monolingual finetuning scored highest for five out of seven languages, improving accuracy by another 9.86% on average.

This section describes the Copenhagen system, which modifies the CoNLL–SIGMORPHON 2018 baseline system, and outlines the baseline architecture before detailing the three augmentations the team introduces.

The section describes the CoNLL–SIGMORPHON 2018 baseline, an encoder-decoder model on character sequences that takes a lemma as input and generates a word form conditioned on context. In track 1 it uses the lemma, word form and MSD of the previous and following word as context, while track 2 only uses the word forms of the previous and next word; context embeddings are concatenated with per-character embeddings of the lemma, encoded by a one-layer LSTM encoder, and decoded by an LSTM decoder with attention. The model uses embedding, LSTM and attention sizes of 100, is trained for 20 epochs with Adam (learning rate 0.001), applies LSTM dropout at 0.3, subsamples training data at a rate of 0.3 per epoch, randomly drops context word forms at 0.1, and is evaluated on development data.

This section describes the authors' system, which encodes the entire past and future context of a target word using forward and backwards LSTMs and introduces an auxiliary objective to predict the target form's MSD tag to increase morphosyntactic awareness. The system uses multilingual training with random groupings of two to three languages (shared MSD decoder parameters, no source-language information), followed by monolingual finetuning at a tenth of the learning rate (0.0001), and produces final predictions via majority vote over an ensemble of the five best models.

The section reports that the Copenhagen system outperforms the baseline across all settings and languages in Track 1 and for almost all in Track 2, except in the high resource setting where it is not definitively superior. It notes the surprising finding that low resource Track 2 results are often higher than Track 1 results despite less explicit contextual information and no multilingual multi-tasking, interpreting this as evidence that a simpler model with fewer parameters performs better with limited training data, and states that the analysis focuses on the low resource setting due to time limitations while considering the analysis valid given the substantially higher Track 1 results than the baseline.

This ablation study analyses the incremental effect of different features in the Copenhagen system on low-resource Track 1 development data, training fifty models per language and architecture to account for the high variance introduced by encoding full context with an LSTM. It finds that encoding the full context with an LSTM improves performance by 11.15% on average, that the auxiliary MSD prediction objective has a mixed effect (positive for de, en, es, sv but negative for others, attributed to insufficient training data), that multilingual training raises accuracy by 7.96% over monolingual models, that monolingual finetuning improves accuracy by 2.72%, and that the multilingual multi-tasking approach outperforms other architectures for five of seven languages (de, en, fr, ru, sv) with an overall 18.30% improvement over the baseline.

This error analysis examines the Copenhagen system's wrong predictions on the English test set, finding that a small portion stem from incorrect interpretation of morphosyntactic conditioning (e.g., predicting "plan" instead of "plans" in "Our _ include raising private capital"), while the majority are nonsensical outputs like "bomb" for "job", "fify" for "fixing", and "gnderrate" for "understand", suggesting the system failed to learn to copy lemma characters into inflected forms, an issue that could be addressed with data augmentation techniques encouraging autoencoding.

This section reports the MSD (multi-sense disambiguation) prediction accuracy from the multi-tasking experiments, where the multilingual finetuned setup for Spanish (66.59%) and the monolingual setup for French (65.35%) scored best, generally outperforming the main task and illustrating the added difficulty of generating correct surface forms even when the morphosyntactic description is correctly identified. It notes a correlation between MSD prediction and main task accuracy for de, en, ru and sv, with French as a notable exception (inflection gains much from multilingual training while MSD prediction suffers greatly), and highlights that the magnitude of change is not always consistent with the direction, using ru as an example where multilingual training benefits inflection more than MSD prediction, illustrating the two-fold effect of multi-task training: informing the main task through shared parameters or helping through regularisation.

This section states that the system is inspired by multi-task and multi-lingual learning, building on the intuitions that jointly learning related tasks and related languages tends to be beneficial, and notes that in computational morphology, multi-lingual approaches have been used for morphological reinflection and paradigm completion, though those datasets covered more languages (40 and 21), enabling linguistically-motivated language groupings and parameter sharing at the character level, while parameter sharing between related languages for dependency parsing was found to be more beneficial for closely related languages.

This section states that the Copenhagen system achieved the best performance in the CoNLL–SIGMORPHON 2018 shared task on Universal Morphological Reinflection (Task 2) with an overall accuracy of 49.87, attributing this success to three core innovations extending a character-based encoder-decoder model: a wide context window encoding the entire available context, multi-task learning with the auxiliary task of MSD prediction acting as a regulariser, and a multilingual approach exploiting information across languages. The authors also identify future work to better understand the increased variance in results introduced by each modification and the varying effects of multi-task learning across different languages.
This acknowledgements section states that the research was supported by the NVIDIA Corporation through the donation of a Titan Xp GPU used for the work.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables, including Table 1 with an example input sentence illustrating context MSD tags and lemmas (available only in Track 1), the main objective of predicting the word form "made," and the auxiliary objective of predicting the MSD tag V;PST;V.PTCP;PASS; Figure 1 schematically representing the approach with focus on predicting the final character "e" of "made," showing the attention matrix and magenta-marked auxiliary decoder input/output; Tables 2 and 3 reporting official shared task test set results and the five best multilingual models per language; and Figures 2 and 3 showing mean accuracy with standard deviation over 100 models per language and architecture (LSTM Enc, Multi-task, Multilingual, Finetuned) and accuracy on the auxiliary MSD prediction task.

The abstract introduces a new task of personalized recipe generation, which expands a recipe name and incomplete ingredient details into complete natural-text instructions aligned with a user's historical preferences. The authors propose a model that attends on technique- and recipe-level representations of previously consumed recipes and fuses these 'user-aware' representations in an attention fusion layer to control recipe text generation, and they evaluate it on a new dataset of 180K recipes and 700K interactions, showing it generates plausible and personalized recipes compared to non-personalized baselines.

This section introduces the task of generating plausible, personalized recipes from incomplete input specifications (dish name, key ingredients, calorie level) by leveraging historical user preferences, combining data-to-text generation and personalized recommendation within an encoder-decoder framework that attends on user profiles (learned latent representations of previously consumed recipes) and fuses user-aware representations with decoder output via an attention fusion layer. The authors release a new dataset of 180K+ recipes and 700K+ user reviews, introduce new evaluation strategies centering on quantitative measures of coherence (perplexity, user-ranking), and report that quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm personalization assists in generating plausible, high-quality, user-specific recipes aligned with historical preferences.

This Related Work section situates the paper within data-to-text natural language generation, noting that prior approaches model recipes as ingredient entities acted upon by cooking actions (BIBREF14, BIBREF15), apply a 'checklist' attention constraint over unused ingredients (BIBREF0), or attend over explicit ingredient references in prior steps (BIBREF16). It argues that hierarchical methods inferring a full ingredient list cannot personalize recipes and are infeasible given the potentially unconstrained number of ingredients (from a space of 10K+), and instead contrasts its approach—attending over historical user preferences from previously consumed recipes—with user- and item-dependent aspect-aware review generation (BIBREF3, BIBREF4).

This section describes a personalized recipe generation model that takes a recipe name, partial ingredient list, and caloric level as input and outputs recipe instructions as a token sequence, using an encoder with vocabulary, ingredient, and caloric-level embedding layers feeding two-layered bidirectional GRUs (BiGRU), an ingredient attention mechanism with an attention-score function $\alpha$ (key $K$, query $Q$, trainable weights $W_\alpha$, bias $\mathbf{b}_\alpha$, normalization $Z$), a two-layer GRU decoder, and an attention fusion layer that concatenates contexts with the decoder GRU output and previous token embedding to compute token probabilities via log-likelihood maximization. It models user preferences through two schemes—Prior Recipe Attention over the $k$-most recent prior recipes $R^+_u$ (with $R^{k+}_u$) to account for temporal drift, using recipe embeddings $\mathcal{R}$ or averaged name tokens, and Prior

This section describes the Food.com recipe dataset, comprising 230K+ recipe texts and 1M+ user reviews collected over 18 years (2000-2018), which after filtering (recipes with at least 3 steps and 4-20 ingredients, users with at least 4 reviews) yields 180K+ recipes and 700K+ reviews. It details the data characteristics (average recipe length of 117 tokens, 13K unique ingredients, 95% of words appearing less than 100 times), the use of Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization producing a 15K token vocabulary, the sequential leave-one-out evaluation split based on review timestamps, and the manual construction of a 58-technique list from 384 cooking actions with technique adherence approximated via string matching.

This section describes the experimental setup and results for generating personalized recipes from the first 3-5 ingredients, using top-$k$ sampling ($k=3$), a hidden size $d_h=256$, Adam optimizer with learning rate $10^{-3}$, and teacher-forcing, comparing personalized models against two baselines (a name-based Nearest-Neighbor model and an Encoder-Decoder with ingredient attention, Enc-Dec). The models are evaluated via BPE perplexity, BLEU-1/4, ROUGE-L, Distinct-1/2, personalization metrics (user matching accuracy and Mean Reciprocal Rank), recipe-level coherence (averaging 1.78-1.82 versus 1.77 for baseline), recipe step entailment, and human evaluation, with the Prior Name model achieving the best performance across most metrics and human evaluators preferring personalized outputs 63% of the time.

The authors propose a novel task of generating personalized recipes from incomplete input specifications and user histories, demonstrating on a dataset of 180K recipes and 700K reviews that their personalized generative models produce plausible, personalized, and coherent recipes preferred by human evaluators, while introducing automatic coherence measures for instructional texts and personalization metrics to support these claims.

This section states that the raw data consists of 270K recipes and 1.4M user-recipe interactions (reviews) scraped from Food.com, covering a period of 18 years (January 2000 to December 2018), with dataset summary statistics in tab:int-stats and sample information about one user-recipe interaction and the recipe involved in tab:samplegk.
This section directs readers to two tabs—samplechx and samplewaffle—containing sample generated recipes for chicken chili and sweet waffles, respectively.

This section describes a human evaluation in which 930 pairwise evaluations (310 per personalized model) were collected over 62 sessions, with 15 pairwise comparisons per session. In each comparison, users received a partial recipe specification (name and 3-5 key ingredients) plus two generated recipes—one from the baseline encoder-decoder model and one from one of three personalized models (Prior Tech, Prior Name, Prior Recipe)—and indicated which recipe was more coherent and which best accomplished the goal indicated by the recipe name.

This section presents the paper's tables and figures, including Table 1 and Table 5 documenting Food.com interaction statistics before and after data processing, Table 6 showing GeniusKitchen sample data, and Tables 2 and 4 reporting metrics (Distinct-1/2, User Matching Accuracy, Mean Reciprocal Rank, and pairwise preference over baseline evaluated for 310 recipe pairs per model) and coherence metrics on generated recipes from the test set. It also includes figures illustrating the model architecture's data flow with prior recipe attention scores, sample generated recipes (such as "Chicken Bell Pepper Chili Weight Watchers" and a waffle recipe) for all models emphasizing personalization and ingredient mentions, and sample questions used in pairwise and coherence evaluation surveys.

The abstract proposes STEP (Sequence-to-Sequence Transformer Pre-training), a Seq2Seq Transformer pre-trained on large-scale unlabeled documents using three tasks—sentence reordering, next sentence generation, and masked document generation—which collectively improve performance over a heavily tuned large Seq2Seq Transformer with a strong pre-trained encoder. Using their best pre-training task, STEP outperforms the best published abstractive model on CNN/DailyMail by 0.8 ROUGE-2 and on New York Times by 2.4 ROUGE-2.

This section introduces Step (Sequence-to-Sequence TransformEr Pre-training), which pre-trains both the encoder and decoder of a seq2seq Transformer using three tasks—Sentence Reordering (SR), Next Sentence Generation (NSG), and Masked Document Generation (MDG)—on large-scale unlabeled documents, then fine-tunes it on the CNN/DailyMail and New York Times datasets, improving ROUGE-2 by 0.8 on CNN/DailyMail and 2.4 on New York Times over a heavily tuned large seq2seq Transformer with a strong pre-trained encoder, with human experiments confirming significantly better summaries.
This section introduces extractive and abstractive document summarization methods as well as pre-training methods for natural language processing tasks.

This section describes extractive summarization as a sentence ranking problem solved via binary (sequence) classification models that score whether each sentence belongs in the summary, with neural models using hierarchical LSTMs/CNNs as feature learners that outperform discrete feature-based models, and more recently pre-trained transformers that further improve performance, while noting limitations such as extracted sentences being too long and redundant and human summaries being inherently abstractive, motivating the paper's focus on abstractive summarization.

This section states that abstractive summarization is a sequence-to-sequence learning problem, and that seq2seq attentive LSTMs (even extended with copy mechanism, coverage model, and reinforcement learning) perform only slightly better than Lead3, likely because LSTMs without pre-training are not powerful enough; it notes that liu2019text used a seq2seq Transformer with its encoder initialized from a pre-trained Transformer (BERT) to achieve state-of-the-art performance, and that the authors' work goes further by pre-training the decoder together with the encoder and initializing both encoder and decoder of a summarization model with pre-trained Transformers.

This section states that pre-training methods such as BERT, XLNet, RoBERTa, and ELMo/GPT focus on pre-training encoders using language modeling objectives, while the authors propose pre-training both the encoder and decoder of a seq2seq Transformer with separate parameters (rather than shared parameters as in a unified Transformer language model), and introduce three pre-training tasks—Masked Document Generation (with a different masking strategy that predicts original text without masked tokens), plus two other tasks—aimed at document-level tasks like abstractive document summarization rather than sentence-level tasks.
This section introduces the backbone architecture of the abstractive summarization model Step, describes methods to pre-train Step, and moves on to fine-tuning on summarization datasets.

This section models abstractive document summarization as a sequence-to-sequence learning problem, adopting the seq2seq Transformer architecture, which consists of an encoder Transformer and a decoder Transformer, each with multiple layers containing a multi-head attentive sub-layer followed by a fully connected sub-layer with residual connections and layer normalization. The encoder transforms the document $X=(x_1,\dots,x_{|X|})$ into contextual representations, while the decoder generates the summary $Y=(y_1,\dots,y_{|Y|})$ one token at a time conditioned on the contextual representations and all preceding tokens $y_{<t}=(y_1,\dots,y_{t-1})$, trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training document-summary pairs.

The section explains that training a seq2seq Transformer summarization model from scratch is difficult due to the limited number of document-summary pairs, so they initialize the encoder of their model Step with a pre-trained Transformer encoder (RoBERTa) to enhance language understanding, then continue pre-training on unlabeled text to develop language generation capabilities and the ability to associate generated text with encoder outputs.

This section describes the Sentence Reordering pre-training task, where a document $X=(S_1, S_2, \dots, S_m)$ is shuffled into $\hat{X}_S=(S_{a_1}, S_{a_2}, \dots, S_{a_m})$ via a permutation $A=\text{\tt permutation}(m)$ and the model Step is trained on $\langle \hat{X}_S, X \rangle$ pairs to recover the original document. The authors motivate this task on three grounds—generating long, coherent multi-sentence summaries, content reordering (which occurs in 40% of document-summary pairs, defined by mapping summary sentences to document sentences via the ROUGE score), and learning to copy tokens—and note that document rotation is a simpler special case they exclude in favor of the general sentence reordering task.

The Next Sentence Generation (NSG) pre-training task uses one span of text $G_1$ to predict the next span $G_2$, splitting documents into two segments (each possibly containing multiple sentences) using option two, where the splitting point can be at any position, potentially producing incomplete sentences. This forces the encoder and decoder to understand incomplete input text and reduces pre-training and fine-tuning input mismatch, training the Step model on large amounts of $\langle G_1, G_2\rangle$ pairs, and differs from skip-thought vectors (which use single-sentence segments to pre-train an encoder) and NSP (a classification task) since NSG is a generation task for pre-training a generation model.

This section describes the third pre-training task, Masked Document Generation (MDG), which learns to recover a document with a masked span of tokens $\mathcal{M}=(x_k, x_{k+1}, \cdots, x_{k+l-1})$, where the span length $l$ is sampled from $\mathcal{U}(a,b)$ and the start position $k$ from $\mathcal{U}(1,|X|-l+1)$. Instead of replacing all masked tokens with [MASK], each token in $\mathcal{M}$ is processed with one of three strategies—replaced with [MASK] (80%), replaced with a random token (10%), or left unchanged (10%)—to produce $\hat{X}_M$, and during pre-training all three tasks (SR, NSG, MDG) can be used together with each task chosen randomly for 1/3 of the time.

After pre-training STEP on the three tasks, the model is fine-tuned on abstractive document summarization datasets by continuing training on supervised document-summary pairs, using beam search during summary generation.
This section introduces the datasets used for the experiments, describes the training details of the models, and outlines the evaluation protocols used to evaluate the summarization models.

The section states that the summarization performance of the models is assessed on two benchmark datasets, CNN/DailyMail (CNNDM) and New York Times (NYT), and that the models are pre-trained on the GIGA-CM dataset.

The section describes the CNN-Daily Mail (CNNDM) dataset, using the non-anonymized version preprocessed with the scripts from see2017get, yielding 287,226 document-summary pairs for training, 13,368 for validation, and 11,490 for test.

This section describes the NYT dataset, which consists of articles with multi-sentence summaries written by library scientists, and explains the preprocessing procedures closely following durrett2016learning and liu2019text. The test set includes all articles published on January 1, 2017 or later (9,076 articles), while the remaining 100,834 articles are split into a training set of 96,834 examples and a validation set of 4,000 examples; after removing articles whose summaries contain fewer than 50 words, the test set contains 3,452 examples.

This section describes the creation of the GIGA-CM dataset, which consists of 6,521,658 unlabeled documents sampled from English Gigaword and CNNDM training documents (with CNNDM's 13,368 validation documents used as the validation set and NYT's test set excluded to avoid overlap), and explains how documents are segmented into 512-token segments and processed for the pre-training tasks: Sentence Reordering (SR), Masked Document Generation (MDG) with masked lengths between 100 and 256 tokens, and Next Sentence Generation (NSG) where each segment predicts its next 256 tokens.

This section describes the implementation details of the Seq2Seq Transformer model, which uses a 24-layer $\text{RoBERTa}_{\text{LARGE}}$-initialized encoder (16 attention heads, hidden size 1,024, feed-forward size 4,096, dropout 0.1) and a shallower 6-layer decoder (feed-forward size 2,048, dropout 0.3), optimized with Adam ($\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.98$) using separate optimizers with learning rates of $2e-5$ (encoder) and $1e-4$ (decoder) and 10,000 warmup steps during pre-training on GIGA-CM, CNNDM, and NYT, and fine-tuned with learning rates of $2e-5$ and 4,000 warmup steps over 50

This section describes the evaluation methodology, stating that ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L scores (full-length F1 on CNNDM, limited-length recall on NYT) were computed using the ROUGE-1.5.5.pl script, and that abstractive systems were additionally evaluated through human judgements in which participants ranked outputs from 20 randomly sampled CNNDM test documents according to informativeness, fluency and succinctness.

This section reports automatic evaluation results on the CNNDM and NYT datasets using ROUGE metrics, showing that Step (pre-trained on GIGA-CM) outperforms all compared extractive and abstractive models, including BERTAbs and UniLM; it finds that Sentence Reordering (SR), Next Sentence Generation (NSG), and Masked Document Generation (MDG) all improve RoBERTa-S2S, with SR being the most effective pre-training task, and that combining all three tasks (ALL) performs best when unlabeled data is limited.

This section describes a human evaluation conducted on 20 documents randomly sampled from the test split of CNNDM, in which participants ranked outputs from the best-performing Step model (pre-trained on the GIGA-CM dataset using the SR task), Gold (human references), RoBERTa-S2S, BERTAbs, and UniLM. The results, reported as proportions of system rankings and mean rank (lower is better) in Table TABREF29, show that Step was selected as best in 25% of cases and achieved the lowest mean rank among all systems except Gold, and a student t-test on ratings (rank $i$ converted to $6-i$) confirmed Step is significantly better than all other systems at $p<0.05$, though it still lags behind human performance, possibly because all systems only take the first 512 tokens of long documents as input and thus lose information from subsequent tokens.

The paper proposes Step, a seq2seq transformer pre-training approach for abstractive document summarization that uses three pre-training tasks—sentence reordering, next sentence generation, and masked document generation—and shows that a summarization model based on pre-trained Step outperforms the best published abstractive system when trained only on unlabeled documents from summarization datasets, with large-scale pre-training data yielding larger gains, achieving 0.8 absolute ROUGE-2 improvements on CNN/DailyMail and 2.4 absolute ROUGE-2 improvements on New York Times.
