This section presents the figures and tables describing STEP's pre-training (using Sentence Reordering, Next Sentence Generation, and Masked Document Generation on the SEQ2SEQ Transformer architecture) along with results on CNNDM and NYT datasets using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L metrics, plus human evaluation rankings.

This work presents an exploration and imitation-learning-based agent that achieves state-of-the-art performance in playing text-based computer games by using the Go-Explore approach, which first extracts trajectories with high rewards during an initial exploration phase and then trains a policy to solve the game by imitating these trajectories. The experiments show that this approach outperforms existing solutions in solving text-based games and is more sample efficient in terms of the number of interactions with the environment, and that the learned policy generalizes better than existing solutions to unseen games without using any restriction on the action space.

This introduction explains that text-based games pose a combinatorially large exploration problem due to the enormous natural-language action space (O(N^m), e.g. 20K^7 ≈ 1.28e30), and proposes using the Go-Explore algorithm to extract high-reward trajectories and train a Seq2Seq model via imitation learning to operate in the full, unconstrained action space. It benchmarks Go-Explore on the CoinCollector games (finding winning trajectories faster than existing solutions) and evaluates generalization on the 4,440 "First TextWorld Problems" games, showing stronger generalization on unseen games compared to competitive baselines.

path: Reinforcement Learning Based Approaches for Text-Based Games
context: This section describes two prominent reinforcement learning approaches for text-based games: the first associates a separate Q-function with each word position in a fixed-length sentence (demonstrated with two-word verb-object sentences like "take apple"), while the second learns a single Q-function that scores all possible actions. The authors note the first approach is limiting due to its fixed word count and lack of temporal dependency, and that the second can face exponentially large action spaces, with BIBREF18 proposing a hierarchical pointer-generator as a solution—though they argue a Q-scorer does not generalize well even when admissible actions are provided (Section 5.2 Zero-Shot).

This section explains that text-based games typically have sparse rewards because the large action space makes random rewards unlikely, requiring longer-term planning. It notes that various exploration-based solutions address reward sparsity—including novelty search, intrinsic motivation, and curiosity-based rewards—and highlights that BIBREF8 demonstrated the effectiveness of the episodic discovery bonus in sparse-reward environments, though this method only works in games with very small action and state spaces because its counting methods depend on the state's explicit raw form.

This section describes Go-Explore, an exploration-based algorithm that uses an archive to track under-explored states and exploits simulator determinism to return to promising states, operating in two phases: exploration (phase 1) and robustification/generalization (phase 2). It frames text-based games as discrete-time Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) defined by $(S, T, A, \Omega, O, R)$, where $S$ is the state set, $T$ the transition function, $A$ the action set (all possible token sequences), $\Omega$ the observation set, $O$ the conditional observation probability, and $R$ the reward function.

Phase 1 implements a Go-Explore variant that builds an archive of cells, where each cell is a set of observations mapped to the same discrete representation by the mapping function $f(x)$, which computes the summed word embedding of each token in an observation, concatenates it with the current cumulative reward, and then compresses and discretizes the result by binning to map similar observations to the same cell; cells store metadata (trajectory, length, cumulative reward) and are added or updated when trajectories are higher-scoring or equal-scoring but shorter, while cell selection and random action selection over the game-provided admissible action set $\mathcal{A}_t$ drive exploration, with adding the cumulative reward to the cell representation described as very effective at increasing the speed of discovering high-reward trajectories, yielding the phase-1 trajectory $\mathcal{T}_g$.

This section describes Phase 2 of the Go-Explore algorithm, which trains a Seq2Seq imitation learning model (using an encoder-decoder LSTM architecture with a word embedding matrix) to generalize the fragile trajectory-based policy into a robust, state-conditioned policy by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of actions given observations, without using reward directly in the loss.

This section describes the experimental setup, introducing two text-based game benchmarks—CoinCollector (a room-navigation game where the agent collects a coin for a sparse +1 reward) and CookingWorld (4,440 games across 222 difficulty levels requiring ingredient collection and recipe-based cooking)—and outlines three research questions: benchmarking phase 1 of Go-Explore against existing exploration approaches on 10 hard-level 30 CoinCollector games, and evaluating generalization on CookingWorld through three settings (Single, Joint, and Zero-Shot), while noting that observations consist of room description, inventory, quest, previous action, and feedback, with only the room description $D$ used in phase 1 of Go-Explore.

This section describes the baseline methods used for comparison: for CoinCollector games, Go-Explore with the episodic discovery bonus (used to improve DQN++ and DRQN++ baselines), and for CookingWorld games, three treatments—LSTM-DQN, LSTM-DQN+ADM, and DRRN.

This section specifies the hyper-parameters used across all games: a maximum of 50 steps, a Go-Explore archive cell representation computed from the sum of 50-dimensional GloVe embeddings of room description tokens concatenated with the cumulative reward, and LSTM hidden states of 300, while CoinCollector baselines reuse the original paper's hyper-parameters and CookingWorld baselines use 100-dimensional GloVe for the single setting and 300-dimensional GloVe for the joint setting.

This section compares the exploration efficiency of Go-Explore, DQN++, and DRQN++ in the CoinCollector setting by measuring the number of environment interactions (frames) and the maximum score achieved, where Go-Explore also counts actions used to restore the environment to a selected cell. The results show that DRQN++ finds a maximum-score trajectory faster than DQN++, while Go-Explore's phase 1 finds an optimal trajectory (30 steps) using approximately half the interactions and always achieves the optimal trajectory length, compared to average lengths of 38 and 42 for DQN++ and DRQN++ respectively.

In CookingWorld, the authors compared models in single, joint, and zero-shot settings, measuring the sum of final scores across all games and trajectory length (number of steps). Phase 1 of Go-Explore on single games achieved a total score of 19,530 (out of a maximum 19,882) with 47,562 steps, finding a winning trajectory in 4,279 out of 4,440 games, confirming the effectiveness of Go-Explore's exploration strategy; the authors then evaluated the simple imitation learning policy trained on the extracted trajectories from Phase 1 of Go-Explore across the three settings.

In the CookingWorld Single setting, where each model is trained from scratch on the 4,440 games using the phase 1 Go-Explore trajectories, the LSTM-DQN approach performs poorly without admissible actions but improves dramatically (+ADM) when admissible actions are used in the $\epsilon$-greedy step; DRRN achieves a very high score by learning to rank admissible actions, while the Seq2Seq model trained on the single Go-Explore trajectory achieves the highest score among all methods despite not using admissible actions, though it scores 9.4% lower than phase 1 Go-Explore due to imperfect trajectory replication, with the gap widening as games become harder.

In the CookingWorld joint setting, a single model is trained on all games simultaneously to test whether one agent can learn to play multiple games, and all evaluated models (including LSTM-DQN and DRRN) achieve lower performance than in the single game setting, partly because learning multiple games at once causes the agent to encounter similar observations across games where the correct action may differ; the order of game presentation strongly affects LSTM-DQN and DRRN, with a shuffled curriculum (shuffling games each epoch) yielding far better performance than an easy-to-hard curriculum, so only the shuffled curriculum is reported, and in FIGREF28's score breakdown all baselines quickly fail, even on easier games.

In the CookingWorld zero-shot setting, 4,440 games are split into training, validation, and test sets stratified by difficulty (recipes 1, 2, and 3), and Table TABREF26 shows that the RL baselines perform poorly, with DRRN substantially underperforming the Go-Explore Seq2Seq model despite DRRN having access to admissible actions at test time while the Seq2Seq and LSTM-DQN models must construct actions token-by-token from a 20,000-token vocabulary; Go-Explore Seq2Seq solves almost half of the unseen games, with most losses occurring in the hardest set requiring very long action sequences (shown in FIGREF62), demonstrating the relative effectiveness of training a Seq2Seq model on Go-Explore trajectories while indicating the need for better RL algorithms that generalize to unseen games.

This section states that the proposed Go-Explore exploration strategy is a viable methodology for extracting high-performing trajectories in text-based games, enabling the training of supervised models that outperform existing models in the experimental settings studied, while acknowledging that several challenges and limitations remain unaddressed by both the proposed methodology and previous solutions.

This section states that the state representation is the main limitation of the proposed imitation learning model, because the descriptions (D) of different games show a large overlap, causing the policy to receive very similar observations while being expected to imitate two different actions, a problem especially evident in the joint setting of CookingWorld where the 222 games are repeated 20 times with different entities and room maps. It notes that a simple Seq2Seq model was used for the policy to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed exploration methods, and that a more complex Hierarchical-Seq2Seq model or a better encoder representation based on knowledge graphs would likely improve the performance of this approach.

This section discusses how Go-Explore's reliance on given admissible actions limits its applicability to more complex text-based games like Zork I and Z-Machine games, where the action space explodes in size. It proposes two viable strategies—leveraging general language models to produce grammatically correct actions or iteratively learning a policy to sample actions while exploring—and notes that a hand-tailored CookingWorld solution from the "First TextWorld Problems" competition achieved up to 91.9% of the maximum possible score across 514 test games, though its reliance on entity extraction and template filling limits generalization, making it complementary rather than competitive to the proposed approach.

This conclusion section states that the authors presented a novel methodology for solving text-based games that first extracts high-performing trajectories using phase 1 of Go-Explore and then trains a simple Seq2Seq model mapping observations to actions using the extracted trajectories, with experiments showing promising results in three settings along with improved generalization and sample efficiency compared to existing methods.
In the hard setting (mode 2), each room on the path to the coin has two distractor rooms, and the level (e.g. 30) indicates the shortest path from the starting point to the coin room.

This section describes how CookingWorld's difficulty is determined by the number and types of skills an agent must master—specifically recipe size (1, 2, or 3 ingredients), take (1, 2, or 3 ingredients to find), open (containers/doors), cook, cut, drop (limited inventory capacity), and go (1, 6, 9, or 12 locations)—with the hardest game being a 3-ingredient recipe requiring ingredients to be picked up across 12 locations, then cut and cooked, with doors or objects opened for access. It also lists the grammar for the text-based games, including actions (go, look, examine, inventory, eat, open/close, take/drop, put/insert) and transformations such as cooking with the BBQ (grilled), oven (roasted), or stove (fried), slicing/chopping/dicing with a sharp object, and preparing the meal.

This section lists the paper's tables and figures, including Table 1 (example CookingWorld observations), Table 2 (statistics of the CookingWorld and CoinCollector text-based game families), Table 3 (CookingWorld results on single, joint, and zero-shot settings), and Figures 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11, which present CoinCollector results comparing DQN++ and DRQN++ versus Go-Explore Phase1, the high-level intuition of the Go-Explore algorithm, an LSTM-DQN schema, and breakdowns of CookingWorld results in the Single, Joint, and Zero-Shot settings normalized and sorted by increasing difficulty level.

This paper describes three discursive segmentation models based solely on resources available in several languages—marker lists and a statistical POS labeling—and presents a preliminary evaluation of segmentation quality. The systems were evaluated automatically against the Annodis corpus, a manually annotated reference, yielding very encouraging results.

This introduction presents Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) as a hierarchical discourse analysis technique and outlines the three steps of discursive analysis—segmentation, relation detection, and tree construction—while motivating the development of a generic, multilingual discourse segmenter. It announces the paper's preliminary results on a generic segmenter combining several segmentation strategies, along with an automatic evaluation protocol, using the Annodis French corpus.

This section describes the Relational-Strategic Text (RST) framework, in which discursive units are classified as nuclei (providing information pertinent to the author's purposes) or satellites (adding dependent information), with nucleus-satellite and multinuclear relationships forming a hierarchical tree structure. It explains that automatic discourse segmentation reduces text into Elementary Discursive Units (EDU) using explicit discursive markers (e.g., "afin de, pour que, donc, cependant, puisque"), and cites research across French, English, Portuguese, Spanish, and other languages that converge on using explicit marker lists to segment texts.

This section describes the Annodis corpus, a French annotated corpus of 687,000 words from four sources (the Est Républicain newspaper, Wikipedia, the TALN 2008 conference proceedings, and IFRI reports), annotated with two types of annotations—Rhetorical relations and multilevel structures—on two levels of analysis (ascendant and descending), using Glozz, and produced by two groups of annotators yielding a "specialist" ($E$) subcorpus and a "naive" ($N$) subcorpus used as references in the experiments.

This section describes the general architecture of the proposed discourse segmenter system, which processes raw UTF-8-encoded text through Part of Speech morphosyntactic Tagging (POS) and sentence-level segmentation as a preprocessing step, then applies rules based on a bank of explicit markers for final discourse segmentation. For the experiments, the system used lists of markers in French, Spanish, English and Portuguese, including the Lexiconn project list regrouping 328 French-language markers, and applied a segmentation strategy according to the POS labelling of the document.

path: Segmentation with explicit use of a marker
context: The elementary baseline system Segmenter$_{\mu}$ performs segmentation using solely a list of discursive markers, replacing each marker's appearance with a special symbol $\mu$ that indicates a boundary between the right segment (SD) and the left segment (SE); for example, it splits the sentence "La ville d'Avignon est la capitale du Vaucluse, qui est un département du Sud de la France" into the left segment "La ville d'Avignon est la capitale du Vaucluse" and the right segment "est un département du sud de la France."

path: Segmentation with explicit use of a marker and POS labels
context: The section describes the Segmenter$_{\mu+}$ system, which improves on Segmenter$_{\mu}$ by incorporating grammar categories (POS labels) from the TreeTagger tool to condition segmentation, and it specifies two strategies: Segmenter$_{\mu+V}$ (verbal version), which uses two rules based on the presence or absence of verbs in the left and right segments, and Segmenter$_{\mu+(V-N)}$ (verb-noun version), which uses four rules based on the presence or absence of verbs and nouns in the segments.

This section describes an evaluation protocol for automatic discourse segmentation that counts common word pairs representing segment borders, comparing the Annodis reference segmentation ($L_r$) with the automatically produced segmentation ($L_c$) using precision $P$, recall $R$, and $F$-score. For the example text, the Segmentator$_{\mu }$ achieved $P$ = 5/11 = 0.45, $R$ = 5/8 = 0.625, and F-score = 0.523. Tests were performed on the $D$ set of 38 common documents (13,364 words) to measure the distance between human markers, and on the "specialist" subcorpus $E$ to benchmark the three automatic systems.

This section compares automatic evaluation results for discourse segmentation systems, using the 78 expert-segmented (E) documents as reference and reporting F-score, precision (P), and recall (R). The grammatical verb-nominal version (V-N) achieved the best F-score, while the verbal version (V) obtained better precision than V-N, and the Naive system's F-score, P, and R proved very similar to those of the Experts.

This section concludes that the authors designed a resource-light discourse segmenter and a simple evaluation protocol (described as the first automatic evaluation in French), finding that a simple baseline employing only a list of markers and words' grammatical categories (obtained via TreeTagger) yields encouraging performance, with Segmentator$_{\mu}$ achieving the best F-score and recall and Segmentator$_{\mu +V}$ excelling in precision, while the impact of markers and grammar tag rules was studied; they plan to improve the segmenters, extend tests to Portuguese, Spanish, English, and other languages using language-specific marker lists, and apply the baselines to tasks such as automatic document summarisation and sentence compression.

This appendix presents the list of French rhetorical connectors used as markers, noting that markers ending in apostrophe (e.g., près qu', à condition d') are deleted from a regular expression implying 'and' (such as près qu' + près que), and provides the resulting enumerated list of markers.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables, including Figure 1 (a Rhetorical Structure Theory tree of a French document), Figure 2 (the system architecture diagram of the proposed Discourse Segmenter), Table 1 (performance of human segmentations), and Table 2 (performance of automatic segmenters versus experts).

This paper quantifies linguistic activities that discriminate answered from unanswered questions on Quora, finding that language use patterns in question text can characterize answerability and predict whether a question unanswered for time period t will eventually be answered, achieving 76.26% accuracy (t = 1 month) and 68.33% accuracy (t = 3 months), with language use feature alone accounting for 74.18% accuracy, and outperforming similar works by Dror et al. and Yang et al. with a maximum improvement of ~39% in accuracy.

This introduction states that Quora is a large community-driven Q&A site where unanswered questions are called "open questions," and it aims to characterize question answerability using linguistic features of question texts as a cheaper alternative to expensive expert human judgment. It notes that appropriate quantification of linguistic activities can correspond to judgment factors (subjective, controversial, open-ended, vague, ill-formed, off-topic, ambiguous, uninteresting) and reviews prior Q&A research using community feedback, textual features, and prediction models for answer quality and unanswered questions.

The dataset was obtained through web-based crawls between June 2014 and August 2014, accumulating a Q&A dataset spanning over four years (January 2010 to May 2014), initiated with 100 randomly selected questions across different topics and crawled using a BFS pattern through related question links, resulting in 822,040 unique questions across 80,253 topics with 1,833,125 answers, for which revision logs (containing edit information) and activity logs of the question asker were separately crawled.

This section identifies linguistic activities on Quora and proposes simple, automatically computable quantifications of language usage, revealing significant differences between open and answered questions: open questions use more words, higher POS tag diversity (POSDiv, computed via the CMU POS tagger as Shannon entropy over POS tag probabilities), and higher ROUGE-LCS recall (indicating less editing), while answered questions contain more content words, personal pronouns, conjunctions, and adverbs. Using LIWC for psycholinguistic analysis, the study finds that answered-question askers use more social, family, and human-related words and express more negative emotions (anger, sadness, anxiety), whereas open-question askers use more function words, impersonal pronouns, and positive emotions, with open questions containing more sexual, body, and health-related words—findings corroborated by example questions in Table 2 that align with factors human judges cite for unanswered questions.

This section describes the prediction framework for whether a Quora question will be answered after a time period $t$, using features based on the linguistic and psycholinguistic aspects of the question asker's language use as discriminatory factors.

This section presents Table 1 (LIWC analysis comparing open and answered questions), Figure 1 (distribution comparisons of word count, fraction of In-Vocabulary words, POS tag diversity, and ROUGE-LCS recall between open and answered questions), Table 2 (examples of open questions across various linguistic activities), and Table 3 (performance of various methods at K = 10, 20, 30, with the first 5 lines for t = 1 month and last 5 lines for t = 3 months).

This paper addresses Prepositional Phrase (PP) attachment disambiguation in English, motivated by NLP applications like Machine Translation where correct preposition attachment is crucial. The authors propose a dual decomposition based algorithm that enforces agreement between parse trees from two languages as a constraint, using alignments from parallel data to correct PP-attachments. Experiments on the English-Hindi language pair showed a 10% performance improvement over the baseline, which used the MSTParser model trained for English.

This section introduces the prepositional phrase (PP) attachment disambiguation problem, illustrating English ambiguity with the examples "I washed the jeans with pockets" (attaching to the noun jeans) and "I washed the jeans with soap" (attaching to the verb washed), and proposes a Dual Decomposition (DD) based algorithm that uses parallel Hindi corpora—where case markers like waali and se resolve attachment—to disambiguate English PP attachments.

This section reviews prior supervised and unsupervised approaches to the PP-attachment problem, including Ratnaparkhi:94's Maximum Entropy Model, Brill:94's transformation-based rule derivation method, Stetina:97's use of a semantic dictionary for word sense disambiguation (WSD), Agirre Agirre:08 and Medimi Medimi:07's WSD-based strategies, Olteanu:05's Support Vector Machines (SVMs) using complex syntactic and semantic features, and Schwartz:03's unsupervised approach using multilingual aligned data transformed into high-level linguistic representations for reattachment decisions.

The section proposes a Dual Decomposition based inference algorithm (rooted in Lagrangian Relaxation) that disambiguates PP-attachment by training separate MSTParser models for English and Hindi and enforcing agreement between the two parse trees via given word alignments, where an edge in one language's parse tree corresponds to a projected edge or path in the other. The problem is formulated as a maximization over parse trees and projected-path scores (computed as the sum of edge scores), solved by alternately fixing one tree and maximizing the other.

This section describes a dual decomposition approach using an iterative Coordinate Descent algorithm (Algorithm 1) that repeatedly calls a Project algorithm (Algorithm 2) until convergence, initializing the English and Hindi parse trees from previously trained MSTParser models. The Project algorithm predicts a target-language parse tree given a source-language tree and word alignments by computing an argmax over parser model parameters and projected path scores, with Lagrangian multipliers initialized to zero and constraints ensuring agreement between projected paths and predicted trees.

This section describes a two-classifier pipeline for predicting the projected path in one language for an edge in the other language, where the first classifier predicts the path length (using five binary perceptrons predicting lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5, with the assumption that projected path lengths are no greater than 5) and the second classifier predicts the path itself (using four structured perceptron classifiers for lengths 2, 3, 4, and 5). Both sets of classifiers were trained on separate annotated data and used the same features: the words and POS tags of the four nodes in the pair of alignments under consideration.

This section describes experiments on prepositional phrase (PP) attachment disambiguation using an MSTParser-based baseline and the paper's bilingual algorithm, trained on Hindi Dependency Treebank (18708 sentences), Penn Treebank (28188 sentences), and the ILCI English-Hindi Tourism parallel corpus (1500 sentences), tested on 100 manually annotated parallel sentences. The baseline achieved 54% PP attachment accuracy (54 correct attachments), while the proposed algorithm improved this by 10% to 64 correct attachments at 30 iterations, though errors from statistical POS taggers and GIZA++ alignments may have caused underperformance.

This section states that the approach achieved 10% accuracy over the baseline on PP-attachment disambiguation but failed to beat the MSTParser model in overall dependency parsing. It identifies future work including testing on a larger dataset and other domains besides Tourism, exploring other languages besides Hindi as aids for PP-attachment disambiguation in English, applying the approach to wh-clause attachment, and analyzing whether using the system's pp-attachments improves machine translation quality.

This section presents dependency parse trees for four example sentences (Figures 1-4), illustrates edge projection from Hindi to English (Figure 6), depicts the optimization problem (Figure 7), and reports test results for English-Hindi parsing (Table 1) alongside a plot of iterations versus correct PP-attachments (Figure 8).

The paper proposes a Tandem Connectionist Encoding Network (TCEN) that bridges the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning in end-to-end speech translation by reusing all subnets in fine-tuning, keeping subnet roles consistent, and pre-training the attention module, along with two methods to ensure consistency between speech encoder outputs and MT encoder inputs in semantic representation and sequence length, achieving a 2.2 BLEU improvement over baselines on a large benchmark dataset.

This section introduces the problem of end-to-end speech translation (ST) and identifies three issues in existing pre-training and fine-tuning approaches—subnet waste, role mismatch, and non-pre-trained attention modules—and proposes a Tandem Connectionist Encoding Network (TCEN) that reuses all pre-trained subnets, maintains role consistency between the speech encoder and text encoder/decoder, and pre-trains the attention module, using CTC-based ASR encoder pre-training, shared projection and word embedding matrices for semantic consistency, and lengthening MT source sentences with word repetitions and blank tokens for length consistency, achieving 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU score improvements over previous methods on the IWSLT18 benchmark for subword-level and character-level decoding, respectively.

This section defines the end-to-end speech translation problem formulation, where an audio piece is converted to acoustic features $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \cdots, x_{T_x})$ and directly translated to a target-language sentence $\mathbf{y^t}$ without generating intermediate transcriptions $\mathbf{y^s}$. It introduces the ASR dataset $\mathcal{A}$, MT dataset $\mathcal{M}$, and ST dataset $\mathcal{S}$ that are assumed available, and states the goal of learning an end-to-end model to generate translations without intermediate results.

path: Multi-Task Learning and Pre-training for ST
context: The section describes three popular multi-task strategies for ST: one-to-many (shared speech encoder between ASR and ST), many-to-one (shared decoder between MT and ST), and many-to-many (shared encoder and decoder). The many-to-many model contains two encoders, two decoders, and three task-specific attentions, and is usually pre-trained on ASR and MT tasks (since $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ are much larger than $\mathcal{S}$) then fine-tuned with multi-task learning, but this method suffers from subnet waste, role mismatch, and non-pre-trained attention issues that limit end-to-end ST performance.

This section introduces the TCEN architecture, which consists of two encoders connected in tandem and one decoder with an attention module, along with the pre-training and fine-tuning strategy for TCEN, and proposes solutions for the semantic and length inconsistency problems caused by multi-task learning.

This section describes the TCEN architecture, which uses a speech encoder $enc_s$ (CNN-BiLSTM with two convolutional layers, max-pooling downsampling by a factor of four, and five bidirectional $d$-dimensional LSTM layers producing $\mathbf{h}^s$), a text encoder $enc_t$ (two bidirectional LSTM layers producing $\mathbf{h}^t$), and a decoder $dec$ (two unidirectional LSTM layers with additive attention $att$) to predict target sequences. The two encoders disentangle acoustic and linguistic feature extraction, enabling knowledge from ASR and MT tasks to be leveraged for ST training, with every module usable in both pre-training and fine-tuning to avoid subnet waste.

The section states that the training procedure is split into pre-training and fine-tuning stages, where in pre-training the speech encoder $enc_s$ is trained toward the CTC objective using dataset $\mathcal{A}$ while the text encoder $enc_t$ and decoder $dec$ are trained on the MT dataset $\mathcal{M}$, and in fine-tuning the model is jointly trained on the ASR, MT, and ST tasks.

In the pre-training stage, the model is trained on a CTC-based ASR task, where the speech encoder $enc_s$ generates subword representations using a CTC loss that maximizes the probability of the golden source transcription $\mathbf {y}^s$ by summing over all legal CTC paths $\Phi _T(y)$, and on an MT task using cross-entropy loss, where $\mathbf {y^s}$ is converted to embeddings $\mathbf {e^s}$ via embedding layer $W_{E^s}$ and processed by $enc_t$ to produce $\mathbf {h^t}$ for the decoder.

In the fine-tune stage, the model is jointly updated on ASR, MT, and ST tasks, where for ST the source encoder $enc_s$ generates $\mathbf{h^s}$ from input $\mathbf{x}$, the target encoder $enc_t$ learns high-level linguistic knowledge into $\mathbf{h^t}$, and the decoder $dec$ predicts the target sentence using the ST loss function. Following the multi-task update strategy of luong2015multi (BIBREF11), a different training ratio $\alpha_i$ is allocated to each task, and tasks are selected randomly with probability $\frac{\alpha_i}{\sum_j \alpha_j}$.

This section addresses the semantic and length inconsistencies that arise because the text encoder consumes $\mathbf{e^s}$ during MT training but accepts $\mathbf{h^s}$ during ST training, and proposes two countermeasures: sharing weights between the CTC classification layer and the source-end word embedding layer during ASR and MT training to keep $\mathbf{e^s}$ and $\mathbf{h^s}$ in the same space, and feeding the text encoder source sentences in the format of CTC paths generated from a seq2seq model to make it more robust toward long inputs.

This section describes a semantic consistency regularization technique that shares the weight $W_{ctc}$ in the CTC classification layer with the source embedding weights $W_{E^s}$ (i.e., $W_{ctc} = W_{E^s}$), so that the CTC loss computes $p(\pi _t=w_i|\mathbf {x})$ by normalizing the product of the hidden vector $h_t^s$ and the $i$-th vector in $W_{E^s}$, thereby closing the distance between $h^s_t$ and the golden embedding vector to encourage $\mathbf {h}^s$ to have the same distribution as $\mathbf {e}^s$ and bridge the space gap between the two latent spaces.

To address length inconsistency between the longer input frames $\mathbf{x}$ and the shorter $\mathbf{e^s}$, the authors train a CTC ASR model on dataset $\mathcal{A}=\{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}^s_i)\}_{i=0}^{I}$ and generate CTC-paths $\mathbf{\pi}_i$ via greedy decoding, then apply a reversible operation $S(\cdot)$ that converts each path $\mathbf{\pi}$ into unique tokens $\mathbf{u}$ and repetition times $\mathbf{l}$ (with $S^{-1}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{l})=\mathbf{\pi}$) to build dataset $\mathcal{P}=\{(\mathbf{y}^s_i,\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{l}_i)\}_{i=0}^{I}$; a seq2seq model (Figure FIGREF2

This section describes experiments conducted on the IWSLT18 speech translation task, where the authors reproduce several competitive baselines based on ESPnet to enable a fair comparison, addressing the fact that IWSLT participants use different data pre-processing methods.

This section describes the datasets used in the experiments: the ST-TED speech translation corpus (272 hours, 171k segments, with 2k dev segments and tst2010/2013/2014/2015 as test sets), the TED-LIUM2 speech recognition corpus (207 hours, 93k sentences), and text translation data from ST-TED, WIT3 (130k and 200k pairs), and WMT2018 (41M pairs). It details data preprocessing steps including feature extraction (80-channel log-Mel filter bank plus 3-dimensional pitch features, yielding 83-dimensional inputs), speed perturbation, lowercasing and punctuation removal, and word/character-level tokenization with a 5k sentencepiece vocabulary, and specifies evaluation using lowercase BLEU after LIUM SpkDiarization and MWER segmentation.

This section describes the baseline models used for comparison, including a vanilla ST baseline, three pre-training baselines (encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder pre-training), three multi-task baselines (one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many settings), and a many-to-many+pre-training baseline, along with the Triangle multi-task strategy from BIBREF18. It specifies implementation details using ESPnet with RNN size $d=1024$, dropout of 0.3, Adadelta with initial learning rate 1.0 for up to 10 epochs, and testing with beam size 10 and length normalization weight 0.2.

Table 2 reports results on four test sets and their average, showing that the proposed method outperforms the strong `many-to-many+pretrain' baseline by 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU scores. The paper finds that pre-training settings (2nd-4th rows) are more effective than multi-task settings (5th-8th rows), observes performance degradation in the `triangle+pretrain' baseline because its ASR decoder only provides lower word-level linguistic information and cannot utilize large-scale MT data, and notes that char-level models outperform subword-level models in all settings—especially the vanilla baseline—because aligning speech frames with subword units in another language is notoriously difficult, while the proposed method brings more gains in the subword setting since it excels at learning text-to-text and subword-level alignments.

This ablation study on subword-level experiments (Table TABREF37) demonstrates that both weight sharing between the CTC classification layer and source embedding layer and using noisy MT input benefit final translation quality, with weight sharing contributing more due to semantic consistency, and that removing the pre-training stage causes a dramatic BLEU score decrease, indicating pre-training is indispensable for end-to-end speech translation.

The section explains that TCEN achieves a higher final result due to a better start-point in fine-tuning, as shown by the learning curves of subword accuracy on the validation set (Figure FIGREF39). While the vanilla model starts at low accuracy because its networks are not pre-trained on ASR and MT data, TCEN and 'many-to-many+pretrain' show similar trends, with TCEN outperforming the latter by about five points throughout fine-tuning, indicating the gain comes from bridging the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning rather than a better fine-tuning process.

The section compares the end-to-end model with cascaded systems built by combining the ASR and MT models used in the pre-training baseline, including a cascaded+re-seg variant that uses a seq2seq model to add sentence boundaries and punctuation to ASR outputs. Results show the end-to-end model outperforms the simple cascaded system by over 2 BLEU scores and achieves comparable performance to the cascaded model with re-segmentation.

This section reviews prior speech translation (ST) approaches, contrasting early pipeline systems that feed ASR lattices (HMM, DenseNet, TDNN) into MT models (attention RNNs, Transformers) with recent end-to-end methods that skip source transcription to avoid error propagation and high latency. It notes strategies to address scarce ST data—pre-training, multi-task learning, curriculum learning, attention-passing, and knowledge distillation—and highlights that while prior work consumes only ASR and ST data, the authors' work sufficiently utilizes large-scale MT data to capture rich semantic knowledge.

This conclusion states that the paper investigated the end-to-end method for speech translation (ST), discussed why there is a huge gap between pre-training and fine-tuning in previous methods, and proposed a method capable of reusing every sub-net and keeping the role of sub-net consistent between pre-training and fine-tuning, with empirical studies demonstrating that their model significantly outperforms baselines.

This section presents the paper's figures and tables, including model architectures for multi-task learning, the seq2seq end-to-end speech translation model, and CTC path decoding, alongside BLEU score results on the IWSLT-18 dataset (averaging tst2010, tst2013, tst2014 and tst2015), ablation studies for subword-level experiments, comparisons of cascaded versus end-to-end results with resegmented ASR outputs, and fine-tuning learning curves.

This abstract states that the authors analyze the geometry of contextualized word representations from ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2 by measuring isotropy, cosine similarity, self-similarity, and variance explained by static embeddings. They find that representations are not isotropic in any layer, that self-similarity for the same word decreases in upper layers (indicating more context-specific representations), and that less than 5% of the variance in contextualized representations can be explained by static embeddings.

This section studies the geometry of the representation space for each layer of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2, finding that contextualized word representations are anisotropic (occupying a narrow cone rather than being isotropic, with GPT-2's last layer so extreme that two random words have almost perfect cosine similarity), that same words in different contexts have non-identical representations that grow more dissimilar in upper layers, that context-specificity manifests differently across models (ELMo representations grow more similar, BERT's become more dissimilar but remain more similar than random words, and GPT-2's show no more similarity than random words), and that after adjusting for anisotropy less than 5% of the variance in a word's representations is explained by its first principal component—suggesting representations do not correspond to a finite number of word senses, though static embeddings from the first principal component still outperform GloVe and FastText on word vector benchmarks.

Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) and GloVe are among the best known models for generating static word embeddings, and although they learn embeddings iteratively, they both implicitly factorize a word-context matrix containing a co-occurrence statistic; because they create a single representation for each word, all senses of a polysemous word must share a single vector.

This section introduces contextualized word representations, describing ELMo (a 2-layer biLSTM), BERT (a 12-layer bidirectional transformer, base, cased), and GPT-2 (a 12-layer uni-directional transformer) as deep neural language models fine-tuned for downstream NLP tasks, noting that BERT achieves state-of-the-art performance on tasks ranging from question-answering to sentiment analysis.

This section describes probing tasks, which train linear models to predict syntactic (e.g., part-of-speech tags) and semantic (e.g., word relations) properties of words, based on the premise that if a linear model can accurately predict a linguistic property, the representations implicitly encode it. While these analyses show that contextualized representations encode semantic and syntactic information, they cannot determine how contextual these representations are or the extent to which they could be replaced with static word embeddings, making this work more similar to the study of static word embedding space geometry (BIBREF13).

The authors study ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2 as their contextualizing models, choosing the base cased version of BERT because it is most comparable to GPT-2 with respect to number of layers and dimensionality. All three models are pre-trained on their respective language modelling tasks and have 2, 12, and 12 hidden layers respectively, with the input layer of each model included as its 0th layer since it is not contextualized and serves as a useful baseline against which to compare the contextualization done by subsequent layers.

This section describes the data used to analyze contextualized word representations: the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity tasks from 2012-2016, chosen because they contain the same words appearing in different contexts (e.g., "dog" in "A panda dog is running on the road." versus "A dog is trying to get bacon off his back."). Words are mapped to the list of sentences they appear in and their index within those sentences, with words appearing in fewer than 5 unique contexts excluded from the analysis.

This section states that the authors measure how contextual a word representation is using three different metrics: self-similarity, intra-sentence similarity, and maximum explainable variance, which they apply to compare the geometry of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 embeddings.

The section defines $\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w)$ as the average cosine similarity between the representations of a word $w$ across its $n$ unique contexts in layer $\ell$ of model $f$, where $f_{\ell}(s,i)$ maps $s[i]$ to its representation in layer $\ell$; it notes that $\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) = 1$ when representations are identical across all contexts (no contextualization), and that more contextualized representations yield lower self-similarity.

This section defines the intra-sentence similarity measure, $\textit{IntraSim}_\ell(s)$, which computes the average cosine similarity between a sentence's word representations and the sentence vector (the mean of those word vectors) in layer $\ell$ of a model. It explains that this measure captures how context-specificity manifests in the vector space: low values of both $\textit{IntraSim}_\ell(s)$ and $\textit{SelfSim}_\ell(w)$ indicate nuanced contextualization where words receive distinct context-specific representations, while high $\textit{IntraSim}_\ell(s)$ with low $\textit{SelfSim}_\ell(w)$ suggests less nuanced contextualization where words simply converge in vector space.

This section defines the Maximum Explainable Variance (MEV) as a measure of contextuality, where for a word $w$ appearing in sentences $\lbrace s_1, ..., s_n \rbrace$ at indices $\lbrace i_1, ..., i_n \rbrace$, the occurrence matrix $[ f_{\ell }(s_1, i_1) ... f_{\ell }(s_n, i_n) ]$ is formed from the word's representations in layer $\ell$ of model $f$, and $\textit{MEV}_\ell(w)$ is the proportion of variance explained by the first principal component (derived from the first $m$ singular values $\sigma_1 ... \sigma_m$), providing an upper bound on how well a static embedding could replace the word's contextualized representations—where values closer to 0 indicate poorer static replacement and $\textit{MEV}_\ell(w) = 1$ indicates a perfect replacement.

This section explains that the authors adjust their contextuality measures for anisotropy by subtracting three anisotropic baselines—one for each contextuality measure: the average cosine similarity between representations of randomly sampled words from different contexts for self-similarity and intra-sentence similarity, and the proportion of variance explained by the first principal component for maximum explainable variance (MEV)—calculated separately for each layer, with both raw measures and baselines estimated using 1K uniformly randomly sampled word representations.

path: Contextualized representations are anisotropic in all non-input layers.
context: This section explains that contextualized word representations are anisotropic (directionally non-uniform) in all non-input layers of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2, meaning the word representations occupy a narrow cone in vector space rather than being uniform in all directions. Anisotropy is measured by the average cosine similarity between randomly sampled words (0 if isotropic, closer to 1 if more anisotropic), and the only exception is ELMo's input layer, which produces static character-level embeddings without contextual or positional information; notably, not all static embeddings are isotropic, as skipgram embeddings are also static but not isotropic.

path: Contextualized representations are generally more anisotropic in higher layers.
context: This section states that contextualized word representations are generally more anisotropic in higher layers, with GPT-2 showing average cosine similarity between randomly chosen words of roughly 0.6 in layers 2 through 8, increasing exponentially from layers 8 through 12 until any two words have an almost perfect cosine similarity in the last layer; this pattern holds for BERT and ELMo as well, though BERT's penultimate layer is much more anisotropic than its final layer, and since all three models' hidden layer representations are almost all more anisotropic than their context-free input layer representations, high anisotropy appears inherent to or a by-product of contextualization.

path: Contextualized word representations are more context-specific in higher layers.
context: Using Definition 1's measure of self-similarity (the average cosine similarity between a word's representations in different contexts within a given layer, adjusted for anisotropy, where 1 means not context-specific and 0 means maximally context-specific), the authors plot the average self-similarity of uniformly randomly sampled words across layers of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 (Figure FIGREF24), finding that in all three models higher layers have lower self-similarity and are thus more context-specific—consistent with lower layers capturing generic features and upper layers capturing class- or task-specific features—though GPT-2 representations are the most context-specific, with its last layer being almost maximally context-specific.

path: Stopwords (e.g., `the', `of', `to') have among the most context-specific representations.
context: Using self-similarity as a metric, the section finds that stopwords (e.g., `the', `of', `to') have among the lowest self-similarity and thus the most context-specific representations across all layers of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2, with ELMo's lowest average self-similarity words being `and', `of', `'s', `the', and `to'; this variation occurs despite stopwords not being polysemous, indicating that the variety of contexts a word appears in—rather than its inherent polysemy—drives variation in contextualized representations, showing that these models do not simply assign one of a finite number of word-sense representations to each word.

path: Context-specificity manifests very differently in ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2.
context: The section measures intra-sentence similarity—the average cosine similarity between each word representation and their mean, adjusted for anisotropy—to investigate how increased context-specificity manifests in the vector space of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2. Plotting the average intra-sentence similarity of 500 uniformly randomly sampled sentences (Figure FIGREF25), they find that context-specificity manifests very differently across the three models.

path: In ELMo, words in the same sentence are more similar to one another in upper layers.
context: The section states that as ELMo word representations become more context-specific in upper layers, the intra-sentence similarity between words in the same sentence rises, suggesting that ELMo extends Firth's distributional hypothesis to the sentence level by making contextualized representations of words sharing the same sentence context more similar.

path: In BERT, words in the same sentence are more dissimilar to one another in upper layers.
context: In BERT, as word representations become more context-specific in upper layers, words in the same sentence drift away from one another and become more dissimilar (with exceptions such as layer 12 in Figure FIGREF25), yet in all layers the average similarity between words in the same sentence remains greater than the anisotropy baseline (the average similarity between randomly chosen words); this indicates a more nuanced contextualization than in ELMo, in which BERT recognizes that although the surrounding sentence informs a word's meaning, two words in the same sentence do not necessarily share a similar meaning simply because they share the same context.

path: In GPT-2, word representations in the same sentence are no more similar to each other than randomly sampled words.
context: The section reports that in GPT-2, the unadjusted intra-sentence similarity is roughly equal to the anisotropic baseline, so the anisotropy-adjusted intra-sentence similarity is close to 0 in most layers (and highest in the non-contextualizing input layer), in contrast to ELMo and BERT, where average intra-sentence similarity exceeds 0.20 in all but one layer; this indicates that high intra-sentence similarity is not inherent to contextualization, though whether these differences trace back to model architecture is left as future work.

path: On average, less than 5% of the variance in a word's contextualized representations can be explained by a static embedding.
context: This section states that the maximum explainable variance (MEV)—the proportion of variance in a word's contextualized representations explained by their first principal component, adjusted for anisotropy by subtracting the proportion explained by the first principal component of uniformly randomly sampled word representations—never exceeds 5% on average in any layer of ELMo, BERT, or GPT-2, indicating that a static embedding cannot replace contextualized representations and suggesting that contextualizing models do not simply assign one of a finite number of word-sense representations; the 5% threshold represents a best-case scenario with no guarantee that embeddings like GloVe would approximate the static embedding maximizing MEV, and while the average raw MEV is below 5% for all layers of ELMo and BERT, it is around 30% for GPT-2 layers 2 to 11 due to extremely high anisotropy.

path: Principal components of contextualized representations in lower layers outperform GloVe and FastText on many benchmarks.
context: This section describes creating static embeddings by taking the first principal component (PC) of contextualized representations in each layer, then evaluating them on semantic similarity (SimLex999, MEN, WS353, RW, SemEval-2012), analogy solving (Google analogy solving, MSR analogy solving), and concept categorization (BLESS, AP). The best-performing PC static embeddings belong to the first layer of BERT, though other layers of BERT and ELMo also outperform GloVe and FastText on most benchmarks; for all three contextualizing models, PCs from lower layers are more effective than those from upper layers, and GPT-2's PCs perform markedly worse than ELMo's and BERT's, suggesting that PCs of highly context-specific representations are less effective on traditional benchmarks.

This Future Work section proposes two directions: first, adding an anisotropy penalty to the language modelling objective to make contextualized representations more isotropic, motivated by BIBREF6's finding that subtracting the mean from static embeddings to make them more isotropic yields large downstream performance improvements; second, extracting static word representations from contextualized models, which are easier to deploy than large models like BERT, with section 4.3 suggesting these extracted vectors perform much better than traditional static embeddings such as GloVe and FastText across a diverse array of tasks.

This conclusion states that upper layers of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2 produce more context-specific representations than lower layers, with increased context-specificity always accompanied by increased anisotropy, though context-specificity manifests differently across models (highest anisotropy-adjusted similarity for words in the same sentence in ELMo, almost non-existent in GPT-2); after adjusting for anisotropy, less than 5% of the variance in a word's contextualized representations could be explained by a static embedding, meaning static word embeddings would be a poor replacement for contextualized ones in all layers of all models.
