This section presents figures and tables characterizing the geometry of contextualized word representations in BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 using statistics such as anisotropy (non-zero average cosine similarity between randomly sampled words), self-similarity, intra-sentence similarity, and maximum explainable variance (MEV), all adjusted for anisotropy. The findings show that representations are generally anisotropic and more so in higher layers, that self-similarity decreases and context-specificity increases in higher layers, that intra-sentence similarity manifests very differently across the three models, and that no more than 5% of a word's contextualized variance can be explained by a static embedding, while ELMo- and BERT-based static embeddings often outperform GloVe and FastText on word embedding benchmark tasks.

The paper addresses cross-domain sentiment classification by minimizing the distance between source and target instances in an embedded feature space, then leveraging unlabeled target data through semi-supervised learning with two regularizations—entropy minimization and self-ensemble bootstrapping—for classifier refinement. Experimental results demonstrate the approach better leverages target-domain unlabeled data and achieves substantial improvements over baseline methods across various experimental settings.

This introduction states that cross-domain sentiment classification transfers knowledge from a labeled source domain to a target domain with few or no labels, but existing pivot-feature techniques depend on heuristic pivot selection and only use unlabeled target data for representation learning while training the classifier solely on the source domain. To address these limitations, the authors propose a novel Domain Adaptive Semi-supervised learning framework (DAS) that jointly performs feature adaptation—explicitly minimizing the distance between encoded representations of the two domains—and semi-supervised learning via entropy minimization and self-ensemble bootstrapping to exploit unlabeled target data for classifier refinement, and they evaluate the method under multiple experimental settings considering label distribution and corpus size, reporting significant improvements over strong baselines.

This Related Work section reviews prior approaches to domain adaptation and semi-supervised learning, covering structural correspondence learning (SCL) with pivot feature prediction, pivot-based feature alignment methods, neural network-based pivot feature prediction with auxiliary tasks using real-valued word embeddings (which showed substantial improvement over SCL), and denoising autoencoders for feature adaptation; it contrasts these with explicit distribution-distance objectives such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and adversarial training frameworks with a domain discriminator, and describes treating domain adaptation as a semi-supervised task using entropy minimization and self-ensemble bootstrapping as regularizations, with experimental results showing both methods are effective when jointly trained with the feature adaptation objective.

This section defines the notations and model overview, describing an unsupervised domain adaptation setting where a neural-based feature encoder (parameterized by INLINEFORM1) maps documents from source and target domains into a shared feature space, combined with a softmax classifier (parameterized by INLINEFORM3). It states that the objective simultaneously considers three factors: minimizing classification error on labeled source examples via cross entropy loss, minimizing domain discrepancy, and leveraging unlabeled data through semi-supervised learning, with additional results presented for a setting using a small number of labeled target examples.

This section describes a feature adaptation approach that minimizes the distance between source and target feature representations by estimating distribution distance as the distance between sample means in the embedding space, rather than aligning domain-specific words through pivot words. The feature adaptation loss uses normalization to rescale vectors so entries sum to 1, combined with a symmetric KL divergence as the distance function, and the authors find this approximation performs comparably to Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) while avoiding the characteristic kernel mapping procedure.

This section describes the Domain Adaptive Semi-supervised Learning (DAS) framework, which exploits target data through semi-supervised learning objectives jointly trained with the main model. It employs two methods to estimate unknown target labels: entropy minimization, which minimizes an entropy penalty to maximize prediction confidence and increase margins between target examples and decision boundaries, and self-ensemble bootstrapping, which estimates labels via ensemble predictions from different training epochs to ensure prediction consistency and serve as regularization. The overall DAS framework (Algorithm SECREF6) jointly trains these losses, using weight parameters to balance their effects, a Gaussian curve to ramp up the bootstrapping loss slowly at the beginning of training, and an exponentially weighted average of recent epochs (with larger weights to recent epochs) to generate estimated one-hot labels, yielding the best results when both methods are jointly employed.

This section describes the CNN encoder used as the feature encoder, adopting a one-layer CNN structure from previous works (BIBREF22, BIBREF4) that has proven effective for sentiment classification. Given a review document of N words, each word is embedded via a continuous word embedding from an embedding matrix W (where V is vocabulary size and d is embedding dimension), jointly updated during training; a convolution layer concatenates dense word embeddings into a vector of length d·k, applies a weight-shared parameter set C with element-wise non-linear activation f to capture local contextual dependencies (producing features similar to n-grams), and a max-over-time pooling layer yields the final document representation.

This section describes the construction of new small-scale datasets (Book, Electronics, Beauty, Music) derived from the large-scale Amazon dataset by McAuley et al., each containing a balanced set 1 (6000 instances) and a real-life-distribution set 2 (6000 instances), along with large-scale datasets (IMDB, Yelp2014, Cell Phone, Baby), and specifies two transductive unsupervised domain adaptation settings for evaluating the max-margin-based semi-supervised method.

This section explains that, since no labeled target data is available during training, the authors sample 1000 examples from the source domain's training set as the development set to select the model with the minimum classification error, and they tune the hyper-parameters INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 on a target domain development set for one problem (e.g., E INLINEFORM4 BK) while fixing their values for the other problems.

This section describes the training configuration, including initializing word embeddings with 300-dimension GloVe vectors and using a top-10000 vocabulary, configuring the CNN encoder (window size 3, hidden layer size 300, ReLU activation, dropout probability 0.5, and weight L2-norm max norm of 3) following previous works. It specifies hyper-parameters such as INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 set to 200 and 1 on small-scale datasets and the Amazon benchmark (tuned on task E's development set under setting 1), and INLINEFORM3 and INLINEFORM4 set to 500 and 0.2 on large-scale datasets (tuned on INLINEFORM5 Y), along with a Gaussian ramp-up of the bootstrapping loss weight, 30 training epochs, batch sizes of 50 and 250, and the RMSProp optimizer with a learning rate of 0.
This section describes the baselines used for comparison: Naive (bag-of-words SVM), mSDA, NaiveNN, AuxNN, ADAN, and MMD, along with variants of the proposed DAS model (DAS-EM, DAS-SE, and FANN).

This section reports main results on the small-scale dataset (using classification accuracy) and large-scale dataset (using macro-F1 due to extremely unbalanced test label distribution), comparing the proposed DAS-EM, DAS-SE, and full DAS models against feature-adaptation-only methods ADAN, MDD, and FANN, finding that DAS methods generally outperform them with DAS achieving the best performance when both techniques are jointly employed; it notes that all domain-adaptive methods perform better under setting 1 (balanced target classes) but argues setting 2 and the large-scale dataset better reflect real-life sentiment distributions, observes that word-embeddings substantially help (NaiveNN outperforming mSDA), and finds that semi-supervised learning alone (with feature adaptation eliminated) performs very badly—entropy minimization giving below-0.4 accuracy and bootstrapping underperforming NaiveNN—demonstrating that feature adaptation is essential.

This section analyzes how accuracy changes with the percentage of unlabeled data used for training (Figure FIGREF23, setting 1) and with the number of labeled target examples added (Figure FIGREF27), comparing the proposed DAS method against NaiveNN and other methods using accuracy as the metric. It finds that DAS shows a nonlinear increasing trend—accuracy quickly improving initially and then stabilizing—demonstrating it better exploits unlabeled data than other methods, whose trends are less obvious and sometimes worsen with more unlabeled data, while DAS remains more effective with few labeled target examples, though performance differences decrease as the number of labeled target examples increases.

This section analyzes sentiment-related CNN filters learned by NaiveNN, FANN, and DAS on task E (E↔BT) under setting 1, identifying the top 10 most related filters per sentiment label based on output-layer weights and representing each filter (window size 3, ReLU activation) as a ranked list of trigrams. The analysis finds that all three methods capture similar expressions on the source domain (including domain-invariant and domain-specific trigrams), but DAS learns more domain-adaptive filters that capture diverse target-specific sentiment expressions, whereas NaiveNN barely captures target-specific expressions and FANN captures only limited ones such as "clean" and "scent."

The conclusion states that the authors proposed DAS, a novel framework that jointly performs feature adaptation and semi-supervised learning, and demonstrated through multiple experiments that DAS better leverages unlabeled data and achieves substantial improvements over baseline methods. It also found that feature adaptation is an essential component, without which semi-supervised learning cannot function properly, and noted that the framework could potentially be adapted to other domain adaptation tasks as the focus of future studies.

This section describes the experimental setup on the Amazon benchmark dataset (Blitzer et al.), which contains four domains (Book, DVDs, Electronics, Kitchen), each with 1000 positive and 1000 negative reviews, plus 4000 balanced unlabeled reviews for both source and target domains. It details the construction of 12 cross-domain binary sentiment classification tasks, where labeled data is split into 1600 training and 400 test reviews, the classifier is trained on the source domain's training set and evaluated on the target domain's test set, and the comparison results are presented in Table TABREF37.

This section states that due to space limitations, only figures are shown in the paper, with all numerical data used for plotting Figure FIGREF17 presented in Table TABREF38. It reports that DAS-EM, DAS-SE, and DAS all achieve substantial improvements over baseline methods under different settings.

This section presents the CNN filter analysis comparing NaiveNN, FANN, and DAS, where for each method the top 10 most related filters for positive, negative, and neutral sentiment labels are identified and represented as ranked lists of trigrams with the highest activation values. Tables TABREF39, TABREF40, and TABREF41 show the trigrams from the target domain (beauty) captured by these filters learned on E INLINEFORM0 BT, and the findings indicate that DAS captures a more diverse set of relevant sentiment expressions on the target domain for each sentiment label compared to NaiveNN and FANN, because DAS refines the classifier on the target domain with semi-supervised learning, forcing the encoder to learn representations that are both domain-invariant and discriminative on both domains.

This section presents the paper's datasets, performance comparisons, and CNN filter analyses. It reports accuracy results across datasets (including the Amazon benchmark and beauty target domain), compares the proposed methods DAS, DAS-EM, and DAS-SE against baselines using one-tailed unpaired t-tests (p < 0.05), and examines trigrams captured by positive-, negative-, and neutral-sentiment-related CNN filters learned on E→BT.

This section proposes a Ghost-VLAD pooling strategy that aggregates local frame level features across time to generate utterance level feature vectors for variable length audio, achieving 98.43% F1-score and outperforming the previous state of the art x-vector method by an absolute improvement of 1.88% in F1-score on 635Hrs of audio data for 7 Indian languages.

This section introduces the language identification task, reviewing prior approaches including i-vectors with GMM-UBM models, deep learning methods such as stacked bottleneck features (Pavel Matejka et al.), frame-level DNNs (I. Lopez-Moreno et al.), LSTM models (J. Gonzalez-Dominguez et al.), CNNs (Alicia et al.), TDNNs with bottleneck features (Daniel Garcia-Romero et al.), and X-vectors (David Snyder et al.), then proposes Ghost-VLAD pooling—inspired by W. Xie et al. [9] and Y. Zhong et al. [10]—and compares it with NetVLAD, average pooling, and statistics pooling, reporting a best accuracy of 98.24% on 635 hours of audio data covering 7 Indian languages from the All India Radio news channel.

This section explains that pooling strategies aggregate frame-level representations into compact, linearly separable utterance-level features for language identification, and it describes the specific pooling methods used—NetVLAD, Ghost-VLAD, Statistic pooling, and Average pooling—with GhostVLAD pooling applied to aggregate local descriptors extracted from ResNet into the global utterance-level feature.

This section describes the NetVLAD pooling strategy, an extension of the VLAD approach that replaces hard assignment based clustering with soft assignment based clustering to enable end-to-end neural network training. The NetVLAD layer maps N local features of dimension D into a fixed dimensional vector by taking N feature vectors and computing a matrix V of dimension KxD, where K is the number of clusters and D is the feature vector dimension, using trainable parameters $w_k$, $b_k$ and $c_k$ for each cluster k, where the first term corresponds to the soft assignment of input $x_i$ to cluster $c_k$ and the second term corresponds to the residual term indicating how far the input descriptor $x_i$ is from the cluster center $c_k$.

This section describes GhostVLAD pooling, an extension of NetVLAD that adds G ghost clusters (typically 2-4) alongside the K normal clusters, resulting in K+G total clusters. The ghost clusters absorb noisy or irrelevant content by receiving most of the weight during aggregation while being excluded from the V matrix concatenation, so that normal VLAD clusters are assigned less weight to noisy features; the resulting concatenated features are then fed into a projection layer followed by softmax to predict the language label.

This section describes two pooling strategies: statistic pooling, which computes first- and second-order statistics (mean and standard deviation) of the local features from the top layer of the ResNet model, unfolds the 3-D feature map into N features of D dimensions, concatenates the resulting two D-dimensional vectors, and feeds them to a projection layer for language label prediction; and average pooling, which computes only the first-order statistic (mean) of the local features from the top layer of the CNN model, producing a single D-dimensional representation that is fed to the projection layer followed by softmax for language label prediction.

This section describes the dataset collection process, in which the authors gathered and curated approximately 635 hours of audio data for seven Indian languages (Kannada, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam, Bengali, and English—though only six are listed) from the All India Radio news channel, crawling data from 2010 to 2019. They segmented the long audio clips into smaller chunks using a Voice activity detector and removed music segments using an Inhouse music detection model, resulting in 635 hours of clean audio divided into 520 hours of training data (165K utterances) and 115 hours of testing data (35K utterances), with per-language breakdowns shown in a table.

This section describes the feature extraction process (257-dimensional spectral features with 512-point FFT, 25ms window, 10ms frame shift, random 5sec cropping producing 257x500 spectrograms) and the Ghost-VLAD pooling network architecture using ResNet-34 to map inputs into a 1x32x512 feature cube converted to 2D 32x512 for the Ghost-VLAD/NetVLAD layer, trained with Adam optimizer (initial learning rate 0.01, final 0.00001) for 15 epochs with early stopping. It also details the baseline methods compared—i-vector+svm (GMM-UBM), tdnn+stat-pool (7-layer TDNN with statistic-pooling), and LSTM+stat-pool (3-layer Bi-LSTM with 256 hidden units)—implemented using Kaldi

This section compares the performance of the Ghost-VLAD pooling system with recent state-of-the-art language identification approaches, compares different pooling strategies, and compares the robustness of the system to the length of the input spectrogram during training. It visualizes the embeddings generated by the GhostVLAD method and concludes that the GhostVLAD embeddings show very good feature discrimination capabilities.

This section compares the authors' Ghost-VLAD pooling system against previous state-of-the-art language identification approaches, specifically the i-vector+svm system (trained using GMM-UBM models to generate i-vectors as proposed in [1]) and the TDNN+stat-pool x-vector system (proposed by David Snyder et al. [11]). The authors report that their method outperforms the x-vector system by an absolute 1.88% improvement in F1-score, as shown in Table 2.

The section compares different pooling strategies for the language identification task using ResNet as the base feature extraction network, keeping the base network constant while varying only the pooling layers. It reports that GhostVLAD pooling outperforms all other pooling methods by achieving a 98.43% F1-Score, as shown in Table 3.

The section describes experiments training the Ghost-VLAD pooling model on 2sec, 3sec, 4sec, and 5sec spectrograms containing 200, 300, 400, and 500 frames respectively, using ResNet as the base feature extractor requiring fixed-length spectrograms, with findings showing the model trained with a 5sec spectrogram achieved the best performance as shown in Table 4.

The section describes visualizing the 512-dimensional embeddings generated by their approach for testing data, which were dimensionality-reduced using t-SNE projection to produce the t-SNE plot shown in Figure 3, demonstrating that the learned embeddings have very good discriminative properties.

This conclusion states that the authors used the Ghost-VLAD pooling approach, originally proposed for face recognition, to improve language identification performance for 7 Indian languages, using 630 hours of audio data collected and curated from the All India Radio news channel. Their experimental results show their approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by an absolute 1.88% F1-score, that GhostVLAD pooling turns out to be the best approach for aggregating frame-level features into a single utterance-level feature compared to other pooling strategies, that their approach works much better even when training input contains smaller durations, and that the embeddings generated have very good language discriminative features that help improve language identification performance.

This section presents the NetVLAD and GhostVLAD architectures (Fig. 1), the dataset used (Table 1), F1-scores for different spectrogram input sizes (Table 4), comparisons with previous methods (Table 2) and different pooling methods (Table 3), and a t-SNE plot of embeddings (Fig. 2).

This abstract states that the paper conducts a systematic study of back-translation in Neural Machine Translation, comparing alternative uses of monolingual target data and multiple data generation procedures. The findings confirm that back-translation is very effective and provide new explanations for why, while also introducing new data simulation techniques that are almost as effective yet much cheaper to implement than back-translation.

This introduction explains that data-hungry Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems underutilize available monolingual and parallel data, especially in domain adaptation, and reviews backward translation (BT) as the most successful current technique, noting its high computational cost and the unresolved question of the right amount and quality of BT data. The paper aims to understand BT's strengths and weaknesses by investigating whether data quality matters, whether BT acts as a regularizer, whether it can be efficiently simulated, how it relates to target-side language modeling, and how its effects can be separated from additional training data, using reimplemented strategies and experiments on two language pairs in a controlled setting.

This section describes the training scenario of using a large out-of-domain parallel corpus with limited monolingual in-domain data, focusing on the Europarl domain for English-German and English-French translation directions, using the Europarl corpus as in-domain data and evaluating on Europarl tests from 2007 and 2008 (with 2006 for development) and WMT newstest 2014 for out-of-domain performance.

This section describes the baseline NMT system, which implements the attentional encoder-decoder approach in Nematus on 4 million out-of-domain parallel sentences using French (News-Commentary-11, Wikipedia from WMT 2014, Multi-UN, EU-Bookshop) and German (News-Commentary-11, Rapid, Common-Crawl WMT 2017, Multi-UN) corpora, with 50k BPE merge operations yielding vocabularies of about 32k/36k for French and 32k/44k for English-German. Both systems use 512-dimensional word embeddings and a single hidden layer with 1024 cells, optimized with Adam and early stopped, training for about three weeks on an Nvidia K80 GPU. The section also details back-translation system training (using the same out-of-domain corpus with swapped source/target sides) and a "fine

path: Using artificial parallel data in NMT
context: This section explores using monolingual data in MT by converting it into synthetic parallel data and training the model as usual, and it first reproduces the results of BIBREF2 using back-translation (BT) of various qualities, which are then analyzed thoroughly.

This section investigates how the quality of the back-translation (BT) system affects NMT performance, comparing three reverse-direction MT systems—backtrans-bad (a poor SMT trained on 50k out-of-domain parallel sentences), backtrans-good (larger SMTs using baseline NMT parallel data plus ~174M English monolingual sentences), and backtrans-nmt (NMT systems replicating forward-translation settings)—alongside a forward-translation system (fwdtrans-nmt) and a combined backfwdtrans-nmt. Using BLEU as the metric, the results show large BT gains (nearly INLINEFORM0 BLEU in French and German), that better artificial data yields better translations, that the best Moses system is nearly as good as the NMT yet an order of magnitude faster to train, that the bad system yields much smaller gains and is detrimental on the out-of-domain test, that forward translation gives about half the gains of BT,

This section compares natural and artificial (back-translated) parallel data sources across linguistic and distributional properties, finding that artificial sources are shorter, have more monotonic word alignments (Kendall coefficients of 0.018 vs. 0.048 for French-English and 0.053 vs. 0.068 for German-English), are syntactically simpler (deeper tree depth differences), and show more concentrated word occurrence distributions with slower type growth and fewer rare events. It confirms via a 10M-word experiment that selecting data by alignment regularity outperforms random selection, explaining why Moses's mostly monotonic back-translation performs nearly as well as NMT's fluid back-translation while both improve the baseline.
This section analyzes simpler data generation schemes for neural machine translation that avoid requiring a backward translation engine, specifically examining "stupid back-translation" approaches.

This section describes three ways to generate pseudo-source texts for monolingual data in NMT: "copy" (copying target sentences and splitting OOVs into source-side units), "copy-marked" (augmenting the source vocabulary with target-word copies marked by a special language identifier to avoid homographic confusion), and "copy-dummies" (replacing words with dummy tokens to study training on noisy, uninformative sources). It also notes that pseudo-source embeddings in the copy-marked setup are pretrained for three epochs on in-domain data with all other parameters frozen.

This section reports that the copy-marked setup yields the best gains for both English-French and English-German, with the model learning to copy source words to target with near-zero cross-entropy (0.33 versus 58.52 for real source), and that adding noise (deleting random words and permuting the rest) brings the out-of-domain French score down to baseline level while producing a significant +1.5 BLEU improvement on German in-domain test sets, nearly matching the backtrans-nmt condition.

This section introduces using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), an idea borrowed from a prior work, to make pseudo-sources look more like natural data by integrating monolingual data into NMT, building on the finding that simply copying the target into the source already yields improvement and adding noise improves performance further.

This section describes the GAN setup, in which a marked target copy serves as a fake (pseudo) source encoded by a pseudo-source encoder that acts as the generator, producing representations that a bidirectional-RNN discriminator (dimension 1024, with averaged states passed to a single feed-forward layer and sigmoid) tries to distinguish from natural (out-of-domain) source encodings. Training optimizes three loss terms—the discriminator loss over natural and pseudo-sentences, the generator loss aimed at fooling the discriminator, and the usual MT objective—requiring three sets of parameters, with the pseudo-source encoder and embeddings updated with respect to both the generator and MT losses, following the GAN practice of updating the discriminator only when the generator's accuracy exceeds a threshold and the generator otherwise, after pre-training the pseudo-encoder and discriminator for 10k updates, and ignoring the pseudo-encoder at test time.

This section reports that adding GANs to the copy-marked setup yields no improvement on both language pairs except a small out-of-domain gain for English-French (indicating robustness to domain variations), and that combined with noise the French model achieves the best performance obtainable with stupid BT on in-domain tests (in BLEU and BEER), while remaining close to baseline on the News domain with slight German improvements. It observes that this method brings stupid BT closer to conventional BT at greatly reduced computational cost, with French still 0.4 to 1.0 BLEU below very good backtranslation while German systems are in the same ballpark. Finally, by reproducing the GAN setup with BT sentences instead of copies, it shows that using a separate pseudo-source encoder can be detrimental to French (degrading all metrics) but that adding GANs allows the German system to slightly outperform backtrans-nmt, demonstrating that GANs help even good systems.

This section compares previous methods with the use of a target-side Language Model (LM), noting that several proposals exist in the literature to integrate LMs in NMT, such as the one in BIBREF3, which strengthens the decoder by integrating an extra, source-independent RNN layer into a conventional NMT architecture, where training is performed either with parallel or monolingual data, and in the latter case word prediction only relies on the source-independent part of the network.

This section describes the language model (LM) setup, in which the authors followed BIBREF29 and reimplemented its deep-fusion technique, which involves first training a one-layer GRU RNN-LM (with hidden dimension 1024, matching the MT decoder) on the in-domain target data using a cross-entropy objective, and then combining the translation and language models by adding the RNN-LM's hidden state as an additional input to the decoder's softmax layer. The RNN-LMs were trained using dl4mt on the target side of the parallel data plus the Europarl corpus (about 6M sentences for both French and German).

The LM Results section (Table TABREF33) shows that deep-fusion barely improves Europarl results but yields about +0.6 BLEU over the baseline on newstest-2014 for both languages, because deep-fusion—unlike stupid BT—does not directly optimize on in-domain data but uses the Europarl-trained LM to maximize the likelihood of out-of-domain training data, so no domain-adaptation improvement is expected and gains appear in the more general domain; combining deep-fusion with copy-marked + noise + GANs produces slight improvements on the German in-domain test sets while out-of-domain performance stays near baseline.

This section analyzes the effect of back-translation (BT) on the internals of the neural machine translation network, specifically examining whether using a copy of the target sentence as a natural source is helpful for the encoder and what effects BT has on the attention model.

This section describes running the same fine-tuning using the copy-marked, backtrans-nmt and backtrans-nmt setups to investigate whether the overall performance of the NMT system degrades when certain sets of parameters are selectively frozen (i.e., not updated during fine-tuning), noting that all training scenarios except the last one have access to the same target training data.

This section reports BLEU scores from selective-update experiments in the backtrans-nmt, copy-marked, and fwdtrans-nmt setups, finding that freezing the decoder degrades performance by at most 0.2 BLEU, while freezing the encoder and/or attention parameters has no impact on the English-German system but slightly degrades the English-French one; the largest degradation (0.4 to over 1.0 BLEU) occurs for the natural setup, indicating that back-translation (BT) impacts the decoder most and that learning to encode a pseudo-source only marginally helps.

This related work section surveys approaches for using monolingual data in NMT, including back-translation and forward-translation (documented in BIBREF2, analyzed in BIBREF19, and studied for data size in BIBREF4, with forward translation considered in BIBREF20 and BIBREF19 and extended to domain adaptation in BIBREF21), target language models (BIBREF3, BIBREF29), multi-task learning to improve the encoder (BIBREF30), multilingual NMT with shared encoder layers (BIBREF31), and round-trip training for semi-unsupervised (BIBREF32) and unsupervised (BIBREF33) NMT, including the use of GANs to reduce the gap between artificial and natural data (BIBREF26), with the authors' own results described as complementary to these prior studies.

This conclusion recaps the paper's systematic study of integrating monolingual data into neural machine translation, confirming the effectiveness of back-translation (BT) while proposing cheaper alternatives using a slightly modified copy of the target instead of full BT, and using GANs to make pseudo-source sentences closer to natural source sentences for domain adaptation. The authors find that BT quality matters for NMT, that artificial sources are lexically less diverse and syntactically simpler but benefit from monotonicity, that properly noised copies (§ SECREF4) and especially GAN-based approaches can be almost as good as low quality BTs (§ SECREF5), that BT is only worth its cost when good BT can be generated, and that BT seems preferable to integrating external LM (§ SECREF6), with future work planned on other cheap data generation methods and refined data selection strategies.

This section presents the datasets, experimental setups, and results used in the study, including Table 1's parallel corpus sizes, Tables 2 and 5's evaluations of BT qualities and "stupid BTs," Table 3's BLEU scores for back-translation into English, Table 8's BLEU scores with selective parameter freezing, and Table 6's GAN setups, alongside Figures 1-3 documenting learning curves and properties of pseudo-English data (shorter sentences, simpler syntax, and lexically richer natural sources) obtained via backtrans-nmt from French and German.

This paper exploits the Facebook reaction feature in a distant supervised fashion to train a support vector machine classifier for emotion detection, using several feature combinations and combining different Facebook pages. Testing on existing benchmarks for emotion detection, the authors show that using only information derived completely automatically (without relying on any handcrafted lexicon) they can achieve competitive results, while also finding large room for improvement, especially by gearing the collection of Facebook pages toward the target domain.

This section introduces the use of Facebook reactions as proxies for emotion labels via distant supervision to train Support Vector Machine models for emotion recognition, achieving competitive or state-of-the-art results on standard evaluation datasets, while also exploring how different sets of Facebook pages provide an intrinsic domain-adaptation method.

This section describes using Facebook's six specific reactions (Like, Love, Haha, Wow, Sad, and Angry) as proxies for emotion labels, collecting the latest 1000 posts from 14 public pages (FoxNews, CNN, ESPN, New York Times, Time magazine, Huffington Post Weird News, The Guardian, Cartoon Network, Cooking Light, Home Cooking Adventure, Justin Bieber, Nickelodeon, Spongebob, Disney) via the Facebook API. For each post, they turned reaction counts into an emotion vector and associated the post with the emotion having the highest count, ignoring "like" as the default generic reaction, as illustrated by the first post in Figure 3 receiving the label "sad" with a score of 284.

This section describes the three emotion datasets used—Affective Text, Fairy Tales, and ISEAR—and provides an overview of the emotions used, their distribution, and how they were mapped to emotions obtained from Facebook posts. It notes that the development portion of the Affective Text dataset was used to develop the models, while all three datasets served as benchmarks for evaluation, with a summary provided in Table TABREF8.

This section describes the Affective Text dataset from SemEval 2007 Task 14, which classifies emotions (Anger, Disgust, Fear, Joy, Sadness, Surprise) and valence (positive/negative) in news headlines collected from Google News, The New York Times, BBC News and CNN. The dataset includes 250 annotated headlines for development and 1000 for testing, with emotions scored 0-100 and evaluated using Pearson's r for fine-grained assessment and precision, recall and f-score for coarse-grained binary classification.

This section describes the Fairy Tales dataset collected by alm2008affect, containing about 1,000 sentences from fairy tales by B. Potter, H.C. Andersen and Grimm, annotated with the six Affective Text emotions (Angry, Disgusted, Fearful, Happy, Sad, and Surprised). Following common usage in prior works, the authors use only sentences where all annotators agreed and merge the angry and disgusted labels.

The ISEAR (International Survey on Emotion Antecedents and Reactions) is a dataset created in the 1990s through questionnaires answered by people of different cultural backgrounds to gather insights into cross-cultural aspects of emotional reactions. Student respondents, both psychologists and non-psychologists, reported situations in which they experienced all seven major emotions (joy, fear, anger, sadness, disgust, shame and guilt), covering how they appraised situations and reacted; the final dataset contains reports by approximately 3000 respondents worldwide, totaling 7665 sentences labelled with an emotion, making it the largest of the three datasets used.

This section summarises the datasets and emotion distributions, mapping all dataset labels to a final subset of four emotions—anger, joy, sadness, and surprise—that are used for training and testing the models (Table TABREF8). It also presents the emotion distributions per dataset and per Facebook page (Figure FIGREF9), observing that news pages tend to have more sadness and anger posts, while cooking and tv-show pages have a high percentage of joy posts, information used to select the best pages for a target domain.

This section describes the two main decisions in developing the model: which Facebook pages to select as training data and which features to use, noting that further exploration of their interaction is left to future work. For development, the authors use a small portion of the Affective dataset (the SemEval 2007 Task 14 development set with 250 annotated sentences), and all results in this section are reported on this dataset, with the Task 14 test set and two other datasets reserved for evaluating the final models.

The section describes how the authors selected Facebook pages for training data using a simple approach: they trained an SVM with a bag-of-words model and default parameters (Scikit-learn) on different combinations of pages, then selected the best model (B-M) based on development data results and emotion distribution. The best model combined Time, The Guardian, and Disney pages, with Time and The Guardian performing well on most emotions while Disney boosted performance for the Joy class.

This section describes the text-based features used for emotion detection, including tf-idf bag-of-words, word (2-3) and character (2-5) ngrams, negation and punctuation features, the NRC10 Lexicon (providing boolean emotion values for anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and positive/negative valence), and three Word Embeddings: Google embeddings (300-dimensional, 3 million words/phrases), Facebook embeddings (trained on 20,000 scraped Facebook sentences with window size 5, learning rate 0.01, dimensionality 100, filtering words with frequency below 2), and retrofitted embeddings (infused with NRC10 emotion-similarity information). Results were evaluated on the Affective development set using the B-M page combination as training data, with the tf-idf bag-of-words feature used only for assessment and ultimately excluded from

This section reports precision, recall, and micro-average f-score on the development set, drawing three observations from Table TABREF20: a simple tf-idf bag-of-words model already achieves a strong f-score of 0.368 (with textual and lexicon-based features not improving the overall score despite per-class variation); Google embeddings outperform Facebook embeddings, likely due to larger training corpus size, with retrofitting not helping Google embeddings but boosting Facebook embeddings; and in combination with embeddings, all features perform better than tf-idf alone, but removing the hand-crafted Lexicon feature yields even better results, so the best model (B-M) relies entirely on automatically obtained information.

The Results section reports the performance of the authors' B-M model on the three standard datasets used for emotion classification evaluation, using a feature set consisting of all features plus Google-based embeddings but excluding the lexicon, which makes the approach independent of any manual annotation or handcrafted resource. The B-M model relies on subsets of Facebook pages selected based on their development set performance and the observation of emotion distributions, and its performance is compared against systems reported in the respective literature without re-implementing any existing model.

This section discusses the potential of distant supervision using Facebook reactions for emotion classification, noting that models enhanced with continuous vector representations achieve competitive results without handcrafted resources, and outlines future work including training emotion-aware embeddings, retrofitting FB-embeddings, selecting training instances via entropy-based measures to capture strong emotions, investigating the choice of Facebook pages in relation to stance-based issues, exploiting vocabulary overlap between pages and datasets, and developing single models per emotion as a multi-label task.

This section presents the tables and figures used in the paper, including Table 1 which shows the emotion labels in existing datasets, Facebook, and the resulting mapping used in the experiments, along with the role each dataset plays. It contains Figure 3 (emotion distribution in the datasets) and Figure 4 (emotion distribution per Facebook page), Table 2 (results on the Affective development set using micro-averaged f-score), and Table 3 (results on test datasets according to Precision, Recall and F-score).

This abstract states that the paper proposes three BERT-based models that leverage gloss (sense definition) knowledge by constructing context-gloss pairs, fine-tuned on the SemCor3.0 training corpus, and reports that the approach outperforms state-of-the-art systems on several English all-words WSD benchmark datasets.

This introduction states that Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is a fundamental NLP task, with previous approaches falling into knowledge-based methods (using WordNet glosses and semantic graph structures) and supervised methods (using manually designed features and word experts), and that recent neural-based methods cannot fully beat the best word expert supervised methods; it then describes the paper's approach of constructing context-gloss pairs from WordNet glosses and treating WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem by fine-tuning the pre-trained BERT model, achieving new state-of-the-art results on several English all-words WSD benchmark datasets, with two contributions: constructing context-gloss pairs and proposing three BERT-based models for WSD, and fine-tuning BERT to significantly outperform state-of-the-art systems.

This section describes GlossBERT, a BERT-based method for word sense disambiguation that incorporates gloss knowledge from lexical databases. The authors explain how their approach leverages the definitions and examples from word senses to improve disambiguation performance.

This section defines the WSD task, where a sentence consists of a series of words, some of which are targets that need to be disambiguated, with candidate senses drawn from entries of the target's lemma in a pre-defined sense inventory (usually WordNet), and the task aims to find the most suitable entry—symbolized as a unique sense key—for each target in a sentence.

This section describes BERT as a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder that is pre-trained on a large corpus using two unsupervised prediction tasks—masked language model and next sentence prediction—and is fine-tuned on the WSD task.

This section describes treating WSD as a token-level classification task where the final hidden state of the target word token (averaging if multiple tokens) is fed into a classification layer added for every target lemma, following the same approach as the last layer of the Bi-LSTM model.

GlossBERT treats word sense disambiguation as a sentence-pair classification problem by constructing context-gloss pairs from all possible senses of the target word in WordNet, leveraging BERT's ability to model the relationship between pairs of texts. Using target word "research" as an example (with four targets in the sentence), the method constructs context-gloss pairs from all possible WordNet senses to fully leverage gloss information.

For each target word, the authors extract glosses of all $N=4$ possible senses from WordNet to construct context-gloss pairs, which are then formatted with [CLS] and [SEP] marks as BERT input, following an approach also used in aspect-based sentiment analysis.

This section describes adding weak supervised signals to context-gloss pairs, where the gloss sentence signal points out the target word and the context sentence signal emphasizes the target word when it occurs multiple times in the same sentence. Each target word generates $N$ context-gloss pair training instances with labels in $\lbrace yes, no\rbrace$, and during testing the sense corresponding to the highest $label=yes$ probability is chosen as the prediction, with the authors experimenting with three GlossBERT models.

GlossBERT(Token-CLS) uses context-gloss pairs as input, highlighting the target word by taking the final hidden state of the token corresponding to the target word (averaging them if more than one token) and adding a classification layer with label ∈ {yes, no}.

GlossBERT(Sent-CLS) uses context-gloss pairs as input, takes the final hidden state of the [CLS] token as the sequence representation, and adds a classification layer with label ∈ {yes, no} that does not highlight the target word.

GlossBERT(Sent-CLS-WS) uses context-gloss pairs with weak supervision as input, taking the final hidden state of the [CLS] token and adding a classification layer with labels in {yes, no} to weakly highlight the target word.
This section states that Table TABREF12 presents the statistics of the WSD datasets used in the experiments.

The section states that, following previous work, the authors choose SemCor3.0 as their training corpus, which is the largest corpus manually annotated with WordNet senses for word sense disambiguation.

This section describes the evaluation datasets used in the study, specifically five standard all-words fine-grained WSD datasets from the Senseval and SemEval competitions: Senseval-2 (SE2), Senseval-3 (SE3), SemEval-2007 (SE07), SemEval-2013 (SE13) and SemEval-2015 (SE15), which were proposed by BIBREF17 for fair comparison. Following BIBREF13, BIBREF12 and BIBREF10, the authors chose SE07, the smallest among these test sets, as the development set.
Since BIBREF17 map all the sense annotations in these datasets from their original versions to WordNet 3.0, the authors extract word sense glosses from WordNet 3.0.

This section describes the experimental settings, stating that the authors use the pre-trained uncased BERT$_\mathrm{BASE}$ model (12 Transformer blocks, 768 hidden layer size, 12 self-attention heads, 110M parameters) for fine-tuning, finding that BERT$_\mathrm{LARGE}$ performs slightly worse than BERT$_\mathrm{BASE}$ on this task. They use the development set (SE07) to find optimal settings, keeping dropout probability at 0.1, number of epochs at 4, initial learning rate at 2e-5, and batch size at 64.

Table TABREF19 reports the performance of GlossBERT and comparison methods on the English all-words WSD benchmark datasets, measured by accuracy, comparing the MFS baseline, knowledge-based systems (Lesk$_{ext+emb}$, Babelfy), traditional supervised systems (IMS, IMS$_{+emb}$), neural-based methods (Bi-LSTM, Bi-LSTM$_{+ att. + LEX + POS}$, GAS$_{ext}$, CAN$^s$, HCAN), and the authors' methods (BERT(Token-CLS), GlossBERT(Token-CLS), GlossBERT(Sent-CLS), GlossBERT(Sent-CLS-WS)); it finds that directly using BERT cannot obtain performance growth, that the improvements come from leveraging BERT to better exploit gloss information, that our method achieves significant improvements in SE07 and Verb (which have the highest ambiguity level among all datasets and all POS tags respectively), and that GlossBERT(Sent-CLS-WS)

This section explains that GlossBERT's improvements stem from constructing context-gloss pairs to convert the WSD problem into a sentence-pair classification task (similar to NLI) and training a single classifier, combined with leveraging BERT to better exploit gloss information. It finds that GlossBERT beats traditional word expert supervised methods by reducing feature engineering effort and avoiding dedicated classifiers per target lemma, that neural methods can now totally beat traditional word expert methods, and that converting fine-tuning into a sentence-pair classification task is an effective approach for using gloss knowledge.

The paper proposes constructing context-gloss pairs and converting WSD into a sentence-pair classification task, then fine-tuning the pre-trained BERT model to achieve new state-of-the-art results on the WSD task.

This paper proposes a multilingual multistage fine-tuning approach for low-resource neural machine translation, benchmarked on a Japanese–Russian pair, which exploits out-of-domain data by first training a multilingual NMT model and then performing multistage fine-tuning on in-domain parallel and back-translated pseudo-parallel data. This approach, combining domain adaptation, multilingualism, and back-translation, improves translation quality by more than 3.7 BLEU points over a strong baseline.

This introduction states that neural machine translation (NMT) outperforms phrase-based statistical machine translation (PBSMT) in resource-rich scenarios but underperforms in low-resource scenarios unless cross-lingual transfer learning is used, and it introduces the paper's focus on the extremely low-resource Japanese-Russian (Ja-Ru) language pair with only 12k lines of news-domain parallel corpus, proposing a novel multilingual multistage fine-tuning approach that combines multilingual modeling and domain adaptation.

This section describes the Japanese–Russian news translation setting (with English as a third language for pivoting), explaining that because clean held-out parallel data was unavailable, the authors manually compiled development and test sets from News Commentary data by first creating tri-text data, manually identifying corresponding parts across languages, splitting unaligned parts into new lines (without merging lines), and obtaining 1,654 lines comprising trilingual, bilingual, and monolingual segments, from which 600 trilingual sentences formed the test set and the rest plus bilingual sentences formed the development sets.

This Related Work section explains that low-resource translation between Japanese and Russian cannot rely on transfer learning (which requires English as a shared language), unsupervised MT, parallel sentence mining, back-translation, or pivot-language MT, because each depends on resources unavailable in this extremely low-resource scenario; it then introduces the paper's approach of combining multilingual modeling (incorporating multiple language pairs into a single model) and domain adaptation (incorporating out-of-domain data) through step-wise fine-tuning.

path: Limit of Using only In-domain Data
context: This section addresses RQ1 by evaluating the translation quality achievable using existing methods with in-domain parallel and monolingual data, then employs the strongest model to experiment with generating and utilizing back-translated pseudo-parallel data to augment NMT, aiming to empirically identify the most effective practices and recognize the limitations of relying only on in-domain parallel corpora.

This section describes the data used to train neural machine translation systems among Japanese, Russian, and English, using parallel data from Global Voices available at OPUS (12k Ja-Ru, 47k Ja-En, and 82k Ru-En sentence pairs), noting that the corpora are not mutually exclusive with 9k of the 12k Ja-Ru sentences also appearing in the other two corpora, which limits the benefit of helping corpora. It also summarizes monolingual corpora across several domains including news, used for pseudo-parallel data augmentation and language modeling, after removing sentences already present in the parallel corpus. Tokenization used Moses' tokenizer.perl for English and Russian, MeCab with the IPA dictionary for Japanese, followed by removal of duplicated sentence pairs and sentences exceeding 100 tokens.

This section describes the MT methods examined, starting with standard PBSMT (BIBREF3) and NMT (BIBREF1), plus advanced PBSMT variants including pivot-based translation using a helping language (BIBREF10) and phrase table induction from monolingual data (BIBREF14). For NMT, they compared attentional RNN-based (RNMT, BIBREF2) and Transformer (BIBREF18) architectures, along with bi-directional (BIBREF11) and multi-to-multi (M2M, BIBREF8) multi-directional models, and evaluated back-translation data augmentation (BIBREF17).

This Results section reports BLEU scores (case-sensitive, tokenized, via Moses's multi-bleu.perl, with statistical significance tested by bootstrap-hypothesis-difference-significance.pl) for Ja–En, Ru–En, and Ja–Ru translation, focusing on the low-resource Ja–Ru pair. It finds that Transformer NMT models outperform RNMT models, that M2M Transformer models benefit from multilingualism (unlike M2M RNMT for Ru–En), and that pivot-based PBSMT with three phrase tables ("Synthesize / Triangulate / Gold") reduces OOV tokens substantially (e.g., 3047 to 1180 for Ja–Ru) but further extension with monolingual-derived phrase tables fails due to poor bilingual word embedding quality. The multistage fine-tuning (models V and VII) achieves significantly higher BLEU scores than both the weak baseline (b3) and strong baseline (#10),

This section describes using the M2M Transformer NMT model (b3) to generate pseudo-parallel data through back-translation of in-domain monolingual data selected via a 4-gram KenLM scoring procedure comparing in-domain (Global Voices) and general-domain (Global Voices, IWSLT, Tatoeba) language models, maintaining a 1:1 ratio with parallel data, then training new NMT models on the concatenation of original and pseudo-parallel data; using all six-way pseudo-parallel data (#10) significantly improved the base model across all translation directions except En–Ru.

This section states that the authors evaluated an extensive variation of MT models relying only on in-domain parallel and monolingual data, but the resulting BLEU scores for the Ja→Ru and Ru→Ja tasks did not exceed 10 BLEU points, implying the inherent limitation of the in-domain data as well as the difficulty of these translation directions.

path: Exploiting Large Out-of-Domain Data Involving a Helping Language
context: This section proposes a multistage fine-tuning method that combines domain adaptation (for Ja→En and Ru→En) and multilingual transfer (via a helping language) to exploit out-of-domain parallel data, relying on the M2M model and examining fine-tuning for iteratively generating and using pseudo-parallel data.

This section describes a multistage fine-tuning approach for domain adaptation and multilingual transfer learning in low-resource neural machine translation. It proposes pre-training a multilingual model on out-of-domain Ja-En and Ru-En parallel data, then fine-tuning on in-domain data (conventional fine-tuning) or a mixture of in-domain and out-of-domain data (mixed fine-tuning), followed by further fine-tuning for the Ja-Ru pair either on in-domain data only or on all in-domain parallel data.

This section describes the selection of out-of-domain parallel data for Ja-En (the cleanest 1.5M sentences from the Asian Scientific Paper Excerpt Corpus, ASPEC) and Ru-En (the UN and Yandex corpora from the WMT 2018 News Translation Task), retaining Ru-En pairs containing at least one OOV token in both sides according to the in-domain language model, with statistics summarized in Table TABREF45.

This section investigates whether back-translation with an improved NMT model yields further gains, generating six-way pseudo-parallel data from the same monolingual sentences used in Section SECREF34 and fine-tuning the model on a mixture of pseudo-parallel and original parallel data using the same over-sampling procedure, repeated five times. Table TABREF51 shows that the from-scratch M2M Transformer "new #10" outperformed #10 in Table TABREF33 due to higher-quality pseudo-parallel data but underperformed the base model VII, whereas the fine-tuned model VIII surpassed VII, and a further iteration (IX) improved BLEU scores across all directions except Ru→En, reaching a much higher plateau than in Section SECREF4.

The paper addresses Ja→Ru news domain translation in an extremely low-resource setting, proposing a multilingual multistage fine-tuning approach that improves translation by over 3.7 BLEU points compared to a strong baseline, as summarized in Table TABREF53.

The authors trained contextualised word embedding ELMo models on raw tokenized corpora and on corpora with word tokens replaced by their lemmas, then evaluated them on the word sense disambiguation task for English and Russian. The experiments showed that lemmatization is not necessary for English but yields small but consistent improvements for Russian, indicating that text pre-processing decisions before training ELMo should consider the linguistic nature of the language.

This section introduces the paper's investigation into whether lemmatization (word normalization) affects ELMo performance in word sense disambiguation (WSD), challenging the deep learning tradition of minimal pre-processing. The authors compare ELMo models trained on the same corpus before and after lemmatization, using contextualized representations from the top layer of ELMo to train word sense classifiers, and report that lemmatization yields small but consistent improvements for Russian (with rich morphology) but negligible differences for English.

This section explains that ELMo learns contextual word representations unsupervised via language modelling using a two-layer BiLSTM over a character-based convolutional layer, which avoids out-of-vocabulary words and leads its authors to recommend using only tokenisation without further normalisation; it also defines WSD as selecting a word sense from a pre-defined sense inventory given context, noting that contextualised embeddings address polysemy and homonymy by producing context-dependent representations for homographs, and states that while no normalisation is needed for English, feeding ELMo lemmas instead of raw tokens can improve WSD performance in other languages.

The authors trained their own ELMo models from scratch using the original TensorFlow implementation (3 epochs, batch size 192, two GPUs, with LSTM dimensionality reduced from 4096 to 2048) on English Wikipedia (February 2017) and a concatenation of Russian Wikipedia (December 2018) and the full Russian National Corpus (RNC) to make the Russian corpus more comparable in size. Texts were tokenized and lemmatized with UDPipe models trained on the Universal Dependencies 2.3 treebanks, yielding lemmatization accuracy of about 96% for English and 97% for Russian, which the authors treated as gold standard.

This section describes the two WSD test sets used for evaluation—Senseval-3 for English (20 noun target words) and RUSSE'18 for Russian (18 noun target words)—and explains that both were pre-processed to produce lemmatized and non-lemmatized versions using UDPipe lemmatization. It notes that the Russian dataset is morphologically far more complex, with 132 distinct inflectional forms across 18 nouns (more than 7 forms per word, covering only half of Russian's inflectional variability), compared to English's 39 distinct forms for 20 nouns, and that the Russian dataset uses a lexical window of 25 words before and after the target word while the English dataset retains the whole paragraph.

This section describes the experimental setup, which uses per-word random splits with 5-fold cross-validation and reports the average of 5 macro-F1 scores per target word, comparing ELMo (used via feature extraction as either a single target word vector or averaged context vectors) against static SkipGram (SGNS) embeddings trained on English and Russian Wikipedia, classified with logistic regression (and verified with an MLP). The findings show that ELMo outperforms SGNS in both languages, that averaging all context vectors is not beneficial (so only the single target word mode is discussed), and that lemmatization does not significantly affect English results but yields a small but significant improvement for Russian ELMo, attributed to the model being able to better learn lexical semantic structures rather than learning morphological idiosyncrasies.

This section qualitatively analyzes the Russian RUSSE'18 dataset, comparing lemma-based and token-based ELMo models using F1 scores and standard deviations. It finds that among 18 target words, only 3 (акция, крона, круп) show significant improvement (differences exceeding one standard deviation) due to their unrelated senses yielding more consistent context differentiation, while домино—being a non-inflected borrowed word—shows a borderline-decreased score because lemmatization loses useful contextual inflectional information; the excluded words байка and гвоздика show great improvement since their senses correspond to different lemmas, making results dependent on lemmatization quality.

This conclusion states that the authors evaluated how ELMo contextualised word embedding models perform on the word sense disambiguation (WSD) task when trained on raw tokenized corpora versus corpora where word tokens are replaced by their lemmas, finding that lemmatization yields small but consistent WSD improvements for the rich-morphology language Russian but not for the simple-morphology language English or for rare words lacking inflected forms, leading to the take-home messages that text pre-processing still matters for deep learning algorithms and that the morphological nature of a language affects optimal training decisions, with future work planned to include more strongly and weakly inflected languages.

This section presents the training corpora (Table 1), target ambiguous words for Russian (RUSSE'18) (Table 2), and characteristics of the WSD datasets including average values (Table 3). It reports averaged macro-F1 scores for WSD (Table 4), visualizes word sense disambiguation performance across words on English and Russian ELMo target models (Figures 1-2), and provides F1 scores for target words from RUSSE'18 showing significant differences between lemma-based and token-based models (Table 5) as well as for excluded target words (Table 6).

This abstract introduces UTCNN, a neural network model that classifies post stance on social media by incorporating user tastes, topic tastes, and user comments on posts, and it also analyzes texts in forums and message boards. Experiments on Chinese Facebook data and English online debate forum data show that UTCNN achieves a 0.755 macro-average f-score for supportive, neutral, and unsupportive stance classes on Facebook data (significantly better than models withholding user, topic, or comment information), mitigates the lack of data for the minor class without oversampling, and yields a 0.842 accuracy on English online debate forum data, outperforming previous work and other deep learning models regardless of language or platform.

This section introduces the UTCNN (user-topic-comment neural network), a deep learning model that incorporates user information (including authors and likers, with user embeddings generable even for users who never posted), topic modeling (to automatically assign topics to posts), and comment information to enhance stance classification on forum-style social media platforms, with the authors claiming it achieves the highest performance across all instances and that each information type (users, topics, comments) makes its own contribution.

This section explains that text features alone are limited for stance classification, so the authors incorporate extra-linguistic features (such as author, user-interaction, and ideology constraints) that previous work has shown improve accuracy by 1–7%. It reviews sequential labeling methods used for online forum text—hidden Markov models (Hasan and Ng), iterative classification (Burfoot et al.), and probabilistic soft logic (Sridhar et al.)—and notes that in the Facebook dataset they use comments as extra information to predict post stance rather than comment stance.

This section reviews prior deep learning approaches for text sentiment classification (adaptive layers in recursive neural networks, recursive neural tensor networks, and paragraph vectors) and extra-linguistic feature methods, specifically the user-word composition vector model (UWCVM) with user embeddings and its extension UPNN with product embeddings, which achieved 2–10% accuracy improvements. It then contrasts this work with Tang et al.'s product-review sentiment classification by noting that UTCNN considers multiple users (an author and many likers) per post and incorporates comment information, generating and utilizing user embeddings for all users—including those who have not authored any posts—to improve post stance classification.

This section describes the UTCNN (user-topic-comment neural network), a deep learning model that first uses CNN-based document composition to capture user- and topic-dependent document-level semantic representations from word representations, then incorporates comment information to construct the full model.

This section describes the User- and Topic-dependent Document Composition module of UTCNN, which uses a general CNN (BIBREF3) combined with two semantic transformations: dot operations that transform word embeddings INLINEFORM4 into user-dependent representations (via INLINEFORM0 modeling user reading preferences) and topic-dependent representations (via INLINEFORM1 modeling topic semantics), with transformed dimensions INLINEFORM2 and INLINEFORM3. The user-dependent and topic-dependent word vectors INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are concatenated into a user- and topic-dependent word vector INLINEFORM3, which serves as CNN input through three convolutional layers (Equation EQREF6/DISPLAYFORM0) using ReLU activation INLINEFORM2 and window sizes of one, two, and three to encode unigram, bigram, and trigram semantics, followed by maximum pooling and average pooling to produce n-gram representations.

This section describes the UTCNN model architecture, which uses maximum pooling layers to form moderator embeddings (representing the pseudo user providing overall semantic/sentiment of engaged users) and joint topic embeddings, with latent user stance modeled by INLINEFORM5 and latent topic stance by INLINEFORM12 for each user and topic respectively. The model treats comments as short documents, applies document composition to generate comment representations, concatenates them with commenter vector embedding INLINEFORM2 and topic vector embedding INLINEFORM3, then applies maximum pooling to select the most important features (chosen over other pooling/merging layers as a reason for UTCNN's performance gains), before feeding the pooled comment representation, user vector embedding INLINEFORM0, topic vector embedding INLINEFORM1, and document representation into a fully connected network with softmax for final stance label prediction.

This section outlines the experimental setup, describing the dataset, training process, and implementation of baselines and variations that reveal the effects of authors, likers, comment, and commenters features, before comparing the model with related work in the results section.

This section describes the two datasets used to evaluate UTCNN: the privately-owned, single-topic, Chinese, unbalanced FBFans dataset (anti-nuclear-power Facebook fan groups, 2,496 authors, 505,137 likers, 33,686 commenters, 505,412 unique users, stance labels Sup/Neu/Uns with Cohen's Kappa of 0.58 for Neu vs not Neu and 0.84 for Sup or Uns, raw agreement 0.91, highly skewed with far more Sup than Uns posts) and the public, multiple-topic, English, balanced CreateDebate dataset (four topics: abortion, gay rights, Obama, marijuana, annotated as for/against, 977 unique users). It reports annotator agreement metrics, validates the assumption that posts attract same-stance users through normalized like statistics across 32,595 posts,

This section describes the UTCNN training settings, including cross-entropy loss, the AdaGrad optimizer, fixed 50-dimensional GloVe word embeddings, a learning rate of 0.03, user and topic embeddings randomly initialized in [-0.1, 0.1], matrix embeddings of size 250, and vector embeddings of length 10. It explains the use of LDA to determine 100 latent topics (with the top three assigned per post) for the FBFans dataset, while CreateDebate used its four existing topic labels directly, and reports class-based and macro-average f-scores for FBFans (due to class imbalance and the importance of minor-class content) and accuracy for CreateDebate to enable comparison with related work.

This section lists the baselines used to evaluate UTCNN: SVM models with unigram/bigram/trigram features, average word embeddings, and average transformed word embeddings (using the INLINEFORM0 transformation from equation EQREF6), plus CNN BIBREF3 and RCNN BIBREF0 deep learning models, all with and without comment information, along with ablation variants of UTCNN (without user information, without the LDA model, and without comments). All models were trained on the training set with parameters and SVM kernel selections (linear or RBF) fine-tuned on the development set, and oversampling was applied to the SVMs, CNN, and RCNN because the FBFans dataset is highly imbalanced.

This section reports the results of UTCNN and baselines on the FBFans dataset, showing that Majority performs well on the neutral class due to the dataset's bias, SVM models perform well on Support and Neutral but poorly on the opposing (minority) class, and CNN/RCNN models perform slightly better but still struggle with the opposing class. It finds that user information is most important among UTCNN's features (a 17.5% improvement when added), followed by topic information (a 4.9% gain from LDA) and comment information (a 4.8% improvement), with the full UTCNN achieving the highest f-scores on all stance classes and the highest macro-average f-score, while the finding that separating author/liker and commenter embeddings yields greater improvement (4.8%) than shared user embeddings (2.5%) leads to training two user matrix embeddings per user.

This section presents the results of UTCNN, baselines, and related work on the CreateDebate dataset, showing that UTCNN significantly outperforms ILP, CRF, PSL, SVM, CNN, and RCNN models, with user embeddings providing a 21% accuracy improvement and topic embeddings adding a further 3.4% improvement, demonstrating that latent representations are more effective than overt model constraints.

The Conclusion states that the authors proposed UTCNN, a neural network model incorporating user, topic, content, and comment information for stance classification on social media texts, where user embeddings are learned for all users with minimum active degree (one post or one like), topic information is obtained from a topic model or pre-defined labels, and comment information provides additional clues. They report that UTCNN achieves promising and balanced results and plan to explore the effectiveness of the UTCNN user embeddings for author stance classification in the future.
