This section presents the UTCNN model architecture and its document composition with user- and topic-dependent semantic transformations (Figures 1-2), along with annotation results for the FBFans and CreateDebate datasets (Table 1), the distribution of like behavior (Table 2), and post stance classification performance showing that UTCNN (full) results are statistically significant (p-value < 0.005) with respect to all other methods except UTCNN shared user embedding on the FBFans dataset (Table 3), and UTCNN results are statistically significant (p-value < 0.001) with respect to other UTCNN settings on the CreateDebate dataset (Table 4).

This abstract states that automatically constructed datasets like WikiBio contain reference texts that diverge from the semi-structured data, causing metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE to show poor correlation with human judgments. The authors propose PARENT, a metric that aligns n-grams from the reference and generated texts to the semi-structured data before computing precision and recall, and through a large-scale human evaluation study of table-to-text models for WikiBio, they show that PARENT correlates with human judgments better than existing text generation metrics, has comparable correlation to the information extraction based evaluation proposed by Wiseman et al (2017) while being easier to use, and is also applicable when reference texts are elicited from humans using data from the WebNLG challenge.

This section explains that automatic metrics like BLEU and ROUGE assume reference texts are gold-standard, but in datasets like WikiBio, WebNLG, and E2E-NLG, references are often "divergent" (containing extra information not entailed by the table). It states that existing metrics correlate poorly with human judgments when divergent references are present, and proposes PARENT (Precision And Recall of Entailed N-grams from the Table), a new metric that uses an entailment model to compute precision via a union of reference and table and recall via an intersection, thereby rewarding correct information missing from the reference and ignoring extra incorrect information.

This section defines the Table-to-Text task as generating fluent, grammatical natural language text INLINEFORM1 that summarizes semi-structured tables expressed as (attribute, value) pairs, and sets up the evaluation framework using reference descriptions INLINEFORM2, with an evaluation set INLINEFORM3 of tables, references, and generated texts, along with n-gram counts INLINEFORM10 and their minimums INLINEFORM13 used to score models in correlation with human judgments.

PARENT evaluates each instance separately by computing the precision and recall of the generated table content (INLINEFORM1) against both the reference text (INLINEFORM2) and the original table (INLINEFORM3).

This section describes training a pointer-generator network as an information extraction system to parse generated text into (attribute, value) tuples for comparison against ground truth tables, achieving an F-score of INLINEFORM0 comparable to other open-domain settings. They then use this system to compute Content Selection (CS) F-score comparing extracted pairs from generated text versus reference, Relation Generation (RG) precision and RG-F comparing extracted pairs against the ground truth table, omitting content ordering since the extraction system does not align records to the input text.

This section describes how the authors compare several automatic evaluation metrics by computing their Pearson correlation with aggregated human evaluation scores assigned to table-to-text models' outputs on an evaluation set, where each model's automatic scores are correlated with the human scores to assess how well each metric aligns with human judgment.

The section describes the WikiBio dataset (and mentions WebNLG) and the models used to generate text from tables, which are divided into two categories: WikiBio-Systems (one model each from four families, testing comparison across model families with large quality variation) and WikiBio-Hyperparams (13 hyperparameter settings of PG-Net, the best-performing system, testing comparison of similar systems with small performance variation).

This section describes a human evaluation in which crowd-sourcing workers performed paired comparisons between generated texts (and between generated texts and reference texts) across the WikiBio-Systems and WikiBio-Hyperparams categories, sampling 1100 tables from the development set and collecting 8800 pairwise comparisons (8 per table) judged by around 500 workers. The comparisons were aggregated into real-valued scores for each of the 16 models using Thurstone's method, and the results showed low variance in the system-level scores, with the reference texts receiving a lower score than PG-Net, highlighting the divergence in WikiBio.

This section describes the metrics used to evaluate Table-to-Text generation, organized into three categories. For Text only, they compare BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr and CIDEr-D using publicly available implementations. For Information Extraction based metrics, they compare CS, RG and RG-F. For Text & Table, they compare a variant of BLEU called BLEU-T (which uses table values as additional references and rewards matching n-grams rather than penalizing them, drawing inspiration from iBLEU), both the word-overlap model (PARENT-W) and co-occurrence model (PARENT-C) of PARENT for determining entailment, and versions where a single INLINEFORM0 is tuned on the entire dataset to maximize correlation with human judgments, denoted as PARENT*-W/C.

This section describes using bootstrap sampling (500 iterations) over the 1100 tables with human annotations to estimate how each metric's correlation with human evaluation varies with the underlying data, reporting average correlations (Table TABREF37) and correlation distributions for the best metrics (Figure FIGREF38). It compares extractive metrics—BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr, BLEU-T, CS, RG-F, and both PARENT variants (PARENT-C and PARENT-W)—finding that reference-only metrics show only weak (often negative in the hyperparams category) correlations, while RG-F and both PARENT variants achieve the highest correlations, with PARENT-W significantly outperforming the others for the systems category; it also notes that word-overlap outperformed co-occurrence for entailment on this dataset (opposite to WebNLG), that PARENT-W can be used out-of-the-box, and that tuning the INLINEFORM0

This Analysis section examines PARENT-W's performance under varying conditions and compares it against other metrics from Table 3, using binary entailment labels (judged by 3 workers with majority vote, Fleiss' kappa indicating fair agreement) to study correlation as the number of divergent references varies. Figure 4 shows that PARENT and RG-F maintain high, stable correlation across the entire range of entailed examples, while BLEU and BLEU-T vary greatly and perform worst when the evaluation set contains only entailed examples—because such subsets omit much table information, penalizing systems that produce more information than the references. Removing the probability of an n-gram being entailed by the table from Eqs. 19 and 23 drops PARENT-W's average correlation to a lower value, and removing Table Recall (Eq. 22) also reduces correlation, demonstrating these components are crucial. Finally, Table 4 shows both PARENT variants achieve significantly higher accuracy than other metrics

This section evaluates how PARENT correlates with human judgments on the WebNLG dataset, where systems generate text describing 1-5 RDF triples and human ratings were collected for 9 participating systems on 223 instances across grammaticality, fluency, and semantics. It finds that both variants of PARENT are competitive or better than other metrics in average correlation across all three aspects, with PARENT-C excelling in grammaticality and fluency while PARENT performs best for semantics, and notes that the INLINEFORM0 parameter influences whether recall is computed against the table or reference, with WebNLG references showing higher recall (often INLINEFORM2) compared to WikiBio.

This Related Work section reviews prior studies evaluating automatic metrics for text generation, concluding that no single metric suits all tasks and that BLEU and NIST fail to judge content quality, while system-level metrics show acceptable but not sentence-level correlation with human judgments; it introduces PARENT as a task-specific metric that discounts non-overlapping n-grams to handle hallucination, drawing on iBLEU (which compares generated text to both source and reference) but rewarding source-matching text to prioritize accuracy over paraphrasing, and notes this is the first study assessing metric quality when table-to-text references are divergent, finding that even system-level correlations become unreliable in that case.

This conclusion summarizes the paper's study of automatically evaluating table-to-text systems when references diverge from the table. It states that the authors propose PARENT, a new metric showing the highest correlation with humans across settings with divergent references in WikiBio, that they perform the first empirical evaluation of information extraction based metrics (finding BIBREF1's RG-F to be effective), and that PARENT is comparable to the best existing metrics when references are elicited by humans on the WebNLG data.

This section describes an information extraction system for evaluating Table-to-Text generation, using a Pointer-Generator Network (PG-Net) trained on WikiBio to generate tables from text. The model uses a sequence-to-sequence architecture with bi-directional LSTMs, attention, and a copy mechanism (but no coverage mechanism), producing a linearized table output. Since references are divergent, the model hallucinates some false information, but it can still be used for evaluation. Extracted (attribute, value) pairs are compared against ground truth using exact string match, with precision, recall, and F-score reported in Table TABREF54.

This section describes the hyperparameters used for both the table-to-text PG-Net and the inverse information extraction PG-Net, including a biLSTM hidden state size of 200, input/output vocabularies of 50000 most common words plus special symbols for table attribute names, GloVe-initialized embeddings, an Adam optimizer, dropout applied to biLSTM outputs, and maximum decoded text and table lengths of 40 and 120 tokens respectively; it also reports that a beam size of 8 with no length penalty produced the highest F-score on the dev set for the information extraction system.
Table TABREF55 presents sample references and the corresponding predictions from the best performing model, PG-Net, for WikiBio.

This section describes the paper's figures and tables, which present the WikiBio dataset and WebNLG challenge data, the PARENT metric (and PRT), models including PG-Net (Pointer-Generator network), human evaluation scores computed using Thurstone's method, and correlations of metrics with human judgments assessed via bootstrap confidence tests and paired McNemar's test, along with an information extraction system using special symbols <R> and <C> to separate (attribute, value) pairs.

The paper assesses the extent to which BERT captures English syntactic phenomena using three types of stimuli: naturally-occurring subject-verb agreement stimuli, "coloreless green ideas" subject-verb agreement stimuli (in which content words in natural sentences are randomly replaced with words sharing the same part-of-speech and inflection), and manually crafted stimuli for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora phenomena, finding that the BERT model performs remarkably well on all cases.

This section introduces the paper's goal of assessing how well BERT captures syntax-sensitive structures, noting that prior work evaluated LSTMs on subject-verb agreement, reflexive anaphora, and negative polarity items using both naturally occurring Wikipedia sentences and controlled "colorless green ideas" stimuli. It highlights that BERT relies on attention mechanisms rather than the explicit word-order modeling of RNNs, and that prior findings on transformer versus LSTM performance are mixed, before stating that the author adapts the evaluation protocol and stimuli of prior work to BERT and finds that out-of-the-box pre-trained BERT (Large and Base) models perform very well on all syntactic tasks.

This section states that the author uses the stimuli provided by the cited works but changes the experimental protocol to adapt it to BERT's bidirectional nature, which requires discarding some stimuli, making the numbers not strictly comparable to those reported in previous work.

This section describes three prior setups (BIBREF1, BIBREF2, BIBREF3) that all use uni-directional, language-model-like LSTM models to assess syntactic abilities. BIBREF1 uses Wikipedia sentences containing a present-tense verb, feeding them word by word into an LSTM up to the focus verb and evaluating on "agreement attractor" sentences via a binary plural/singular prediction (supervised) or by comparing assigned probabilities to plural vs. singular verb forms (LM setup). BIBREF2 controls for semantic selectional-preference cues by replacing content words with random words of the same part-of-speech and inflection to produce "coloreless green ideas" nonce sentences, then scores correctness by comparing probabilities of correct versus incorrect verb inflections. BIBREF3 uses manually constructed minimal pairs of grammatical and ungrammatical sentences fed in their entirety into a pre-trained LSTM-LM, scoring correctness by whether the grammatical sentence receives higher probability, a method that also

The author adapts the uni-directional setup to the bi-directional BERT model by feeding the complete sentence while masking out the single focus verb and comparing the scores assigned to the correct versus incorrect verb at the masked position, using the PyTorch implementation with pre-trained bert-large-uncased and bert-base-uncased models. This differs from prior work by considering the entire sentence (excluding the verb) and conditioning the focus verb on bidirectional context, and the author discards NPI stimuli from BIBREF3 (minimal pairs differing in two words), agreement cases involving is or are from BIBREF1 and BIBREF2 (copular constructions), and stimuli where the focus verb or its inflection is out-of-vocabulary, resulting in 23,368 discarded pairs from BIBREF3, 680 sentences from BIBREF1, and 28 sentence-pairs (8 tokens) from BIBREF2.

Tables 1, 2 and 3 show the results, in which all cases exhibit high scores—substantially higher than reported in previous work—indicating that the purely attention-based BERT models are likely capable of capturing the same kind of syntactic regularities that LSTM-based models capture, at least as well and probably better. The results are not directly comparable to previous work because the BERT models are trained on different and larger data, can access the suffix of the sentence in addition to its prefix, and are evaluated on somewhat different data due to discarding OOV items, and a noticeable trend is that larger is not necessarily better, with the BERT-Base model outperforming the BERT-Large model on many of the syntactic conditions.

This Discussion section states that BERT models performed remarkably well on all syntactic test cases, surprising the authors who expected attention-based mechanisms to fail compared to LSTM-based models. The BIBREF2 and BIBREF3 conditions rule out reliance on selectional preference cues or memorizing Wikipedia training data, suggesting real syntactic generalization, and the authors identify exploring how deep purely-attention-based architectures like BERT capture hierarchy-sensitive and syntactic dependencies as a promising area for future research.

This section presents three tables reporting BERT's accuracy on syntactic stimuli from Linzen et al. (2016), the EN NONCE condition of Gulordava et al. (2018), and Marvin and Linzen (2018), noting that the numbers reported by Linzen et al. (2016) and Gulordava et al. (2018) for the 2, 3 and 4 attractor cases are substantially lower, that Gulordava et al. (2018) report an LSTM accuracy of 74.1±1.6 on All in the EN NONCE condition, and that the BERT and M&L numbers are not directly comparable because the experimental setup differs in many ways.

This paper proposes using dice loss, based on the Sorensen-Dice coefficient or Tversky index, as a replacement for the standard cross-entropy objective to address data imbalance in NLP tasks, and associates training examples with dynamically adjusted weights to deemphasize easy-negative examples, which theoretical analysis shows narrows the gap between F1 score in evaluation and dice loss in training. The authors report significant performance boosts on data-imbalanced NLP tasks, achieving SOTA results on CTB5, CTB6 and UD1.4 for part-of-speech tagging, SOTA results on CoNLL03, OntoNotes5.0, MSRA and OntoNotes4.0 for named entity recognition, along with competitive results on machine reading comprehension and paraphrase identification.

This introduction identifies data imbalance as a common problem in NLP tasks like tagging and machine reading comprehension, citing the CoNLL03 and OntoNotes5.0 datasets (where class $O$ tokens are 5 and 8 times more frequent than entity labels) and MRC tasks with negative-positive ratios of 50-200. It explains that imbalance causes (1) training-test discrepancy and (2) the overwhelming effect of easy-negative examples, both of which cross-entropy (CE) or maximum likelihood (MLE) objectives fail to address. The authors propose replacing CE/MLE with Sørensen–Dice coefficient (dice loss) or Tversky index losses to handle imbalance, plus a dynamic weight adjusting strategy based on $(1-p)$, inspired by focal loss, to deemphasize confident examples and mitigate easy-negative dominance. This section describes data resampling approaches for handling training example weighting, including importance sampling, boosting algorithms like AdaBoost, hard example mining, oversampling, focal loss's soft weighting scheme, self-paced learning, loss-based weight adjustment, and networks that learn to predict sample weights.

path: Data Imbalance Issue in Object Detection
context: This section describes the severe background-object label imbalance issue in object detection and the methods developed to address it, including hard negative mining (HNM), online hard example mining (OHEM) by shrivastava2016ohem which makes training progressively more difficult, SSD's approach by ssd2016liu that sorts negative samples by confidence loss with a 3:1 negative-positive ratio, IoU-balanced sampling by pang2019rcnn, and the average-precision loss ranking model by aploss2019chen, all of which inspired solving data imbalance in NLP.

This section introduces the notation used throughout the paper, illustrating with binary classification how different losses work (extendable to multi-class). It defines a set of instances $\lbrace x_i\rbrace$, each with a golden label vector $y_i = [y_{i0},y_{i1}]$ where $y_{i1}$ and $y_{i0}$ denote the positive and negative classes, and a probability vector $p_i = [p_{i0},p_{i1}]$ representing the model's assigned probabilities for the positive and negative labels.

This section describes the vanilla cross entropy (CE) loss and two strategies for handling data imbalance—weighting classes by a factor $\alpha_i$ (which the authors compute as $\lg (\frac{n-n_t}{n_t}+K)$, where $n_t$ is the number of samples of class $t$ and $n$ is the total number of training samples, with $K$ a tunable hyperparameter) and resampling the dataset—both of which change the data distribution and are equivalent in nature, but are not widely used because selecting $\alpha$ is tricky and can easily bias towards rare classes.

This section defines the Sørensen–Dice coefficient (DSC) as an F1-oriented similarity measure between predicted positives (set A) and golden positives (set B), expressed via true positives, false positives, and false negatives, and derives the corresponding DSC loss for each example $x_i$ with a smoothing $\gamma$ factor that lets negative examples contribute to training; it also notes milletari2016v's squared-denominator variant for faster convergence, the choice of summing individual DSC losses over set-level dice for easier optimization, and the Tversky index (TI)/Tversky loss (TL) as a generalization approximating $F_\beta$ that controls the false-negative/false-positive tradeoff via $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and reduces to DSC when $\alpha=\beta=0.5$.

This section proposes a self-adjusting Dice Loss that multiplies the soft probability $p_{i1}$ by a decaying factor $(1-p_{i1})$, yielding $(1-p_{i1})p_{i1}$, to reduce the influence of easy examples (whose probabilities approach 0 or 1) and prevent easy-negatives from dominating training, thereby improving F1 performance on hard-negatives; it explains this via the derivative of $\frac{(1-p)p}{1+(1-p)p}$ approaching 0 once examples are correctly classified, and notes the similarity to focal loss's $(1-p)^\beta$ down-weighting of well-classified examples.

The Experiments section states that the proposed method is evaluated on four NLP tasks—part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, machine reading comprehension, and paraphrase identification—with baseline models optimized using the standard cross-entropy training objective.

This section describes using BERT as the backbone for part-of-speech tagging experiments conducted on three Chinese POS datasets, evaluating with span-level micro-averaged precision, recall and F1, with hyperparameters tuned on each dataset's development set.

This section describes the datasets used for the POS tagging experiments: Chinese Treebank 5.0 (CTB5, containing 507,222 words, 824,983 characters and 18,782 sentences), Chinese Treebank 6.0 (CTB6, containing 781,351 words, 1,285,149 characters and 28,295 sentences), and UD 1.4 (Universal Dependencies version 1.4) for Chinese POS tagging.

This section lists the baseline methods used for the POS tagging experiments: Joint-POS (shao2017character), which jointly learns Chinese word segmentation and POS; Lattice-LSTM (lattice2018zhang), which constructs a word-character lattice; and Bert-Tagger (devlin2018bert), which treats part-of-speech tagging as a tagging task.

The section reports POS tagging results showing that the proposed DSC loss outperforms the best baseline (BERT-tagger) by +1.86 F1 on CTB5, +1.80 on CTB6, and +2.19 on UD1.4, achieving SOTA on all three datasets, whereas weighted cross entropy and focal loss yield only marginal gains on CTB5 and CTB6 and dice loss gains heavily on CTB5 but not CTB6, indicating these three losses are not consistently robust to data imbalance, while DSC loss performs robustly across all three datasets.

This section describes the Named Entity Recognition experiments, which use the BERT-MRC model (with BERT Large English checkpoints for English datasets and official Chinese checkpoints for Chinese datasets) as the backbone, and report span-level micro-averaged precision, recall and F1-score with hyperparameters tuned on each dataset's development set.

This section describes the four NER datasets used—Chinese OntoNotes4.0 and MSRA, and English CoNLL2003 and OntoNotes5.0—detailing their entity types, domains, and the train/dev/test splits employed, including the 9:1 random split of the MSRA training set for development since no official development set is provided.

This section lists the baseline models used for comparison: ELMo, Lattice-LSTM (used only in Chinese datasets), CVT, Bert-Tagger, Glyce-BERT, and BERT-MRC, which is described as the current SOTA model for both Chinese and English NER datasets.

The section states that on the CoNLL2003, OntoNotes5.0, MSRA, and OntoNotes4.0 NER datasets, the proposed Dice Loss method outperforms BERT-MRC by +0.29 and +0.96 in F1 on the English datasets, and achieves F1 improvements of +0.97 and +2.36 on the Chinese MSRA and OntoNotes4.0 datasets, setting new state-of-the-art performances on all four datasets.

This section describes the Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) experiments, focusing on SQuAD-style MRC tasks where the model predicts answer spans in a passage given a question and passage. The authors report Extract Match (EM) and F1 scores on the validation set, with all hyperparameters tuned on each dataset's development set.

This section describes the five datasets used for the Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) task: SQuAD v1.1, SQuAD v2.0, and Quoref. SQuAD v1.1 contains 100K crowdsourced question-answer pairs, SQuAD v2.0 extends SQuAD v1.1 by allowing questions with no answer in the passage, and Quoref contains 24K questions over 4.7K paragraphs from Wikipedia to test coreferential reasoning.

This section lists the baseline models used for the machine reading comprehension experiments: QANet (a convolution and self-attention-based model), BERT (which treats NER as a tagging task), and XLNet (a generalized autoregressive pretraining method enabling bidirectional context learning).

The section reports Machine Reading Comprehension results showing that the proposed DSC loss obtains significant performance boosts on both EM and F1 with either BERT or XLNet. Specifically, it outperforms XLNet by +1.25 in F1 and +0.84 in EM on SQuADv1.1, achieves 87.65 on EM and 89.51 on F1 for SQuAD v2.0, and surpasses XLNet by +1.46 on EM and +1.41 on F1 on QuoRef, with XLNet outperforming BERT by a huge margin and the DSC loss providing further improvement averaging above 1.0 in both EM and F1, indicating it is complementary to the model structures.
This section describes using BERT and XLNet as backbones for the paraphrase identification task, reporting F1 scores with hyperparameters tuned on each dataset's development set.

This section describes the two datasets used for the Paraphrase Identification task: MRPC, a corpus of sentence pairs from online news with imbalanced classes (68% positive, 32% negative), and QQP, a collection of question pairs from Quora with unbalanced class distribution (37% positive, 63% negative).

This section reports the Paraphrase Identification (PI) task results, showing that replacing the training objective with Dice Score Consistency (DSC) loss improves performance for both BERT and XLNet, increasing the F1 score by +0.58 on MRPC and +0.73 on QQP.

path: The Effect of Dice Loss on Accuracy-oriented Tasks
context: The authors fine-tune BERT$_\text{Large}$ on the SST-2 and SST-5 sentiment classification datasets using cross-entropy (CE), dice loss (DL), and DSC losses, reporting accuracy as the metric. They find that for SST-5 BERT with CE achieves 55.57 accuracy while DL and DSC slightly degrade performance to 54.63 and 55.19, and for SST-2 CE achieves 94.9 accuracy with slight drops for DL and DSC, concluding that dice loss works well for F1 but not for accuracy.

path: The Effect of Hyperparameters in Tversky index
context: This section describes an ablation study examining the effect of the hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the Tversky index (TI) on the tradeoff between false-negatives and false-positives, conducted on the Chinese OntoNotes4.0 NER dataset and English QuoRef MRC dataset. The results show that the highest F1 is 84.67 for Chinese OntoNotes4.0 when $\alpha$ is set to 0.6, and 68.44 for QuoRef when $\alpha$ is set to 0.4, with performance varying significantly as $\alpha$ changes across datasets, demonstrating that the hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ play an important role in the proposed method.

The paper proposes using dice loss, described as a soft version of the F1 score, in place of the standard cross-entropy loss to narrow the gap between training objectives and evaluation metrics. Empirically, they show this training objective leads to significant performance boosts for part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, machine reading comprehension, and paraphrase identification tasks.

This section presents eight tables and one figure summarizing the data imbalance ratios across NLP tasks (Table 1), loss function formulas (Table 2), an illustration of the derivative of f1 and f2 (Figure 1), and experimental results for POS tagging, NER, MRC, PI, and sentiment classification tasks (Tables 3–7), comparing WeightCE, focal loss, dice loss, and adjusted dice coefficient, along with the effect of α in the Tversky Index (Table 8).

The paper proposes augmenting BERT's next sentence prediction (NSP) task with a previous sentence prediction (PSP) task to form a 3-class categorization that distinguishes entailment from shallow correlation, and further expands the scope of NSP and PSP to include close but nonsuccessive sentences to incorporate document-level information, with noise mitigated by label-smoothing. This simple modification yields remarkable improvements over vanilla BERT on NLI and MRC benchmarks, including the challenging HANS dataset, demonstrating that the document-level task is promising for pre-training.

This section argues that BERT's next sentence prediction (NSP) task does not fully exploit document-level knowledge because its negative samples are randomly drawn from other documents, encouraging the model to rely on shallow semantic cues (e.g., topic) and to recognize sentence correlation rather than semantic entailment, and that BERT's order-sensitivity degrades performance on NLI tasks when sentence order is reversed. To address these issues, the authors propose introducing a symmetric previous sentence prediction (PSP) task with an IsPrev label that is the reverse of NSP's IsNext label, which forces the model to extract more detailed semantics, alleviates order sensitivity through symmetric regularization, and improves semantic reasoning across sentence-pair tasks, with NSP and PSP further extended to non-successive sentences using label smoothing, yielding considerable improvements on standard NLI and MRC benchmarks including the challenging HANS dataset.

This section reviews pair-wise semantic reasoning, noting that pre-training models like BERT, StructBERT, ERNIE, RoBERTa and XLNet achieve significant improvements on these tasks, with BERT's Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) objective showing a positive effect on NLI and MRC tasks despite its reported inefficiency at large sequence lengths. The work aims to enhance the NSP task and verify whether document-level information helps pre-training, evaluating regularization ability on the HANS dataset, where previous models like BERT fail with test accuracy that can barely exceed 0%.

This section discusses unsupervised sentence pre-training methods, including Skip-Thought (an encoder-decoder model predicting surrounding sentences), Quick-Thought (a faster variant using sampled softmax that is rotation invariant and does not distinguish previous from next sentences), and InferSent (which pre-trains using a large-scale NLI dataset in a supervised manner), noting that BERT is order-dependent and thus provides more supervision signal for semantic learning, before stating that the paper's work focuses on designing a more effective document-level objective extended from the NSP task.

This section states that the method retains BERT's input format and architecture but focuses on extending the NSP task with previous sentence prediction (PSP) and expanding the scope to include more surrounding sentences, motivated by NSP's two deficiencies: the semantically shallow discrimination between IsNext and DiffDoc labels, and BERT's order-sensitivity combined with NSP's uni-directionality. It reports that BERT achieves 97%-98% accuracy on NSP, that swapping sentence order degrades performance by about 0.5% on MNLI and 0.4% on QNLI, and that the proposed PSP extension is beneficial for downstream NLI and MRC tasks.

This section argues that Previous Sentence Prediction (PSP) is essential for BERT pre-training because BERT is order-sensitive, unlike Quick-Thought which uses a rotating symmetric function that makes the IsPrev label redundant; it further states that PSP enhances document-level supervision by forcing the model to extract detailed semantics to distinguish PSP from Next Sentence Prediction (NSP).

The section proposes expanding the discrimination task to incorporate document-level information by including in-adjacent sentences (the sentences next to the immediately adjacent sentences) in the sentence-pair classification task, labeled as IsPrevInadj and IsNextInadj. Because these in-adjacent sentences introduce more training noise, the model adopts label smoothing (e.g., transforming target probabilities from (1.0, 0.0) to (0.8, 0.2)) to reduce this noise, and the pre-training examples are constructed using five labels: IsNext, IsPrev, IsNextInadj, IsPrevInadj, and DiffDoc.

This section describes the experiment settings, including the BERTbase model (12 layers, 12 self-attention heads, hidden size 768), two-phase training (sentence lengths 128 and 512, 50K and 40K training steps), AdamW optimizer with learning rate 1e-4, β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, L2 weight decay 0.01, 10% learning rate warmup with linear decay, dropout 0.1, and pre-training on English Wikipedia (2500M words) and BookCorpus (800M words). It introduces three method settings—BERT-PN (3-class task with IsNext, IsPrev, DiffDoc), BERT-PN5cls (5-class task adding IsNextInadj and IsPrevInadj), and BERT-PNsmth (label-smoothed version with

This section states that BERT trained with NSP is order-sensitive, as reversing the input sentence order during fine-tuning decreased accuracy by 0.5% on MNLI and 0.4% on QNLI (verified via the validation set), confirming that NSP-only training makes BERT dependent on input order; it further reports that BERT-PN is order-invariant, with performance remaining stable when input order is reversed, demonstrating that the method remedies the order-sensitivity problem.

This section reports GLUE results across the NLI tasks (MNLI, QNLI, RTE), STS tasks (QQP, STS-B, MRPC), and text classification tasks (SST-2, CoLA), using fine-tuning for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 2e-5 and selecting the best validation checkpoint. It finds that the proposed method improves all NLI tasks (with a significant ~4% absolute gain on RTE over BERTBase), outperforms BERTBase on STS tasks, and even slightly improves single-sentence problems, with PN5cls outperforming PN and BERTBase-PNsmth achieving an averaged score of 81.0.

This section reports the HANS NLI evaluation results, comparing BERTBase and the proposed BERTBase-PNsmth on the Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems (HANS) dataset, which tests the lexical overlap, sub-sequence, and constituent heuristics; it finds that BERTBase-PNsmth clearly outperforms BERTBase, achieving a 160% relative improvement on lexical-overlap non-entailment examples and a 20% accuracy gain on entity-swapped samples, attributing the improvement to the NSP/PSP discrimination helping the model capture entity relationships.

This section evaluates the method on the SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0 MRC (question answering) datasets using the same fine-tuning procedure as BERT (3 epochs, learning rate 3e-5), with output vectors used to compute start and end token scores and selecting the maximum-scoring valid span as the prediction. It reports that including the PSP subtask (BERTBase-PN) yields a 2.4% absolute improvement over BERTBase on SQuAD v1.1, BERTBase-PNsmth adds another 0.3% EM increase, and the method achieves about 4% absolute improvement in both EM and F1 against BERTBase on SQuAD v2.0.

This section reports the Results of MRC Tasks on the RACE dataset, where the question, document, and option are concatenated as a single sequence separated by [SEP] tokens (truncated to 40/432/40), scored by a scalar and passed through a softmax layer, with fine-tuning for 5 epochs, batch size 32, and learning rate 5e-5. The proposed method significantly improves performance, with BERTBase-PN achieving a 2.6% accuracy improvement and BERTBase-PN5cls further adding a 0.4% absolute gain, demonstrating that additional sentence and discourse information benefits MRC tasks that rely on global semantic understanding and sophisticated reasoning.

This section reports results on five Chinese NLP tasks—XNLI, LCQMC, NLPCC-DBQA, CMRC-2018, and DRCD—using a model pre-trained on 10879M tokens of Chinese corpus (Hudong Baike, Zhihu, Sohu News, and Wikipedia). For the first three tasks, the proposed method achieves comparable or better results than ERNIE 2.0 despite ERNIE 2.0 using five objectives and more training data (14988M tokens), demonstrating that PSP alone achieves results on par with multiple objectives; for CMRC-2018 and DRCD, the method shows similar effectiveness for Chinese QA tasks, though results are incomparable with ERNIE 2.0 due to a smaller batch size of 12.

This section concludes that the authors enriched the NSP task with a Pairwise Sentence Prediction (PSP) objective that differentiates sentence orders by exploiting the in-symmetric property of NSP, enabling the BERTbase model to achieve improved pair-wise semantic reasoning, and they plan to combine this document-level objective with large-scale training in future work.

This section presents the figures and tables illustrating the proposed Symmetric Regularization method (with DiffDoc, IsNext, IsPrev labels and label smoothing for in-adjacent sentences), the accuracy of BERT and BERT-PN on the MNLI and QNLI validation sets, results on the GLUE benchmark, SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0, HANS evaluation (including its six sub-components and thirty detailed sub-components defined by Lexical overlap, Sub-sequence and Constituent heuristics), the RACE dataset, and Chinese NLP tasks (including CMRC-2018 and DRCD), reporting accuracy, F1 scores, Spearman correlations, and exact match (EM) metrics.

This abstract introduces a conversational forecasting model that learns an unsupervised representation of conversational dynamics to predict future derailment in an online fashion as conversations develop, addressing the challenge that real conversations have an unknown horizon and require risk assessment as they unfold rather than analyzing single comments in isolation. By applying this model to two new diverse datasets of online conversations with labels for antisocial events, the authors show that it outperforms state-of-the-art systems at forecasting derailment.

This section introduces a model for forecasting conversational events that processes comments and their relations in an online fashion, decoupling the learning of a neural representation of conversational dynamics (pre-trained on unsupervised data) from predicting future events (fine-tuned on small labeled data). It describes two datasets—the `Conversations Gone Awry' dataset (tripled in size) and a new ChangeMyView dataset—and reports that the model outperforms fixed-window approaches and simpler sequential baselines, triggering on average 3 comments (or 3 hours) before an overtly toxic comment is posted.

This section reviews related work on antisocial behavior online, post-hoc classification of conversations, conversational forecasting, and pre-training for NLP, contrasting each with the paper's goal of forecasting conversational events (such as derailment) before they occur while conversations are ongoing. It notes that prior forecasting work relies on hand-crafted features (e.g., similarity between utterances, sentiment imbalance, flow of ideas, increase in hostility, reply rate, and graph representations) extracted from fixed-length windows, and that multiple models trained for different window-lengths are treated as independent without aggregating them into a single forecast; it also describes pre-training objectives like next-word prediction, sentence autoencoding, machine translation, and BERT's sentence prediction, contrasting them with the paper's conversation-level, generative conversational modeling objective.

This section describes two datasets used for forecasting conversation derailment: an expanded version of the "Conversations Gone Awry" Wikipedia dataset (4,188 conversations with 4+ comments preceding a personal attack, released via ConvoKit, using topic-control pairing and civil-pre-attack filtering, split 80-20-20 with 1 million WikiConv conversations for unsupervised pre-training) and a secondary subreddit ChangeMyView (CMV) dataset (6,842 conversations labeled by moderator removal of comments violating Rule 2, using same-post pairing and same-user controls, with a pair-preserving 80-20-20 split and 600,000 clean conversations for pre-training).

This section describes CRAFT (Conversational Recurrent Architecture for ForecasTing), a forecasting model that combines a generative hierarchical recurrent encoder-decoder (HRED) dialog model—comprising an utterance encoder, context encoder, and attention-augmented decoder—that learns conversational dynamics unsupervised, with a supervised 3-layer MLP predictor (leaky ReLU activations, sigmoid output) that fine-tunes the encoder representations via backpropagation to forecast whether a to-be-forecasted event (e.g., conversation derailment) will occur, outputting a probability $p_{\text{event}}(c_{n+1})$; the model is implemented in PyTorch and released with the data as part of ConvoKit.

This section describes the evaluation of CRAFT for forecasting conversational derailment on the Wikipedia and CMV datasets, where comment-level predictions are aggregated to conversation-level outcomes (true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives) using a threshold learned on the development split. CRAFT is compared against fixed-window baselines (Awry and BoW), online forecasting baselines (Cumulative BoW and Sliding Awry), and CRAFT ablations (a no-pre-training variant that performs at random-guessing level, and CRAFT−CE, which zeroes the context encoder's memory to eliminate inter-comment dependency modeling), with results showing CRAFT outperforms all baselines in accuracy and F1 and achieves a superior precision-recall curve and larger area under the curve (AUPR), demonstrating the value of full conversational context and pre-training.

This Analysis section investigates CRAFT's early-warning capability and whether it learns an order-sensitive representation of conversational context. It finds that the model warns on average 3 comments (4 for CMV) before an attack, with over 50% of conversations getting at least 3 hours of advance warning (2 hours for CMV) and 39% getting at least 12 hours; a prefix-shuffling experiment shows the model changes its prediction in roughly one fifth of cases (12% for CMV), indicating it does not simply compute a bag-of-features, while a pre-training/fine-tuning/testing shuffle experiment that disables order-sensitive dynamics drops performance to 65% accuracy for Wikipedia and 59.5% for CMV, similar to disabling the context encoder entirely.

This Conclusions and Future Work section summarizes the paper's model for forecasting conversational derailment that processes comments as they happen while taking full conversational context into account to make updated predictions at each step, filling a void in conversational forecasting literature by addressing inter-comment dynamics and an unknown horizon; it reports state-of-the-art performance on forecasting derailment across two publicly released datasets, with the system providing substantial prior notice of derailment to enable preemptive interventions by human moderators (BIBREF65), and notes an AUPR of 0.7 indicating robustness across thresholds. The section outlines future work including adapting the CRAFT architecture to other forecasting tasks, running user studies with actual moderators to address questions about warning timing, the optimal balance between precision, recall, and false positive rate, and ethical implications, while acknowledging limitations such as reliance on balanced datasets despite derailment being a rare event, and the assignment of a single label to each conversation rather than finer-grained forecasting of conversational trajectories

This section presents the CRAFT architecture (Figure 2), a comparison of baseline and CRAFT models (full and without Context Encoder) regarding their capabilities for capturing inter-comment dynamics, online processing, and automatic feature learning, along with performance metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, false positive rate, and F1 score (Table 1), and describes precision-recall curves for Wikipedia data (Figure 3), the distribution of comments elapsed between the model's first warning and the attack (Figure 4), and the prefix-shuffling procedure (Figure 5).

The abstract states that existing GANs for text generation suffer from instability due to reinforcement learning algorithms like policy gradient, and proposes Adversarial Reward Augmented Maximum Likelihood (ARAML), a framework in which the discriminator assigns rewards to samples from a stationary distribution near the data rather than the generator's distribution, while the generator is optimized via maximum likelihood estimation augmented by the discriminator's rewards instead of policy gradient. Experiments show the model outperforms state-of-the-art text GANs with a more stable training process.

This introduction explains that natural text generation typically relies on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), which suffers from exposure bias, and that GANs with reinforcement learning (RL) training have been introduced but suffer from training instability due to high variance in reward signals from policy gradient updates. The authors propose Adversarial Reward Augmented Maximum Likelihood (ARAML), a framework that trains the discriminator to assign higher rewards to real data, then updates the generator via MLE on samples from a stationary distribution weighted by the discriminator's rewards, using RAML instead of policy gradient to obtain more stable training.

This Related Work section explains that text generation via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) tends to produce universal text and suffers from exposure bias, motivating reinforcement learning approaches like policy gradient, actor-critic, and Reward Augmented Maximum Likelihood (RAML). It reviews adversarial training methods for discrete text generation—including SeqGAN, MaliGAN, LeakGAN, MaskGAN, RankGAN, inverse reinforcement learning, and DPGAN—and contrasts the proposed ARAML with RAML (adding a discriminator to learn reward signals rather than using existing metrics) and MaliGAN (sampling from a fixed distribution near real data instead of the generator's distribution to stabilize training).

This section formulates text generation as training a generative model to fit the real data distribution, where words are drawn from a vocabulary, and describes ARAML's two-phase adversarial training framework: training a discriminator to assign higher rewards to real data than generated data, and training the generator via reward augmented MLE on samples from a stationary distribution, which constrains the search space with the MLE objective to alleviate unstable training.

This section describes the discriminator INLINEFORM0, which distinguishes real data from generated data like other GANs, and specifies its loss function based on Least-Square GAN, which forces the discriminator to assign higher rewards to real data than to generated data so it can learn to provide more proper rewards as training proceeds.

This section describes the generator's training framework, which uses an exponential payoff distribution to connect the RL loss with RAML loss, then applies importance sampling to derive a stable loss function that avoids policy gradient variance. It constructs a sampling distribution based on edit distance, decomposing sample generation into three steps—sampling an edit distance, selecting substitution positions, and filling new words via constrained sampling—and devises a reward function based on the discriminator's output and the stationary distribution to train the generator stably near real data.

This section states that ARAML's adversarial training framework can be extended to conditional text generation tasks like dialogue generation by modifying the generator's objective function given the data distribution where contexts and responses are denoted, with a component trained to distinguish whether a response is the true response to a given context.

This section compares ARAML with RAML and MaliGAN, noting that the main difference lies in the generators' training objectives (shown in Table TABREF26). Unlike RAML, which uses samples from a non-parametric distribution based on a specific reward, ARAML's reward comes from a learnable discriminator that varies during adversarial training, enabling adaptation to tasks without explicit reward metrics. Unlike MaliGAN, which samples from the generator's fixed distribution (often yielding low-reward samples and instability), ARAML samples from a stationary distribution around real data, resulting in more stable training.

This section describes the three datasets used to evaluate ARAML: the COCO image caption dataset, the EMNLP2017 WMT dataset, and the WeiboDial single-turn dialogue dataset. COCO and EMNLP2017 WMT serve as common benchmarks with no input for evaluating discrete GAN performance (preprocessed following existing works), while WeiboDial tests the model's performance with an input trigger, after removing post-response pairs containing low-frequency words and randomly selecting a subset for training/testing, with statistics presented in Table TABREF28.

This section lists the baselines used for comparison, which include MLE, Seq2Seq, SeqGAN, LeakGAN, MaliGAN, IRL, RAML, DialogGAN, and DPGAN, and specifies that MLE, SeqGAN, LeakGAN, MaliGAN, and IRL are used as baselines on COCO and EMNLP2017 WMT, while MLE, RAML, DialogGAN, and DPGAN are used on WeiboDial.

This section describes the implementation details of the ARAML model, including the use of a 128-cell LSTM generator and discriminator for COCO/EMNLP2017, an encoder-decoder structure with two-layer 128-cell GRU and attention mechanism for WeiboDial, and a language model for constrained sampling pre-trained on each dataset's training set. It also explains that baseline generators match ARAML's except LeakGAN (which uses a hierarchical LSTM), with discriminators implemented per original papers and hyper-parameters (batch size, learning rate, pre-training epochs) set based on original codes due to their sensitivity.

path: Language Generation on COCO and EMNLP2017 WMT
context: This section describes the evaluation of generated text quality on the COCO and EMNLP2017 WMT datasets using forward perplexity (PPL-F), reverse perplexity (PPL-R), and Self-BLEU (S-BLEU), along with standard deviation to reflect performance stability. It reports that LeakGAN performs best on forward perplexity due to generating more fluent samples, while ARAML outperforms all baselines on reverse perplexity and Self-BLEU, demonstrating better fitting of the data distribution, avoidance of mode collapse, and generation of more diverse sentences, and that ARAML nearly achieves the smallest standard deviation across all metrics, indicating superior stability compared to policy gradient.

This section describes a manual evaluation on WeiboDial where five annotators compared 200 sampled posts' responses (ARAML vs. baselines) on grammaticality and relevance, measuring inter-annotator agreement with Fleiss' kappa (showing moderate agreement) and testing significance with a sign test, finding that ARAML performs significantly better than all baselines in both metrics.

To verify training stability, the authors conducted multiple COCO experiments and selected the best 5 trials for SeqGAN, LeakGAN, IRL, MaliGAN and ARAML, presenting the forward/reverse perplexity during training in Figure FIGREF38. They found that ARAML has a smaller standard deviation and is more stable than the other GAN baselines in both metrics, while LeakGAN, despite reaching the best forward perplexity, has an extremely large standard deviation and performs badly in reverse perplexity, indicating it generates limited expressions that are grammatical yet divergent from the data distribution.

This ablation study investigates the impact of the temperature parameter (which controls the search space around real data) and two sampling strategies (random sampling and constrained sampling) on ARAML, evaluated on COCO. The results show that as temperature increases, forward perplexity gradually increases while Self-BLEU decreases (since larger temperatures encourage exploration of samples distant from the real data distribution, improving diversity but hurting fluency), with the model at temperature INLINEFORM0 reaching the best reverse perplexity; additionally, random sampling hurts model performance on automatic metrics except Self-BLEU-1 (because it exposes the generator to low-quality samples that degrade quality and diversity), though it does not affect training stability, as ARAML-R's standard deviation remains smaller than other GAN baselines.

This Case Study section presents qualitative examples generated by ARAML and baseline models (MLE, IRL) on the COCO and WeiboDial datasets, showing that baselines suffer from grammatical errors, repetitive expressions, incoherent statements, and failure to capture topic words (e.g., "late"), whereas ARAML produces grammatical and coherent outputs closely relevant to the input.

The authors propose ARAML, a novel adversarial training framework that incorporates RAML into the adversarial training paradigm to give the generator stable rewards and address the instability caused by policy gradient in current GANs for text generation. Experiments show that their model outperforms several state-of-the-art GAN baselines with lower training variance and achieves better performance on three text generation tasks.

This abstract states that the article describes the authors' experiences with computational text analysis to achieve three goals: shedding light on thorny issues not always prominent in discussions of these methods, providing best practices for working with thick social and cultural concepts based on their own (inherently imperfect) experiences, and promoting interdisciplinary collaborations. The paper draws on the authors' diverse disciplinary backgrounds and research practices to capture a range of ideas, identify commonalities, and argue that interdisciplinary insights and partnerships are essential for realizing the full potential of computational text analysis involving social and cultural concepts.

This introduction explains that computational text analysis offers exciting opportunities to address "thick" cultural and social questions at scale, but also carries significant challenges because texts are culturally and socially situated and many concepts (like hate speech) are highly contested. It outlines the paper's goal of guiding readers through a typical research process—identification of research questions, data selection, conceptualization, operationalization, analysis, and interpretation—while providing best practices and promoting interdisciplinary collaborations informed by the humanities and social sciences.

This section explains that research questions in computational text analysis are often theory-grounded and insight-driven, aiming to describe or explain phenomena (e.g., how and why hate speech is used, whether it comprises multiple forms, and its boundaries with other speech), and are shaped by data availability; it contrasts this with application-focused tasks measured by prediction accuracy, describes how domain experts provide feedback to revise questions, notes the possibility of connecting multiple disciplines, and addresses concerns about potential "dual use" of the research.
This section states that the next step involves deciding on the data sources, collecting and compiling the dataset, and inspecting its metadata.

This section describes data acquisition, contrasting analogue and born-digital sources (e.g., social media, web archives, Twitter, Facebook, campaign manifestos, traditional media) and noting that born-digital data enable unobtrusive measurements and large-scale studies but often require multiple collection methods combined with surveys, laboratory experiments, or field observations. It highlights ethical concerns around privacy and informed consent, access restrictions from providers like Facebook and Twitter via black box APIs, problems of provenance and contextualisation (e.g., the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine), data biases limiting generalization, the usefulness of non-representative data for within-sample comparisons (e.g., the Reddit hate speech example, skewed toward young white men), the appeal and pitfalls of large datasets (e.g., Google Books' over-representation of scientific articles versus the Gutenberg archive), fairness and representation of marginalized groups, the role of local experts and informants, and the need to report dataset choices and acknowledge limitations.

This section describes compiling data by defining a "core" set of documents and a "comparison" set, expanding the collection to increase sample size and notice consistent patterns, and using matching designs to support causal inference by estimating counterfactual scenarios, as illustrated by Chandrasekharan et al.'s study of Reddit forums closed as a treatment group versus similar non-banned forums as a control. It also notes the removal of potentially useless documents, such as meta-discourse, non-primary-language texts, and duplicates, while cautioning researchers to consider the consequences of such removal on the data and its interpretation.

This section explains that metadata—information about document creation (date, author, forum) or reception (flagged as hate speech, helpful review)—can be valuable for understanding documents and checking a collection's balance and representativeness, but it is prone to errors, inconsistencies, bias, and missing information, and using metadata as "ground truth" labels for machine learning requires caution because labels can mean different things than expected (e.g., a down vote could indicate offensive content or simply disagreement with the expressed view).

This section describes the conceptualization phase, in which social and cultural concepts (such as hate speech, rumor, or conversion) are defined into measurable quantities before operationalization, using Adcock and Collier's distinction between the "background concept" (the full, diverse set of meanings) and the "systematized concept" (the definition adopted for the study). It notes that social and cultural concepts have no absolute ground truth, that multiple valid definitions may exist and be contested over time, and that the machine learning reliance on ground truth or gold standard is uncommon in the humanities and social sciences, where concepts are often fundamentally unobservable and validation is challenging.

This section states that operationalization is the phase in which researchers develop measures (also called "operationalizations" or "indicators") for concepts of interest, translating systematized concepts into concrete outputs—Adcock and Collier's "scores"—as numbers or labels. It emphasizes that choices here must address the question "Are we measuring what we intend to measure?" by ensuring operationalizations match conceptual definitions and by recognizing gaps between what is important and what is easy to measure, before discussing modeling considerations and several frequently used computational approaches along with their strengths and limitations.

This section discusses modeling considerations for text as social and cultural data, emphasizing that variables (predictors and outcomes) are rarely simply binary or categorical and can be modeled in different ways, such as discretizing age into categories or keeping variables in their most precise form (e.g., using latitude and longitude coordinates from geotagged tweets rather than aggregating into administrative units like counties or cities, as done in a study on dialect differences). It notes that choosing a classification scheme determines which variations are visible or hidden, that schemes rarely are consistent, mutually exclusive, and complete, and that borderline cases—especially for social and cultural concepts—are challenging, with ethical implications (e.g., gender often modeled as binary, reinforcing gender-stereotypical patterns). Supervised learning (learning from labeled data to predict labels) suits clear conceptual definitions with available labels, while unsupervised learning (e.g., topic models) aids exploration, with conceptualization and operationalization occurring simultaneously, and is also used when concepts are measured via

This section explains that annotation schemes (codebooks) are developed through iterative updates, often using a mixed deductive-inductive strategy grounded in "content validity," and collected via crowdsourcing, highly-trained annotators, or experts depending on the concept's complexity. It measures inter-annotator agreement (intercoder reliability) using Krippendorff's alpha, with an acceptable threshold of 0.80 or above for manual content analysis, and notes that disagreement can reveal scheme weaknesses or inherent ambiguity and be integrated into subsequent analyses.

This section describes text pre-processing steps that significantly impact operationalizations, analyses, and reproducibility, including OCR error correction, tokenization (which can be confused by emoticons, creative orthography, missing whitespace, and multi-word terms), lowercasing, punctuation removal, stemming, lemmatization, and normalization, all aimed at improving the token-to-type ratio. It notes that these choices affect results—such as potentially hiding social meaning, that inflection handling matters more for Romance and indigenous languages, that stoplists remove function or infrequent words depending on research goals, that stemming offers little benefit for topic modeling, and that entity/part-of-speech marking tools struggle with linguistic variation and drop in performance outside their training domain.

This section explains that dictionaries consist of one or more categories (word lists) used to code texts in content analyses, with words either counted equally or assigned continuous scores, and that they offer high transparency but should only be used when their word scores match how words are actually used in the data. It notes that off-the-shelf dictionaries like LIWC are well-validated but may not transfer to new domains without validation, and that semi-automatically constructed dictionaries—using automation to generate initial word lists and human insight to filter them—can overcome these limitations, as illustrated by the SAGE-based study that identified hate speech words distinguishing closed treatment subreddits from control subreddits, which was then manually filtered against the European Court of Human Rights hate speech definition to show that hate speech on Reddit declined after the treatment subreddits were closed.

This section explains that supervised learning is used to scale up analyses, such as expanding a Movember motivations analysis to over 90k participants via a classifier trained on a small set of annotations. It notes that model choice depends on the task and label types (e.g., sequential or time series algorithms for stance toward rumors), that features range from content-based (words, word sequences, syntactic structure) to meta-information (user or network data), and that feature engineering requires experimentation and expert insight; it warns that supervised models can latch onto spurious features—illustrated by hate speech annotations derived from banned subreddits and by the name of an Australian TV show emerging as a strong feature for sexism on Twitter—and stresses that interpretability, through interpretable models or post-hoc explanations, is needed to support insight-driven analysis.

Topic models (e.g., LDA) are unsupervised methods suited for insight-driven exploration because their constrained output is interpretable, though raw word features are better for search and document classification and LSTMs and continuous word embeddings are better as language models. A topic model creates probability distributions over the vocabulary that, combined in different proportions, best match the collection's content, with each text segment having its own distribution over topics; the number of topics is treated as a scale or magnification determined by user needs rather than an inherent "right" number, and after fitting the model analysts may need to revisit preprocessing to address spurious patterns such as topics dominated by French stopwords or word fragments like "ing", "tion", and "inter".

This section states that measurement outputs ("scores") must be assessed for reliability (repeatability) and validity (measuring what is intended), noting that in NLP models are typically evaluated against a human "gold standard" while inter- and intra-coder reliability factors in chance agreement. It argues that accuracy, precision, recall, and F-score indicate reliability rather than validity when there is no objective ground truth, and describes alternative validation approaches including close reading (illustrated by Piper's identification of a new "conversional novel" form in 450 18th-century novels in three languages), stratified random-sample content validation, comparison with other approaches or external measures (e.g., public opinion polls, future events), uncertainty interval assessment via human judgments, and task-based evaluation using human experts.

This section describes the "Analysis" phase, where computational models are used to explore research questions by examining connections between topics and metadata elements, and where supervised learning "errors" or "failures" (such as a "dog that didn't bark") serve as "opportunities for interpretation" revealing interesting cases. It emphasizes that computational text analysis complements qualitative approaches, and by moving between large-scale computational and small-scale qualitative analyses, researchers can identify large-scale trends while telling individual stories, as illustrated by the Reddit hate speech study that raised follow-up questions about distinguishing hate speech from discussion of it.

This conclusion states that insight-driven computational analysis of text increasingly enables scholars to see more broadly, detect subtle patterns more clearly, and explore new questions about culture and society. It summarizes that analyzing text as social and cultural data is a labor-intensive, multi-step research process involving cross-disciplinary discussion and negotiation about operationalization and analysis approaches, and that with perseverance and mutual understanding this yields conceptually sound and meaningful work that makes use of the opportunities offered by rich textual data.

This abstract states that the authors train a recurrent neural network sentiment analysis model on English reviews and reuse it for Russian, Spanish, Turkish, and Dutch by translating reviews, addressing the challenge that sentiment analysis is highly language dependent and that collecting annotated data for different languages is challenging. They report that their single-model approach trained on English reviews statistically significantly outperforms the baselines in several different languages.

This section introduces a reusable, lexicon-free sentiment analysis framework that trains a recurrent neural network (RNN) on English reviews from multiple domains (movie and product reviews) to predict polarity, then specializes the model for a target domain using transfer learning from the larger English data. The authors evaluate reusability by translating non-English test sets into English and scoring them with the pre-trained model, demonstrating that this machine-translation-based approach eliminates the need for language-specific feature extraction, lexicons, and word embeddings, and that it statistically significantly outperforms baselines on multilingual sentiment analysis when data is limited.

This Related Work section reviews prior sentiment analysis research that relies on language-dependent features such as sentiment lexicons (e.g., SentiWordNet), polarity dictionaries, word vectors, and emotion tokens, and surveys machine translation-based multilingual approaches (Hiroshi et al., Balahur and Turchi, Boyd-Graber and Resnik, Mohammed et al., Tellez et al., Wan, Brooke et al.) that still require resource extraction in one or both languages, then states that the paper's approach uses off-the-shelf machine translation to translate corpora into a language with more available training data combined with a deep learning model that performs intrinsic feature learning without relying on any dictionaries other than English word embeddings.

This section describes a multilingual sentiment analysis approach where a single RNN-based model (using LSTM/GRU with two bidirectional layers of 40 neurons each and dropout of 0.2) is trained on English product reviews, first on a large generic dataset and then fine-tuned on domain-specific English reviews, before scoring reviews in other languages via machine translation to English. The model uses pre-trained global vectors (GloVe) with an embedding length of 100, takes text and pre-trained word embeddings as inputs, and predicts review polarity without utilizing any resources from the test set languages.

This section states that the authors conducted experiments to evaluate their proposed RNN-based framework for multilingual sentiment analysis, using SAS Deep Learning Toolkit for the experiments and Google translation API for machine translation, with the section first presenting the corpora used in the study followed by experimental results.

This section describes the corpora used in the study, consisting of two sets of publicly available data: English reviews and restaurant reviews from four languages (Spanish, Turkish, Dutch, Russian), all with two class values (positive, negative) for polarity detection. It details three training sets (Amazon reviews, Yelp restaurant reviews, and a Kaggle restaurant reviews dataset) used to build a generalizable model, and four SemEval-2016 Challenge Task 5 datasets for evaluating the multilingual approach.

This section reports experimental results comparing the RNN-based method against a majority baseline and a SentiWordNet-based lexicon approach across four multilingual datasets, using accuracy, false positive/false negative distributions, Tukey HSD tests (family-wise error rate=0.06), and Cohen's d effect sizes. It finds that the RNN outperforms both baselines in all four datasets, that the lexicon-based baseline falls below the majority baseline for Spanish restaurant reviews (indicating that mere translation and lexicons are insufficient), that false negatives exceed false positives due to the imbalanced training data (59,577 positive vs 17,132 negative reviews), and that the RNN's superiority is statistically significant with very large effect sizes relative to the baselines.

This Discussion section analyzes the impact of machine translation errors by computing the ratio of misclassifications containing non-English words, finding that 25.84% of Dutch, 21.76% of Turkish, 24.46% of Spanish, and 10.71% of Russian misclassified reviews contained non-English words, leading to the conclusion that machine translation errors have a non-noticeable effect and preserve most information necessary for sentiment analysis. The paper proposes a multilingual sentiment analysis framework using a recurrent neural network (RNN) trained on the largest available corpus, employing a general-to-specific strategy where a multi-domain corpus trains the model and a smaller single-domain corpus specializes it, with scoring performed by translating domain-specific corpora from different languages into English. Experimental results showed the approach outperformed both the majority baseline and the lexicon-based baseline, and future work will investigate the model on other review domains (such as hotel reviews) and problems like stance detection.

This section presents the figures and tables illustrating the multilingual sentiment analysis approach, including training and testing datasets (Tables 1 and 2), the RNN-based training process (Figure 2), accuracy results (%) comparing the RNN approach with majority and lexicon-based baselines (Table 3), percentages of false positives and false negatives (Table 4), visual comparisons between the three approaches (Figure 3), and multiple comparison of means (Table 5).

This paper analyzes gender representation in four major French broadcast corpora used for training ASR systems, finding that women are under-represented in terms of speakers and speech turns, with even fewer women in the Anchor category of prominent speakers. The gender imbalance causes ASR performance to decrease on women, though this can be counterbalanced for speakers who regularly appear in media when sufficient training data is available.

This introduction highlights that women are under-represented in media (e.g., representing only 40% of French media speakers, dropping to 29% during peak hours 6:00-8:00pm per the CSA report), and raises the concern that this gender imbalance in broadcast recordings—used as training data for ASR systems—may negatively impact ASR performance, given the male-oriented focus of AI and documented gender bias in NLP tools. The paper outlines its aim to analyze gender representation in four state-of-the-art French broadcast corpora and assess its impact on ASR systems.

context: This section argues that data quality and quantity are crucial for system performance, noting that despite data being called "the new oil," few corpora exist for ASR due to the cost of gathering and annotating audio data. It highlights that telephone conversations and broadcast recordings are primary sources of spontaneous speech, with only ~14% of the 130 English audio resources from LDC based on broadcast news and conversation, and identifies the four most widely used French broadcast corpora: ESTER1, ESTER2, ETAPE, and REPERE.

path: From gender representation in data to gender bias in AI
context: This section reviews prior research on gender bias in AI technologies (face recognition, NLP, machine translation) and ASR, noting that speech recognizers tend to perform better on female voices (BIBREF22, BIBREF23) while YouTube captioning shows gender bias (BIBREF24) but Bing Speech and YouTube captions show race/dialect bias favoring General American and white speakers (BIBREF8); it then outlines the paper's plan to statistically analyze gender representation across four French broadcast corpora using the notion of speaker's role to assess voice professionalism and to investigate the impact of this representation on an ASR system trained on these data.

This section outlines the methodology, beginning with a description of the French broadcast corpora used, followed by an explanation of how gender representation is analyzed and the notion of speaker's role is introduced, and concluding with the presentation of the ASR system and the metrics employed to evaluate gender bias in performance.

This section describes the two French broadcast speech corpora used to train and evaluate the ASR system, namely the ESTER1, ESTER2, ETAPE and REPERE datasets, which contain radio and TV broadcasts aired between 1998 and 2013. The training set contains 27,085 utterances from 2,506 speakers (approximately 100 hours), while the evaluation set contains 74,064 utterances from 1,268 speakers (70 hours) with a higher variety of prepared (P) and spontaneous (S) speech types.

path: Methodology for descriptive analysis of gender representation in training data
context: This section describes how gender representation in French broadcast training data is measured in terms of number of speakers, number of utterances, and turn lengths, and introduces the notion of speaker's role—defined by two criteria (number of speech turns and cumulative speaking duration, each compared against a 1% threshold of the show's totals)—to distinguish two salient roles: Anchor speakers (A), who exceed the 1% threshold on both criteria, and Punctual speakers (PS), who fall below it on both.

context: This section describes the ASR system used in the study, which is based on the KALDI toolkit with a hybrid HMM-DNN acoustic model trained on 100h of non-spontaneous broadcast speech from radio and TV shows, a 5-gram language model trained on 3,323M words from several French corpora using SRILM, and a pronunciation model built from the BDLEX lexical resource plus automatic grapheme-to-phoneme transcription with a vocabulary limited to 80K words, all following speaker adaptive training (SAT) using fMLLR-adapted features in per-speaker mode to reduce training-evaluation mismatch.

context: This section describes how Word Error Rate (WER) was computed for each speaker at the episode (show occurrence) level to investigate the impact of speaker gender and role on ASR performance, with gender obtained from metadata and role derived using criteria from Section SECREF6, and results analyzed across gender and role categories using Wilcoxon rank sum tests (Mann-Whitney U test, α=0.001) chosen due to the non-normality of the data.
